# Decolonisation of Knowledge Production and Knowledge Transmission in the Global South: Stalled, Stagnated or Full Steam Ahead?

##### By:

October 21, 2020  
  
**On the Question**

The question of whether decolonisation stalled in the Global South has been addressed in some form for as long as the concept of decolonisation has been present in our world. As many educational institutions across the world, and especially in the Global North, begin to include ‘decolonising’ in their knowledge transmission agendas, connecting this question with the past, present and future of all aspects of the colonial project has never been more important. This short essay argues firstly that the question itself relies on certain presumptions that should be revisited. Secondly, the essay argues that the answer itself is complex and depends on where our gaze primarily lies – state or people.

The question we are attempting to answer is predicated on the presumption that decolonisation has occurred and may now have stalled. Therefore, the answer to that question is itself dependent on whether we consider colonisation itself to be merely a physical and administrative project or also an epistemic one. Also, whether this epistemic nature of the colonial project was an incidental or rather an integral part of colonisation. [Mignolo](https://muse.jhu.edu/article/30745), in particular, argues that the colonial project was driven by supplanting one knowledge system over all others. Or as [Boaventura de Sousa Santos](https://books.google.co.uk/books?hl=en&lr=lang_en&id=7fpjDwAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PT5&dq=boaventura+de+sousa+santos+cognitive&ots=Ts5bYhf8An&sig=SfBuelRULbfYThmB7lrhj0szJ1w#v=onepage&q=boaventura%20de%20sousa%20santos%20cognitive&f=false) explains, the colonial project was reliant on massive epistemicides – the killing of ways of knowing and being, that lay on the other side of the abyssal line… in other words what we may call, for our purposes here, in the Global South. ‘Killing’ here is achieved by replacing different ways of knowing with one way of knowing, which is then considered superior and therefore universal. This framing of colonisation is especially pertinent when we ask if the processes of knowledge production and transmission have become trapped in what one may consider to be an overarching structure of stalled decolonisation. This is because, if one considers colonisation to merely be the overseas administration of colonies, then decolonisation occurs at independence with the replacement of the foreign administrators with local administrators. However, because it is widely accepted that colonisation included not just political administration but also relied upon economic and knowledge hegemonies and dependencies, I agree with [Nkrumah’s](https://www.marxists.org/subject/africa/nkrumah/neo-colonialism/) argument, colonisation did not end; it changed form but not ideology. Therefore, decolonisation in terms of knowledge structures can be said, at the very least, to have stalled. But then there are other non-statist structures that can be observed, especially in the sphere of knowledge production, where innovation continues to happen beyond the centre – in the creative, business and technology sectors, for example. Nevertheless, it is in the question of whether these innovations can successfully break away from the Global North-dependent capitalist centre that I think the answers lie as to what the state of play is in decolonisation of knowledge production in the Global South.

**A Short Aside on Decolonisation and Who Determines the Global South**

For the coloniser, decolonisation serves the purpose of keeping what has been gained without the extra expense of continually administering colonies. [El-Enany makes an argument for this in her book, [*Bordering Britain: Law, race and empire*](https://manchesteruniversitypress.co.uk/9781526145420/)*.*] Depending on which section of the colonised one considers however, the purposes of decolonisation range from ideas of freedom or justice, to an opportunity to occupy the privileged position of the departing colonisers. [Ekeh’s concept of two publics in Africa](https://www.jstor.org/stable/178372?casa_token=lvwJlZm2yiEAAAAA%3AAiEKMul-PoBSW-8u-13_D7DnqOlD_9fVpC1u1lBTcMHSPGSLKxfAvGK_va8QorWqIz-HtupASF8ACHmclwxvzPvUlfPZaS0OT1-fORo3EaKvIe1R9y0&seq=1#metadata_info_tab_contents) illustrates the public schism caused by colonialism into an outward-facing and an inward-facing public. One could thus argue that both colonisation and purported decolonisation, suggest ruptures and continuities of purpose and place that do not exist, or are brought about by the suggestion of rupture or continuity themselves.

Thus, while I accept that the Global South is a concept that we all use and collectively understand, there are power and positional complexities in the identifying the Global South as a homogenous entity. These serve to obscure the power implications in who gets to declare a region decolonised or designated as Global South. Such terminology often obscures regions within this designation which operate as sites of exploitative labour and consumption which are contingent on the Global North’s primitive accumulation. In other words, the Global North and South are co-constitutive of each other. Or as [Olaniyan](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0yKhmpTpG4) says, in explaining why African poverty is predicated on Euro-modern extraction and accumulation, *‘it is absolutely ridiculous to think that Congo is not modern, but Belgium is…’* alluding here to [Belgium’s colonial reign](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/40961621-king-leopold-s-ghost) of terror in what was called the Belgian Congo. Thus, these zones are closer than the geographical global North-South demarcation suggests. [Grosfoguel](http://jwsr.pitt.edu/ojs/jwsr/article/view/609) argues that they overlap, with both the designated North and South containing within them zones of being and zones of non-being. Thus, in this essay, my treatment of the Global South attempts to be alive to these complexities especially in how they affect knowledge production. Consequently, I use the phrase ‘designated Global South,’ to reflect the power to name – either the moment of decolonisation or a space as Global South.

**Stalled Decolonisation of Knowledge?**

Colonisation was operationalised by and as an epistemic project. Therefore, knowledge hierarchies and epistemicides formed a major mechanism by which colonisation was achieved – at home and abroad. Not a by-product. The consequence of the encounter between coloniser and the colonised was to establish thereafter the parameters for [global power and the gateway of acceptable language, knowledge, jurisprudence and thought](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2883552). The effects of this encounter are illustrated not only in knowledge systems that were destroyed at the time of encounter, but also in the structure and method by which knowledge is transferred in the ‘Global South’ after the colonial encounter. For example, [language in education](https://folukeafrica.com/language-in-african-education/), [education institutionalisation](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v40/n14/mahmood-mamdani/the-african-university) and [certification](https://bristoluniversitypress.co.uk/who-are-universities-for). The overall result is an overwhelming silence about indigenous knowledge systems as they continue to be replaced and subjugated by the knowledge systems introduced by the colonial project. It is these same colonial knowledge systems that subjugated knowledges in what is designated the Global South, that are being relied upon to reignite the fires of decolonisation.

Thus, the starting position of the anticolonial postcolonial wishing to decolonise knowledge and education and carry on the work of decolonisation is inherently limited. For example, on African continent, at independence, there were attempts to decolonise knowledge, as well as more generally improve standards in education. Inadequate personnel and research impeded continental efforts to reform curricula, while international efforts continue to be contextually uninformed, sporadic, and isolated.  Furthermore, the [Structural Adjustment Programmes](https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/140111/1/v23-i01-a06-BF02929964.pdf) introduced to Africa by international financial institutions in the 1980s and 1990s resulted in massive reductions to governmental spending on education.  Global North-South collaborations in these efforts, are often encumbered by comparatively higher costs of travel, [gatekeeping practices](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/africaatlse/2019/05/29/decolonizing-scholarly-data-and-publishing-infrastructures/), [harmful partnership practices](https://www.tandfonline.com/toc/cjac20/31/3?nav=tocList), difficulties in [obtaining visas](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/africaatlse/2019/07/10/visa-applications-emotional-tax-privileged-passports/) or visiting fellowships etc. This continuing epistemic violence is indicative of stalled, or even non-existent decolonisation.  Decolonisation of knowledge production and transmission is thus caught in a bind. The ‘Global South’ intellectual lacks the structural capacity to adequately represent silenced voices, while even the well-intentioned ‘Global North’ intellectual runs the risk of distorting knowledge while ‘speaking for’… Spivak explains this process in her essay ‘[Can the Subaltern Speak?](http://users.uoa.gr/~cdokou/TheoryCriticismTexts/Spivak-Subaltern.pdf)’.

The use of language in education in the Global South also illustrates the stagnation of the decolonial project, as schooling is often done in European languages. [Wa Thiong’o](https://books.google.co.uk/books/about/Decolonising_the_mind.html?id=z60udlv1F_cC) is famed for making the point that many African literature prizes only recognise works in a European language. Consequently, this means that in many areas designated ‘Global South’, education structures do not operate to assist knowledge production, as learners simultaneously struggle with language and text; doubling the mental effort required to learn. Furthermore, this use of language has contributed to the disappearance of indigenous languages. Inadvertently, the ability to speak a colonial language influences the measure of success attainable. In other words, social mobility is more likely for those who can speak an European language, than for those that speak their indigenous languages only. This explains why, across the African continent, but most especially in South Africa, there are increasingly vocal arguments for [decolonisation to include use of indigenous languages](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-030-15689-3.pdf) in education.

As [Paulo Freire](https://www.goodreads.com/en/book/show/72657) argues, ‘*Education either functions as an instrument that is used to facilitate the integration of the younger generation into the logic of the present system and bring about conformity to it, or it becomes “the practice of freedom”, the means by which men and women deal critically and creatively with reality and discover how to participate in the transformation of their world.’* I suggest that education in the designated Global South, as I have summarised above is NOT the practice of freedom, as it is quite closely linked to the logic of the colonial system of epistemicides and not transformation of the world.

**Decolonial Progress?**

Despite the above, it is vital to note that there are ways in which decolonisation has not entirely stalled… in the informal economy, in intra-continental and trans-Diasporic communication. The beauty of the informal economy is that it reflects everyday realities and is divorced from the statist structures and strictures of neo-liberalism. The informal economy involves practices, knowledge and values that are related to, and grow out of, local and community circumstances. Some of these are linked to knowledge systems that were nearly wiped out during the overt colonial encounter. Traditional practices relating to [orthography](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gIbIewxHQrk&list=WL&index=83&t=4s), [environmental conservation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hklt2xW2DCg&list=WL&index=185&t=0s), [health and beauty](https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/evewoman/beauty/article/2001260933/beauty-secrets-our-african-ancestors-used-for-flawless-skin), music and art, [finances](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SO7pX6ojJQ0&t=15s) and self-help still exist today. On the other hand, the dominant discourse is that indigenous practices are outmoded, archaic and out of tune with [modernity](http://qz.com/599483/dont-underestimate-the-power-of-africas-informal-sector-in-a-global-economy/). Yet, these practices, as they are engaged with today, are not trapped in time, but have evolved in tandem with society’s many iterations. Thus, while cross-continental and precolonial trade routes mostly no longer exist, Africans have found new ways to communicate and share knowledge about art, music, writing and science that often bypass the state structures imposed by colonisation. These forms of knowledge production and transmission may not be curated or valued by the ‘Global North’, but they exist. And knowledge is being exchanged and produced in new ways. For example, as [Siyanda Mohutsiwa](https://www.ted.com/talks/siyanda_mohutsiwa_how_young_africans_found_a_voice_on_twitter?language=en) states quite succinctly, social media has finally given Pan-Africanism a new voice.

**The Hope of a Decolonial Tomorrow?**

Going forward, we need to consider who should be at the forefront of restarting areas of stalled decolonisation, and what decolonisation should achieve in what is designated the Global South. In the ideas of stalled decolonisation, we see the conflation of seemingly similar but actually distinct ideologies and aspirations. There is some underlying presumption than **post**colonial states, peoples and populations will inevitably be **anti**colonial. As if the passage of time will of itself repudiate what has gone before. Contradictorily, postcolonial states often tend to be nearly as colonial as the colonies that preceded them, relying as they do on the same systems of production, international relationships, political structures and definitely the same knowledge systems of production – both in content and structure. Thus, if the ‘Global North’ and leaders in the ‘Global South’ are left to drive decolonisation, it will inevitably stall as imperialism inexorably reproduces itself. However, one hopes that if the people who are most affected – those at the grassroots, at the coalface, locked in crowded garment factories and below the earth in unsafe mines – drive decolonisation based on their aspirations, then it is possible that decolonisation will move from being post- to anti-colonial. One hopes.

My last reflection is: what would we consider to be successful and complete decolonisation? Development on par with the ‘Global North?’ Democratic states modelled to mimic those of the ‘Global North?’ Knowledge production and transmission, as the practice of freedom requires more than low-level and intermittent transnational engagement on counter-normative platforms. It requires engagement with the informal sector that moves beyond speaking for and distorting aspirations. It requires theoretical, radical and critical thought of what freedom actually looks like through the eyes of those who aspire to true freedom.

This is an opinion/analysis essay published on October 21, 2020, by Afronomicslaw, examining whether the decolonisation of knowledge production and transmission in the Global South has stalled, stagnated, or is progressing. The author argues that the question itself presumes decolonisation has already occurred, and that this presumption depends on whether colonisation is viewed as merely a physical/administrative project or also an epistemic one.

Key arguments include:
- Colonisation was fundamentally an epistemic project that relied on "epistemicides" (killing of ways of knowing), as argued by scholars like Mignolo and Boaventura de Sousa Santos.
- The author agrees with Nkrumah that "colonisation did not end; it changed form but not ideology," meaning decolonisation in knowledge structures has at minimum stalled.
- Structural barriers to decolonisation include: Structural Adjustment Programmes in the 1980s-90s that cut African education spending, gatekeeping practices in publishing, harmful Global North-South partnership practices, visa difficulties, and the continued use of European languages in education (as highlighted by Wa Thiong'o).
- The "Global South" is not a homogenous entity; the author uses the term "designated Global South" to reflect the power dynamics in naming, citing scholars like Grosfoguel and Olaniyan.
- Despite stagnation in formal structures, decolonisation has not entirely stalled: the informal economy, intra-continental and trans-Diasporic communication, social media (citing Siyanda Mohutsiwa on Pan-Africanism's new voice on Twitter), and traditional practices in orthography, environmental conservation, health, music, art, and finance continue to evolve outside statist structures.
- The essay concludes that if Global North leaders and Global South elites drive decolonisation, it will inevitably stall; instead, decolonisation must be driven by grassroots people (workers in garment factories, miners, etc.) to move from "post-colonial" to truly "anti-colonial."
- It poses a final question: what constitutes successful decolonisation—development on par with the Global North, or something more radical that requires "theoretical, radical and critical thought of what freedom actually looks like through the eyes of those who aspire to true freedom"?
- The essay draws on Paulo Freire's argument that education either integrates younger generations into the present system's logic or becomes "the practice of freedom."
- Spivak's "Can the Subaltern Speak?" is referenced regarding the risk of Global North intellectuals distorting knowledge while "speaking for" silenced voices.
args.key_excerpts: "Colonisation did not end; it changed form but not ideology." — Nkrumah (as cited by the author)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Process of undoing colonial influences on knowledge

This article is about the undoing of colonial influences on knowledge. For the legacy of colonialism within the domain of knowledge, see [Coloniality of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_knowledge "Coloniality of knowledge").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/-RMF_Statue_Removal_32_Desmond_Bowles.jpg/330px--RMF_Statue_Removal_32_Desmond_Bowles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:-RMF_Statue_Removal_32_Desmond_Bowles.jpg)

Removal of the statue of [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes") from the campus of the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town") on 9 April 2015. [Rhodes Must Fall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Must_Fall "Rhodes Must Fall") movement is said to have been motivated by a desire to decolonize knowledge and education in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa").[[1]](#cite_note-Chowdhury2019-1)

**Decolonization of knowledge** (also **epistemic decolonization** or **epistemological decolonization**) is a concept advanced in [decolonial scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoloniality "Decoloniality")[[note 1]](#cite_note-3)[[note 2]](#cite_note-5) that critiques the perceived [hegemony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemony "Hegemony") of [Western knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_knowledge "Western knowledge") systems.[[note 3]](#cite_note-7) It seeks to construct and legitimize other knowledge systems by exploring alternative [epistemologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology"), [ontologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontology "Ontology") and [methodologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology").[[4]](#cite_note-Dreyer1-6) It is also an intellectual project that aims to "disinfect" academic activities that are believed to have little connection with the objective pursuit of knowledge and truth. The presumption is that if curricula, theories, and knowledge are colonized, it means they have been partly influenced by political, economic, social and cultural considerations.[[5]](#cite_note-Broadbent_2017-8) The decolonial knowledge perspective covers a wide variety of subjects including [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") ([epistemology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology") in particular), [science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science "Science"), [history of science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_science "History of science"), and other fundamental categories in [social science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science").[[6]](#cite_note-Hira1-9)

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Main article: [Coloniality of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_knowledge "Coloniality of knowledge")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Destruction_of_Mexican_Codices.jpg/250px-Destruction_of_Mexican_Codices.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Destruction_of_Mexican_Codices.jpg)

In his 1585 *Descripción de Tlaxcala*, [Diego Muñoz Camargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Muñoz_Camargo "Diego Muñoz Camargo") illustrates the destruction of Mexican codices by [Franciscan friars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans").[[7]](#cite_note-10)

Decolonization of knowledge inquires into the historical mechanisms of knowledge production and their perceived [colonial and ethnocentric foundations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_knowledge "Coloniality of knowledge").[[8]](#cite_note-Heleta1-11) Budd L. Hall et al argue that knowledge and the standards that determine the validity of knowledge have been disproportionately informed by Western system of thought and ways of being in the world.[[9]](#cite_note-Hall_Tandon_2017_pp._6–19-12) According to Jaco S. Dreyer, the western knowledge system that emerged in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") during [renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") and [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") was deployed to legitimise Europe's colonial endeavour, which eventually became a part of colonial rule and forms of civilization that the colonizers carried with them.[[4]](#cite_note-Dreyer1-6) This perspective maintains that the knowledge produced by the Western system was deemed superior to that produced by other systems since it had a universal quality. [Decolonial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoloniality "Decoloniality") scholars concur that the western system of knowledge still continues to determine as to what should be considered as scientific knowledge and continues to "exclude, marginalise and dehumanise" those with different systems of knowledge, expertise and worldviews.[[4]](#cite_note-Dreyer1-6) [Anibal Quijano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anibal_Quijano "Anibal Quijano") stated:

> In effect, all of the experiences, histories, resources, and cultural products ended up in one global cultural order revolving around European or Western hegemony. Europe's hegemony over the new model of global power concentrated all forms of the control of subjectivity, culture, and especially knowledge and the production of knowledge under its hegemony... They repressed as much as possible the colonized forms of knowledge production, the models of the production of meaning, their symbolic universe, the model of expression and of objectification and subjectivity.[[10]](#cite_note-Ivanovic_2019_pp._82–102-13)

In her book *[Decolonizing Methodologies: Research and Indigenous Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonizing_Methodologies:_Research_and_Indigenous_Peoples "Decolonizing Methodologies: Research and Indigenous Peoples")*, [Linda Tuhiwai Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Tuhiwai_Smith "Linda Tuhiwai Smith") writes:

> Imperialism and colonialism brought complete disorder to colonized peoples, disconnecting them from their histories, their landscapes, their languages, their social relations and their own ways of thinking, feeling and interacting with the world.[[11]](#cite_note-Rohrer_2016_p._35-14)

According to this viewpoint, [colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism") has ended in the legal and political sense, but its legacy continues in many "colonial situations" where individuals and groups in historically colonized places are marginalized and exploited. Decolonial scholars refer to this continuing legacy of colonialism as "[coloniality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_knowledge "Coloniality of knowledge")", which describes the oppression and exploitation left behind by colonialism in a variety of interrelated domains, including the domain of subjectivity and knowledge.[[4]](#cite_note-Dreyer1-6)

## Origin and development

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin and development")]

In community groups and social movements in the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas"), decolonization of knowledge traces its roots back to resistance against colonialism from its very beginning in 1492.[[6]](#cite_note-Hira1-9) Its emergence as an academic concern is rather a recent phenomenon. According to [Enrique Dussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Dussel "Enrique Dussel"), the theme of epistemological decolonization has originated from a group of Latin American thinkers.[[12]](#cite_note-Dussel1-15) Although the notion of decolonization of knowledge has been an academic topic since the 1970s, [Walter Mignolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mignolo "Walter Mignolo") says it was the ingenious work of Peruvian sociologist [Anibal Quijano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anibal_Quijano "Anibal Quijano") that "explicitly linked [coloniality of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_power "Coloniality of power") in the political and economic spheres with the [coloniality of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_knowledge "Coloniality of knowledge")."[[13]](#cite_note-Andraos1-16) It has developed as "an elaboration of a problematic" that began as a result of several critical stances such as [postcolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcolonialism "Postcolonialism"), [subaltern studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subaltern_studies "Subaltern studies") and [postmodernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism"). Enrique Dussel says epistemological decolonization is structured around the notions of [coloniality of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloniality_of_power "Coloniality of power") and [transmodernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmodernism "Transmodernism"), which traces its roots in the thoughts of [José Carlos Mariátegui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Carlos_Mariátegui "José Carlos Mariátegui"), [Frantz Fanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frantz_Fanon "Frantz Fanon") and [Immanuel Wallerstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immanuel_Wallerstein "Immanuel Wallerstein").[[12]](#cite_note-Dussel1-15) According to [Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabelo_J._Ndlovu-Gatsheni "Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni"), although the political, economic, cultural and epistemological dimensions of decolonization were and are intricately connected to each other, attainment of [political sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westphalian_sovereignty "Westphalian sovereignty") was preferred as a "practical strategic logic of struggles against colonialism." As a result, political decolonization in the twentieth century failed to attain epistemological decolonization, as it did not widely inquire into the complex domain of knowledge.[[14]](#cite_note-Gatsheni1-17)

## Themes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

According to Alex Broadbent, decolonization is sometimes understood as a rejection of the notion of [objectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objectivity_(philosophy) "Objectivity (philosophy)"), which is seen as a legacy of colonial thought. He argues that universal conception of ideas such as "[truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth "Truth")" and "[fact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fact "Fact")" are Western constructs that are imposed on other foreign cultures. This tradition considers notions of truth and fact as "local", arguing that what is "discovered" or "expressed" in one place or time may not be applicable in another.[[5]](#cite_note-Broadbent_2017-8) The concerns of decolonization of knowledge are that the western knowledge system has become a norm for global knowledge and that its methodologies are the only ones deemed appropriate for use in knowledge production. This perceived hegemonic approach towards other knowledge systems is said to have reduced epistemic diversity and established the center of knowledge, eventually suppressing all other knowledge forms.[[15]](#cite_note-Naude_2017_pp._23–37-18) [Boaventura de Sousa Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boaventura_de_Sousa_Santos "Boaventura de Sousa Santos") says "throughout the world, not only are there very diverse forms of knowledge of matter, society, life and spirit, but also many and very diverse concepts of what counts as knowledge and criteria that may be used to validate it."[[16]](#cite_note-de_Sousa_Santos_2015_p._192-19) However, it is claimed that this variety of knowledge systems has not gained much recognition.[[17]](#cite_note-Sousa2-20) According to [Lewis Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Gordon "Lewis Gordon"), the formulation of knowledge in its singular form itself was unknown to times before the emergence of European [modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity"). Modes of knowledge production and notions of knowledge were so diversified that *knowledges*, in his opinion, would be more appropriate description.[[18]](#cite_note-Gordon1-21)

According to [Walter Mignolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mignolo "Walter Mignolo"), the modern foundation of knowledge is thus territorial and [imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism"). This foundation is based on "the socio-historical organization and classification of the world founded on a macro narrative and on a specific concept and principles of knowledge" which finds its roots in European modernity.[[19]](#cite_note-Mignolo1-22) He articulates epistemic decolonization as an expansive movement that identifies "geo-political locations of [theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theology "Theology"), [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularity "Secularity") [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") and scientific reason" while also affirming "the modes and principles of knowledge that have been denied by the rhetoric of [Christianization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianization "Christianization"), civilization, progress, development and [market democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_capitalism "Democratic capitalism")."[[14]](#cite_note-Gatsheni1-17) According to [Achille Mbembe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achille_Mbembe "Achille Mbembe"), decolonization of knowledge means contesting the hegemonic western epistemology that suppresses anything that is foreseen, conceived and formulated from outside of western epistemology.[[20]](#cite_note-Paddy1-23) It has two aspects: a critique of Western knowledge paradigms and the development of new epistemic models.[[15]](#cite_note-Naude_2017_pp._23–37-18) Savo Heleta states that decolonization of knowledge "implies the end of reliance on imposed knowledge, theories and interpretations, and theorizing based on one's own past and present experiences and interpretation of the world."[[8]](#cite_note-Heleta1-11)

## Significance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Significance")]

According to [Anibal Quijano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anibal_Quijano "Anibal Quijano"), epistemological decolonization is necessary for opening up new avenues for [intercultural communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercultural_communication "Intercultural communication") and the sharing of experiences and meanings, laying the groundwork for an alternative [rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality "Rationality") that could rightfully stake a claim to some degree of universality.[[21]](#cite_note-Quijano2-24) [Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabelo_J._Ndlovu-Gatsheni "Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni") says epistemological decolonization is essential for addressing the "asymmetrical global intellectual division of labor" in which Europe and [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America") not only act as teachers of the rest of the world but also serve as the centers for the production of theories and concepts that are ultimately "consumed" by the entire human race.[[22]](#cite_note-Gatsheni2-25)

## Approaches

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Approaches")]

According to [Linda Tuhiwai Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Tuhiwai_Smith "Linda Tuhiwai Smith"), decolonization "does not mean a total rejection of all theory or research or Western knowledge".[[23]](#cite_note-Kemp_Samuels_2019_pp._102–128-26) In [Lewis Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Gordon "Lewis Gordon")'s view, decolonization of knowledge mandates a detachment from the "commitments to notions of an epistemic enemy."[[24]](#cite_note-Fanon1-27) It rather emphasizes "the appropriation of any and all sources of knowledge" in order to achieve relative [epistemic autonomy and epistemic justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_justice "Cognitive justice") for "previously unacknowledged and/or suppressed knowledge traditions."[[25]](#cite_note-Olivier1-28)

### Indigenous decolonization

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Indigenous decolonization")]

This section is an excerpt from [Indigenous decolonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_decolonization "Indigenous decolonization").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Indigenous_decolonization&action=edit)]

[Indigenous decolonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_decolonization "Indigenous decolonization") describes ongoing theoretical and political processes whose goal is to contest and reframe narratives about indigenous community histories and the effects of [colonial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism") expansion, [cultural assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_assimilation "Cultural assimilation"), exploitative [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture") research, and often though not inherent, [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide").[[26]](#cite_note-Indigenous_decolonization_:4-29) [Indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples "Indigenous peoples") engaged in decolonization work adopt a critical stance towards [western-centric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocentrism "Eurocentrism") research practices and discourse and seek to reposition knowledge within Indigenous cultural practices.[[26]](#cite_note-Indigenous_decolonization_:4-29)

The [decolonial work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decoloniality "Decoloniality") that relies on structures of western political thought has been characterized as paradoxically furthering cultural [dispossession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dispossession,_oppression_and_depression "Dispossession, oppression and depression"). In this context, there has been a call for the use of independent intellectual, spiritual, social, and physical reclamation and rejuvenation even if these practices do not translate readily into political recognition.[[27]](#cite_note-30) Scholars may also characterize indigenous decolonization as an [intersectional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersectionality "Intersectionality") struggle that "cannot liberate all people without first addressing [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism") and [sexism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexism "Sexism")."[[26]](#cite_note-Indigenous_decolonization_:4-29)

Beyond the theoretical dimensions of indigenous-decolonization work, [direct action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action "Direct action") campaigns, healing journeys, and embodied social struggles for decolonization are frequently associated with ongoing native resistance struggles and disputes over [land rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_rights "Land rights"), ecological extraction, political [marginalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginalization "Marginalization"), and [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty"). While native resistance struggles have gone on for centuries, an upsurge of indigenous [activism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activism "Activism") took place in the 1960s - coinciding with [national liberation movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_liberation_movements "National liberation movements") in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Africa "Decolonisation of Africa"), [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Asia "Decolonisation of Asia"), and the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization_of_the_Americas "Decolonization of the Americas").[[28]](#cite_note-31)

#### Relational model of knowledge

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Relational model of knowledge")]

Decolonial scholars inquire into various forms of [indigenous knowledges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_knowledge "Traditional knowledge") in their efforts to decolonize knowledge and worldviews.[[29]](#cite_note-Botha_Griffiths_Prozesky_2021_p.-32) Louis Botha et al make the case for a "[relational model of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relational_model_of_knowledge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Relational model of knowledge (page does not exist)")," which they situate within indigenous knowledges. These indigenous knowledges are based on indigenous peoples' perceptions and modes of knowing. They consider indigenous knowledges to be essentially relational because these knowledge traditions place a high value on the relationships between the actors, objects, and settings involved in the development of knowledge.[[29]](#cite_note-Botha_Griffiths_Prozesky_2021_p.-32) Such "networked" relational approach to knowledge production fosters and encourages connections between the individuals, groups, resources, and other components of knowledge-producing communities. For Louis Botha et al, since it is built on an ontology that acknowledges the spiritual realm as real and essential to knowledge formation, this relationality is also fundamentally spiritual, and feeds axiological concepts about why and how knowledge should be created, preserved, and utilized.[[29]](#cite_note-Botha_Griffiths_Prozesky_2021_p.-32)

### In academia

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: In academia")]

Shose Kessi et al argue that the goal of academia is "not to reach new orders of homogeneity, but rather greater representation of pluralistic ideas and rigorous knowledge". They invite academics to carefully scrutinize the authors and voices that are presented as authorities on a subject or in the classroom, the methods and epistemologies that are taught or given preference, as well as the academic concerns that are seen as fundamental and the ones that are ignored. They must reconsider the pedagogical tools or approaches used in the learning process for students, as well as examine the indigenous or community knowledge systems that are followed, promoted, or allowed to redefine the learning agenda. The purpose and future of knowledge must also be reevaluated during this process.[[30]](#cite_note-Kessi_Marks_Ramugondo_pp._1–9-33) There have been suggestions for expanding the reading list and creating an inclusive curriculum that incorporates a range of voices and viewpoints in order to represent broader global and historical perspectives. Researchers are urged to investigate outside the Western canons of knowledge to determine whether there are any alternative canons that have been overlooked or disregarded as a result of colonialism.[[31]](#cite_note-THE_Campus_Learn,_Share,_Connect_2021-34)

[Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngũgĩ_wa_Thiong'o "Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o"), who emphasizes the significance of decolonizing history, memory, and language, has stated that language, not geopolitics, should serve as the initial point of decolonization.[[32]](#cite_note-Mamdani_pp._15–28-35) According to [Mahmood Mamdani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmood_Mamdani "Mahmood Mamdani"), the idea of a university based on a single language is a colonial heritage, as in the case of African universities, which began as a colonial project, with English or French being the project language, and it recognized only one intellectual tradition—the Western tradition.[[32]](#cite_note-Mamdani_pp._15–28-35) According to Mamdani, university education needs to be more diverse and multilingual, with a focus on not only providing Westernized education in a variety of languages but also on ways to advance non-Western intellectual traditions as living traditions that can support both scholarly and public discourse. Mamdani makes the case for allocating funds to the creation of academic units that may research and instruct in non-Western intellectual traditions. He believes that learning the language in which the tradition has been historically developed is necessary if one wants to access a different intellectual tradition.[[32]](#cite_note-Mamdani_pp._15–28-35)

### In various disciplines

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In various disciplines")]

In order to overcome the perceived constraints of the Western canons of knowledge, proponents of knowledge decolonization call for the decolonization of various academic disciplines, including [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History"),[[33]](#cite_note-Behm_Fryar_Hunter_Leake_2020_pp._169–191-36) [science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science "Science") and the [history of science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_science "History of science"),[[34]](#cite_note-Roy_2018-37)[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38) [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy"),[[36]](#cite_note-The_Express_Tribune_2022-39) (in particular, [epistemology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology")),[[37]](#cite_note-Mignolo_pp._19–43-40) [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology"),[[38]](#cite_note-Kessi_2016-41)[[39]](#cite_note-Bhatia_pp._257–266-42) [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology"),[[40]](#cite_note-Connell_pp._399–407-43) [religious studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_studies "Religious studies"),[[41]](#cite_note-Nye_2019_p.-44)[[42]](#cite_note-Tayob_2018_p.-45) [legal studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"),[[43]](#cite_note-Unsettling_Eurocentrism_in_the_Westernized_University_p.-46) and [ethnomusicology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnomusicology "Ethnomusicology").[[44]](#cite_note-Agawu,_Kofi_2003-47)

#### History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: History")]

According to the official web page of the [University of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Exeter "University of Exeter"), the "colonialist worldview," which allegedly prioritises some people's beliefs, rights, and dignity over those of others, has had an impact on the theoretical framework that underpins the modern academic field of history.[[45]](#cite_note-History_2022-48) This modern field of study has first developed in Europe during a period of rising [nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalism "Nationalism") and colonial exploitation, which determines the historical narratives of the world.[[45]](#cite_note-History_2022-48) This account suggests "that the very ways we are conditioned to look at and think about the past are often derived from imperialist and racialised schools of thought".[[45]](#cite_note-History_2022-48) Decolonial approach in history requires "an examination of the non-western world on its own terms, including before the arrival of European explorers and imperialists". In an effort to understand the world before the fifteenth century, it attempts to situate [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe") in relation to other historical "[great powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_power "Great power")" like the [Eastern Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") or the [Abbasid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate").[[45]](#cite_note-History_2022-48) It "requires rigorous critical study of [empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire "Empire"), [power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_(social_and_political) "Power (social and political)") and political contestation, alongside close reflection on constructed categories of social difference".[[33]](#cite_note-Behm_Fryar_Hunter_Leake_2020_pp._169–191-36) According to [Walter Mignolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mignolo "Walter Mignolo"), discovering the variety of local historical traditions are crucial for "restoring the dignity that the Western idea of universal history took away from millions of people".[[46]](#cite_note-McClure1-49)

#### Modern science

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Modern science")]

The decolonial approach contests the notion of science as "purely objective, solely empirical, immaculately rational, and thus, singularly truth confirming".[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38) According to this account, such an outlook towards science implies "that reality is discrete and stagnant; immune to its observer's [subjectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subjectivity "Subjectivity"), including their cultural suasions; and dismountable into its component parts whose functioning can then be ascertained through [verificationist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verificationism "Verificationism") means". Laila N Boisselle situates modern science within [Western philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_philosophy "Western philosophy") and Western paradigms of knowledge, saying that "different ways of knowing how the world works are fashioned from the [cosmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmology "Cosmology") of the observer, and provides opportunities for the development of many sciences".[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38) Margaret Blackie and Hanelie Adendorff argue "that the practice of science by scientists has been profoundly influenced by [Western modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity")".[[47]](#cite_note-The_Mail_&_Guardian_2020-50) According to this perspective, modern science thus "reflects foundational elements of [empiricism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empiricism "Empiricism") according to [Francis Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bacon "Francis Bacon"), [positivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivism "Positivism") as conceptualized by [Comte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Comte "Auguste Comte"), and neo-positivism as suggested by the [School of Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Circle "Vienna Circle") in the early 1900s." Boisselle also suggests that the mainstream scientific perspective that downplays the function or influence of Spirit or [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God") in any manifestation in its processes, is not only Western and modern but also [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism "Secularism") in orientation.[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38)

Boisselle sought to identify two issues with Western knowledge, including "Western Modern Science". For her, it starts off by seeking to explain the nature of the universe on the basis of [reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason "Reason") alone. The second is that it considers itself to be the custodian of all knowledge and to have the power "to authenticate and reject other knowledge."[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38) The idea that modern science is the only legitimate method of knowing has been referred to as "scientific fundamentalism" or "[scientism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientism "Scientism")". It assumes the role of a gatekeeper by situating "science for all" initiatives on a global scale inside the framework of scientism. As a result, it acquires the power to decide what scientific knowledge is deemed to be "epistemologically rigorous".[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38) According to [Boaventura de Sousa Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boaventura_de_Sousa_Santos "Boaventura de Sousa Santos"), in order to decolonize modern science, it is necessary to consider "the partiality of scientific knowledge", i.e. to acknowledge that, like any other system of knowledge, "science is a system of both knowledge and ignorance". For Santos, "scientific knowledge is partial because it does not know everything deemed important and it cannot possibly know everything deemed important".[[48]](#cite_note-Jandrić_Ford_2022_p._107-51) In this regard, Boisselle argues for a "relational science" based on a "relational ontology" that respects "the interconnectedness of physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual aspects of individuals with all living things and with the star world, and the universe".[[35]](#cite_note-Boisselle_p=215824401663525-38)

Samuel Bendeck Sotillos, with reference to [perennial philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perennial_philosophy "Perennial philosophy"), critiques modern science for its rejection of [metaphysics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysics "Metaphysics") and spiritual traditions from around the world. He states that "the belief that only the [scientific method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method "Scientific method") gives access to valid forms of knowledge is not only flawed but totalitarian, having its roots in the [European Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") or the so-called [Age of Reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment")". For him, "This dogmatic outlook is not science, but an ideology known as scientism, which has nothing to do with the proper exercise of the scientific method".[[49]](#cite_note-Sotillos_2021-52) This viewpoint challenges the idea that science is Truth, with a capital "T", saying that "contemporary science is largely relegated to dealing with [approximations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approximation "Approximation"); in doing so, it is always modifying its understanding and thus is in no position to declare what can be finally known with certainty", and it promotes an understanding of science within the confines of its underlying philosophical assumptions concerning [physical reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe "Universe"). In this context, Sotillos seeks to revive traditional metaphysics, also known as sacred science or [scientia sacra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientia_sacra "Scientia sacra"), which is guided by metaphysical principles and is based on the sapiential teachings of [world religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_religions "World religions").[[49]](#cite_note-Sotillos_2021-52)

#### History of science

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: History of science")]

Beginning in the middle of the 1980s, postcolonial histories of science is said to constitute a "decentered, diasporic, or 'global' rewriting of earlier nation-centred imperial grand narratives." These histories seek to uncover "counter-histories of science, the legacies of precolonial knowledge, or residues and resurrections of the constitutive relations of colonial science."[[50]](#cite_note-NEALE_KOWAL_2020_pp._403–412-53) Instead of "centering scientific institutes in colonial metropoles," this history attempts to examine what [Warwick Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick_Anderson "Warwick Anderson") refers to "as the unstable economy of science's shifting spatialities as knowledge is transacted, translated, and transformed across the globe". It seeks to eradicate "imperial grand narratives", which is said to provincialize science into a single "indigenous knowledge tradition".[[50]](#cite_note-NEALE_KOWAL_2020_pp._403–412-53) Instead, it seeks to recognise "the culturally diverse and global origins of science", and build a cosmopolitan model of science history in place of the narrow view of science as the creation of "lone geniuses".[[34]](#cite_note-Roy_2018-37) This perspective acknowledges the contributions of other civilizations to science, and offers a "contrageography of science that is not [Eurocentric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocentrism "Eurocentrism") and [linear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearity "Linearity")". The central tenet is that the history of science should be seen as a history of transmissions. In this, Prakash Kumar et al cite [Joseph Needham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Needham "Joseph Needham") as saying, "modern science...[is] like an ocean into which the rivers from all the world's civilizations have poured their waters".[[51]](#cite_note-Project_Muse_2018_p=24-54)

#### Philosophy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Philosophy")]

[Nelson Maldonado-Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Maldonado-Torres "Nelson Maldonado-Torres") et al see the decolonial turn in philosophy "as a form of liberating and decolonising [reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason "Reason") beyond the liberal and Enlightened emancipation of [rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality "Rationality"), and beyond the more radical Euro-critiques that have failed to consistently challenge the legacies of Eurocentrism and white male heteronormativity (often Euro-centric critiques of Eurocentrism)".[[52]](#cite_note-Toress18-55) According to [Sajjad H. Rizvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajjad_H._Rizvi "Sajjad H. Rizvi"), the shift toward global philosophy may herald a radical departure from colonial epistemology and pave the way for the decolonization of knowledge, particularly in the study of the humanities.[[36]](#cite_note-The_Express_Tribune_2022-39) In opposition to what is said to have been the standard method in philosophy studies, he argues against focusing solely on Western philosophers. Rizvi makes the case for the inclusion of [Islamic philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_philosophy "Islamic philosophy") in the discussion because he thinks it will aid in the process of decolonization and may eventually replace the Eurocentric education of philosophy with an expansive "pedagogy of living and being".[[36]](#cite_note-The_Express_Tribune_2022-39) Philip Higgs argues for the inclusion of [African philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_philosophy "African philosophy") in the context of decolonization.[[53]](#cite_note-56) Similar suggestions have been made for [Indian philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_philosophy "Indian philosophy")[[54]](#cite_note-Raina_2012_pp._187–201-57) and [Chinese philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_philosophy "Chinese philosophy").[[55]](#cite_note-Song_p.-58) Maldonado-Torres et al discuss issues in the philosophy of race and gender as well as [Asian philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_philosophy "Asian philosophy") and Latin American philosophy as instances of the decolonial turn and decolonizing philosophy, contending that "Asia and Latin America are not presented here as the continental others of Europe but as constructed categories and projects that themselves need to be decolonized".[[52]](#cite_note-Toress18-55)

#### Psychology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Psychology")]

According to many influential colonial and postcolonial leaders and thinkers, decolonization was "essentially a psychological project" involving a "recovery of [self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self "Self")" and "an attempt to reframe the damaging colonial discourses of selfhood".[[39]](#cite_note-Bhatia_pp._257–266-42) According to the decolonial perspective, Eurocentric psychology, which is based on a specific history and culture, places a strong emphasis on "experimental positivist methods, languages, symbols, and stories". A decolonizing approach in psychology thus seeks to show how colonialism, [Orientalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalism "Orientalism"), and Eurocentric presumptions are still deeply ingrained in modern psychological science as well as psychological theories of culture, identity, and human development.[[39]](#cite_note-Bhatia_pp._257–266-42) Decolonizing psychology entails comprehending and capturing the history of colonization as well as its perceived effects on families, nations, nationalism, institutions, and knowledge production. It seeks to extend the bounds of cultural horizons, which should serve as a gateway "to new confrontations and new knowledge". Decolonial turn in psychology entails upending the conventional research methodology by creating spaces for indigenous knowledge, oral histories, art, community knowledge, and lived experiences as legitimate forms of knowledge.[[39]](#cite_note-Bhatia_pp._257–266-42) Samuel Bendeck Sotillos seeks to break free from the alleged limits of modern psychology, which he claims is dominated by the precepts of modern science and which only addresses a very "restricted portion of human individuality". He instead wants to revive the traditional view of the human being as consisting of a spirit, a soul, and a body.[[49]](#cite_note-Sotillos_2021-52)

#### Sociology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Sociology")]

See also: [Sociology of absences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology_of_absences "Sociology of absences")

Decolonial scholars argue that sociological study is now dominated by the viewpoints of academics in the [Global North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South "Global North and Global South") and empirical studies that are concentrated on these countries. This leads to sociological theories that portray the Global North as "normal" or "modern," while anything outside of it is assumed to be either "deviant" or "yet to be modernized." Such theories are said to undermine the concerns of the [Global South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South "Global North and Global South") despite the fact that they make up around 84% of the world population.[[56]](#cite_note-Baur_p.-59) They place a strong emphasis on taking into account the problems, perspectives, and way of life of those in the Global South who are typically left out of sociological research and theory-building; thus, decolonization in this sense refers to making non-Western social realities more relevant to academic debate.[[56]](#cite_note-Baur_p.-59)

#### Religious studies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Decolonization_of_knowledge&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Religious studies")]

According to the decolonial perspective, the study of religion is one of many humanities disciplines that has its roots in European colonialism. Because of this, the issues it covers, the concepts it reinforces, and even the settings in which it is taught at academic institutions all exhibit colonial characteristics. According to Malory Nye, in order to decolonize the study of religion, one must be methodologically cognizant of the historical and intellectual legacies of colonialism in the field, as well as fundamental presuppositions about the subject matter, including the conception of religion and world religions.[[41]](#cite_note-Nye_2019_p.-44) For Adriaan van Klinken, a decolonial turn in the study of religions embraces reflexivity, is interactive, and challenges "the taken-for-granted Western frameworks of analysis and scholarly practice." It must accept "the pluriversality of ways of knowing and being" in the world.[[57]](#cite_note-van_Klinken_pp._148–155-60) The interpretation of the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") in the Euro-American academic community has been cited as one such example, where "the phenomenon of revelation (Wahy)" as it is understood in [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") is very often negated, disregarded, or regarded as unimportant to comprehending the scripture.[[58]](#cite_note-Lumbard_p=176-61)[[59]](#cite_note-Rizvi_2020_pp._122–138-62) According to [Joseph Lumbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_E._B._Lumbard "Joseph E. B. Lumbard"), Euro-American analytical modes have permeated [Quranic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quranic_studies "Quranic studies") and have a lasting impact on all facets of the discipline. He argues for more inclusive approaches that take into account different forms of analysis and make use of analytical tools from the classical Islamic tradition.[[58]](#cite_note-Lumbar

This is a Wikipedia article on "Decolonization of knowledge" (also called epistemic or epistemological decolonization), a concept in decolonial scholarship that critiques the hegemony of Western knowledge systems and seeks to construct and legitimize other knowledge systems through alternative epistemologies, ontologies, and methodologies.

**Background:** The concept inquires into historical mechanisms of knowledge production and their colonial and ethnocentric foundations. Scholars like Budd L. Hall, Jaco S. Dreyer, and Anibal Quijano argue that Western knowledge systems, which emerged during the Renaissance and Enlightenment, were deployed to legitimize European colonial endeavors and continue to "exclude, marginalise and dehumanise" those with different systems of knowledge. Linda Tuhiwai Smith's book "Decolonizing Methodologies" is a foundational text. Colonialism has ended legally and politically, but its legacy continues in "colonial situations" referred to as "coloniality."

**Origin and Development:** While rooted in resistance since 1492, its academic emergence is recent. It traces to Latin American thinkers, particularly Peruvian sociologist Anibal Quijano, who linked "coloniality of power" with "coloniality of knowledge." It developed from critical stances including postcolonialism, subaltern studies, and postmodernism, drawing on José Carlos Mariátegui, Frantz Fanon, and Immanuel Wallerstein. Political decolonization in the 20th century failed to achieve epistemological decolonization.

**Themes:** The concept involves a critique of objectivity as a colonial legacy, arguing that notions of truth and fact are "local" rather than universal. It holds that the Western knowledge system reduced epistemic diversity and suppressed other knowledge forms. Scholars like Lewis Gordon argue "knowledges" (plural) is more appropriate than "knowledge" (singular). Walter Mignolo describes the modern foundation of knowledge as territorial and imperial. Achille Mbembe says decolonization means contesting hegemonic Western epistemology.

**Significance:** Anibal Quijano argues epistemological decolonization is necessary for intercultural communication and alternative rationality. Ndlovu-Gatsheni says it addresses the "asymmetrical global intellectual division of labor" where Europe and North America produce theories consumed globally.

**Approaches:**
- **Indigenous decolonization:** Contests and reframes narratives about indigenous histories and colonial effects, adopts critical stance toward western-centric research, and seeks to reposition knowledge within Indigenous cultural practices. Some decolonial work relying on Western political thought has been criticized as paradoxically furthering dispossession.
- **Relational model of knowledge:** Louis Botha et al argue indigenous knowledges are relational, valuing relationships between actors, objects, and settings, and are fundamentally spiritual.
- **In academia:** Calls for greater representation of pluralistic ideas, inclusive curricula, expanded reading lists, and scrutiny of authority figures and epistemologies. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o emphasizes language as the starting point of decolonization; Mahmood Mamdani argues single-language universities are a colonial heritage and advocates for multilingual, diverse academic traditions.
- **Disciplines:** Proponents call for decolonization of history, science and history of science, philosophy (especially epistemology), psychology, sociology, religious studies, legal studies, and ethnomusicology.
  - **History:** The "colonialist worldview" has impacted the field; decolonial approach examines non-Western world on its own terms.
  - **Modern science:** Contests science as "purely objective, solely empirical, immaculately rational"; critics identify scientism as an ideology rooted in the Enlightenment. Boisselle argues for a "relational science" based on "relational ontology"; Samuel Bendeck Sotillos critiques modern science's rejection of metaphysics and promotes sacred science (scientia sacra).
  - **History of science:** Since the mid-1980s, postcolonial histories seek "decentered, diasporic, or 'global' rewriting" of nation-centred imperial grand narratives, acknowledging diverse global origins of science.
  - **Philosophy:** The decolonial turn liberates reason beyond Enlightenment rationality; scholars argue for inclusion of Islamic, African, Indian, Chinese, Asian, and Latin American philosophy.
  - **Psychology:** Decolonization is "essentially a psychological project" involving "recovery of self"; seeks to show colonialism and Eurocentric presumptions are ingrained in modern psychological science, creating space for indigenous knowledge and lived experiences.
  - **Sociology:** Decolonial scholars argue the Global North dominates sociological study, portraying the Global South as "deviant" or "yet to be modernized" despite constituting ~84% of world population.
  - **Religious studies:** The study of religion has colonial roots; decolonization requires methodological awareness of colonial legacies, reflexivity, and acceptance of "pluriversality of ways of knowing and being." Quranic studies in Euro-American academia is cited as an example where the Islamic concept of revelation (Wahy) is often negated or disregarded.
