***Orientalism*** is a 1978 book by [Edward Said](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Said "Edward Said"), in which he establishes the term "[Orientalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalism "Orientalism")" as a [critical concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_theory "Critical theory") to describe the [Western world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world")'s commonly contemptuous depiction and portrayal of the [Eastern world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") (or, the [Orient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient "Orient")). Societies and peoples of the Orient are those who inhabit regions throughout [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia") and [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"). Said argues that Orientalism, in the sense of Western scholarship about the Eastern world, is inextricably tied to the [imperialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism") societies that produced it, which makes much [Orientalist work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental_studies "Oriental studies") inherently political and servile to [power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_(social_and_political) "Power (social and political)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

According to Said, in the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East"), the social, economic, and cultural practices of the [ruling Arab elites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruling_class "Ruling class") indicate they are imperial [satraps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satrap "Satrap") who have [internalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internalization_(sociology) "Internalization (sociology)") a romanticized version of [Arab culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_culture "Arab culture") created by French and British (and later, American) Orientalists. Examples used in the book include critical analyses of the colonial literature of [Gustave Flaubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Flaubert "Gustave Flaubert").

Through the critical application of [post-structuralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-structuralism "Post-structuralism") in its scholarship, *Orientalism* influenced the development of [literary theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_theory "Literary theory"), [cultural criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_critic "Cultural critic"), and the field of [Middle Eastern studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Eastern_studies "Middle Eastern studies"), especially with regard to how academics practice their intellectual inquiries when examining, describing, and explaining the Middle East.[[2]](#cite_note-newhumanist-2) Moreover, the scope of Said's scholarship established *Orientalism* as a foundational text in the field of [post-colonial studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcolonialism "Postcolonialism") by denoting and examining the connotations of Orientalism, and the history of a given country's post-colonial period.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

As a [public intellectual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual "Intellectual"), Said debated historians and scholars of [area studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_studies "Area studies"), notably historian [Bernard Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lewis "Bernard Lewis"), who described the thesis of *Orientalism* as "[anti-Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Western_sentiment "Anti-Western sentiment")" in nature.[[4]](#cite_note-4) For subsequent editions of *Orientalism*, Said wrote an Afterword (1995)[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 329–52 and a Preface (2003)[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): xi–xxiii addressing discussions of the book as cultural criticism.

## Overview

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

### "Orientalism"

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: ")]

The term *[Orientalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalism "Orientalism")* denotes the exaggeration of difference, the presumption of Western superiority, and the application of [clichéd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliché "Cliché") analytical models for perceiving the "[Oriental world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental_world "Oriental world")." This intellectual tradition is the background for Said's presentation of Orientalism as a European *viewpoint* reflecting a contrived [Manichean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manichean "Manichean") duality.

As such, Orientalism is the pivotal source of the inaccurate cultural representations that form the foundations of [Western thought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_thought "Western thought") and perception of the Eastern world, specifically in relation to the Middle East region.

Said distinguishes between at least three separate but interrelated meanings of the term:[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 2–3

1. an academic tradition or field;
2. a worldview, representation, and "style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between 'the Orient' and (most of the time) 'the Occident';" and
3. as a powerful political instrument of domination.

In other words, Said had in mind the "Occidental" (or Western) views of eastern cultures that mirrored the prejudices and ideologies that the colonial experience of Western individuals was shaded by. Said's work drew attention to the obsession of Western writers with women and their role in the preservation (or destruction) of so-called cultural mores, viewing them as either "pristine" (redeemed) or "contaminated" (fallen).[[6]](#cite_note-6)

According to an article published by *[The New Criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Criterion "The New Criterion")*, the principal characteristic of Orientalism is a "subtle and persistent [Eurocentric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocentrism "Eurocentrism") prejudice against Arab-Islamic peoples and their culture,"[[7]](#cite_note-7) which derives from Western images of what is Oriental (i.e., cultural representations) that reduce the Orient to the fictional [essences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essentialism "Essentialism") of "Oriental peoples" and "the places of the Orient;" such representations dominate the [discourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discourse "Discourse") of Western peoples with and about non-Western peoples.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

These cultural representations usually depict the '[Orient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient "Orient")' as primitive, irrational, violent, despotic, fanatic, and essentially inferior to the westerner or native informant, and hence, 'enlightenment' can only occur when "traditional" and "reactionary" values are replaced by "contemporary" and "progressive" ideas that are either western or western-influenced.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

In practice, the imperial and colonial enterprises of the West are facilitated by [collaborating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborationism "Collaborationism") régimes of [Europeanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europeanisation "Europeanisation") Arab élites who have [internalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internalization_(sociology) "Internalization (sociology)") the fictional, and romanticized representations of [Arabic culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_culture "Arabic culture"). The idea of the "Orient" was conceptualized by French and English Orientalists during the 18th century, and was eventually adopted in the 20th century by American Orientalists.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) As such, Orientalist stereotypes of the cultures of the Eastern world have served, and continue to serve, as implicit justifications for the [colonial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism") ambitions and the [imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism") endeavors of the U.S. and the European powers. In that vein, about contemporary Orientalist stereotypes of Arabs and Muslims, Said states:

> So far as the United States seems to be concerned, it is only a slight overstatement to say that Moslems and Arabs are essentially seen as either [oil suppliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC "OPEC") or [potential terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_terrorism "Islamic terrorism"). Very little of the detail, the human density, the passion of Arab–Moslem life has entered the awareness of even those people whose [profession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalism "Orientalism") it is to report the Arab world. What we have, instead, is a series of crude, essentialized [caricatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caricatures "Caricatures") of the Islamic world, presented in such a way as to make that world vulnerable to military aggression.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Moving from the assertion that 'pure knowledge' is simply not possible (as all forms of knowledge are inevitably influenced by ideological standpoints), Said sought to explain the connection between ideology and literature. He argued that "Orientalism is not a mere political subject or field that is reflected passively by culture, scholarship, or institutions," but rather "a distribution of geopolitical awareness into aesthetic, scholarly, economic, sociological, historical, and philological texts."[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13) European literature for Said carried, actualised, and propelled Orientalist notions forward and constantly reinforced them. Put differently, literature produced by Europeans made possible the domination of the people of the 'East' because of the Orientalist discourse embedded within these texts. Literature here is understood as a kind of carrier and distributor of ideology.

He repeatedly underscored the importance of understanding the intimate relationship between knowledge and power, declaring: "If the knowledge of Orientalism has any meaning, it is in being a reminder of the seductive degradation of knowledge, of any knowledge, anywhere, at any time."[[14]](#cite_note-14)

### Thesis of representation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Thesis of representation")]

*Orientalism* (1978) proposes that much of the Western study of Islamic civilization was an exercise in political [intellectualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectualism "Intellectualism"); a psychological exercise in the self-affirmation of "[European identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essentialism "Essentialism")"; not an objective exercise of intellectual enquiry and the academic study of Eastern cultures. Therefore, Orientalism was a method of practical and cultural discrimination that was applied to non-European societies and peoples in order to establish European imperial [domination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominance_hierarchy "Dominance hierarchy"). In justification of empire, the Orientalist claims to know more—essential and definitive knowledge—about the Orient than do the Orientals.[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 2–3

One of the main themes of Said's critique is that the representations of the Orient as "different" from the West are based entirely on accounts taken from textual sources, many of them produced by Westerners. Modern on-the-ground reality is heavily discounted such that the Orient is implicitly disregarded as incapable or not credible to describe itself.[[15]](#cite_note-:1-15)

Western writings about the Orient—the perceptions of the East presented in Orientalism—cannot be taken at face value, because they are cultural representations based upon fictional, Western images of the Orient. The history of European colonial rule and political domination of Eastern civilizations distorts the intellectual [objectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrality_(philosophy) "Neutrality (philosophy)") of even the most knowledgeable, well-meaning, and culturally sympathetic Western Orientalist; thus did the term "Orientalism" become a pejorative word regarding non–Western peoples and cultures:[[16]](#cite_note-16)

> I doubt if it is controversial, for example, to say that an Englishman in India, or Egypt, in the later nineteenth century, took an interest in those countries, which was never far from their status, in his mind, as British colonies. To say this may seem quite different from saying that all academic knowledge about India and Egypt is somehow tinged and impressed with, violated by, the gross political fact—and yet *that is what I am saying* in this study of Orientalism.[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 11

The notion of cultural representations as a means for domination and control would remain a central feature of Said's [critical approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_theory "Critical theory") proposed in *Orientalism*. Towards the end of his life, Said argued that while representations are essential for the function of human life and societies—as essential as language itself—what must cease are representations that are authoritatively repressive, because they do not provide any real possibilities for those being represented to intervene in this process.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)

The alternative to an exclusionary representational system for Said would be one that is "participatory and collaborative, non-coercive, rather than imposed," yet he recognised the extreme difficulty involved in bringing about such an alternative due to advances in the "electronic transfer of images" which are increasing media concentration in the hands of powerful, transnational conglomerates.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13) This concentration is of such great magnitude that 'dependent societies' situated outside of the "central metropolitan zones" are reliant upon these systems of representation for information about themselves, known as self-knowledge.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13) For Said, this process of gaining self-knowledge by peripheral societies is insidious, because the system upon which they rely is presented as natural and real, such that it becomes practically unassailable.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)

### Geopolitics and cultural hierarchy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Geopolitics and cultural hierarchy")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Kaulbach%2C_Wilhelm_von_-_Die_Seeschlacht_bei_Salamis_-_1868.JPG/250px-Kaulbach%2C_Wilhelm_von_-_Die_Seeschlacht_bei_Salamis_-_1868.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kaulbach,_Wilhelm_von_-_Die_Seeschlacht_bei_Salamis_-_1868.JPG)

*The Sea Battle at Salamis* (1868) envisages the [Greco-Persian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars "Greco-Persian Wars") as an East–West clash of civilisations.

 [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Anonymous_Venetian_orientalist_painting%2C_The_Reception_of_the_Ambassadors_in_Damascus%27%2C_1511%2C_the_Louvre.jpg/250px-Anonymous_Venetian_orientalist_painting%2C_The_Reception_of_the_Ambassadors_in_Damascus%27%2C_1511%2C_the_Louvre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anonymous_Venetian_orientalist_painting,_The_Reception_of_the_Ambassadors_in_Damascus',_1511,_the_Louvre.jpg)

*The Reception of the Ambassadors in Damascus* (1511) depicts the "[Arabic culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_culture "Arabic culture")" of 16th-century Syria as part of a "romanticized" Orient.

Said said that the Western world sought to dominate the Eastern world for more than 2,000 years, since [Classical antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity") (8th c. BC – AD 6th c.), the time of the play *[The Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Persians "The Persians")* (472 BC), by [Aeschylus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeschylus "Aeschylus"), which celebrates a [Greek victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis "Battle of Salamis") (Battle of Salamis, 480 BC) against the Persians in the course of the [Persian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars "Greco-Persian Wars") (499–449 BC)—imperial conflict between the Greek West and the Persian East.[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 1–2[[17]](#cite_note-17) Europe's long military domination of Asia ([empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism") and [hegemony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemony "Hegemony")) made unreliable most Western texts about the Eastern world, because of the implicit [cultural bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_bias "Cultural bias") that permeates most Orientalism, which was not recognized by most Western scholars.

In the course of empire, after the physical-and-political conquest, there followed the intellectual conquest of a people, whereby Western scholars appropriated for themselves (as European intellectual property) the [interpretation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantics "Semantics") and [translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation "Translation") of Oriental languages, and the critical study of the cultures and histories of the Oriental world.[[18]](#cite_note-18) In that way, by using Orientalism as the intellectual norm for cultural judgement, Europeans wrote the history of Asia, and invented the "exotic East" and the "inscrutable Orient", which are cultural representations of peoples and things considered inferior to the peoples and things of the West.[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 38–41

The contemporary, historical impact of *Orientalism* was in explaining the *how?* and the *why?* of imperial impotence; in the 1970s, to journalists, academics, and Orientalists, the [Yom Kippur War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War "Yom Kippur War") (6–25 October 1973) and the [OPEC petroleum embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") (October 1973 – March 1974) were recent [modern history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_history "Modern history"). The Western world had been surprised, by the pro-active and decisive actions of non-Western peoples, whom the ideology of Orientalism had defined as [essentially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essentialism "Essentialism") weak societies and impotent countries. The [geopolitical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopolitics "Geopolitics") reality of their actions, of military and economic warfare, voided the fictional nature of [Orientalist representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_(arts) "Representation (arts)"), attitudes, and opinions about the non-Western [Other self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Other_(philosophy) "Other (philosophy)").[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 329–54

## Influence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Influence")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_-_Le_charmeur_de_serpents.jpg/250px-Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_-_Le_charmeur_de_serpents.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerome_Snake_Charmer.jpg)

The Eastern world depicted in *The Snake Charmer* (1880), by [Jean-Léon Gérôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Léon_Gérôme "Jean-Léon Gérôme"), illustrates the sensuous beauty and cultural mystery of the fiction that is "the exotic Orient".

The greatest intellectual impact of *Orientalism* (1978) was upon the fields of [literary theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_theory "Literary theory"), [cultural studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_studies "Cultural studies"), [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History"), and [human geography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_geography "Human geography"), by way of which originated the field of [Post-colonial studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcolonialism "Postcolonialism"). Edward Said's method of [post-structuralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poststructuralism "Poststructuralism") analysis derived from the analytic techniques of [Jacques Derrida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Derrida "Jacques Derrida") and [Michel Foucault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Foucault "Michel Foucault"); and the perspectives to Orientalism presented by [Abdul Latif Tibawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Latif_Tibawi "Abdul Latif Tibawi"),[[19]](#cite_note-19) [Anouar Abdel-Malek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anouar_Abdel-Malek "Anouar Abdel-Malek"),[[20]](#cite_note-20) [Maxime Rodinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Rodinson "Maxime Rodinson"),[[21]](#cite_note-21) and [Richard William Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._W._Southern "R. W. Southern").[[22]](#cite_note-22)

### Post-colonial culture studies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-colonial culture studies")]

As a work of [cultural criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_critic "Cultural critic"), *Orientalism* (1978) is a foundational document in the field of [postcolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-colonialism "Post-colonialism"), providing a framework and method of analysis to answer the *how?* and the *why?* of the [cultural representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_(arts) "Representation (arts)") of "Orientals," "[The Orient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Orient "The Orient")," and "[The Eastern world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world")," as presented in the [mass-media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_media "Mass media") of the [Western world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world").[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Postcolonial theory studies the [power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_(philosophy) "Power (philosophy)") and continued dominance of Western ways of [intellectual enquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research"), as well as the [production of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology") in the academic, intellectual, and cultural spheres of [decolonised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization "Decolonization") countries. Said's survey concentrated upon the British and the French varieties of Orientalism that supported the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") and the [French Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire "French colonial empire") as commercial enterprises constructed from colonialism, and gave perfunctory coverage, discussion, and analyses of German Orientalist scholarship.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Such disproportional investigation provoked criticism from opponents and embarrassment for supporters of Said, who, in "Orientalism Reconsidered" (1985), said that no single opponent provided a rationale, by which limited coverage of German Orientalism limits either the scholarly value or the practical application of *Orientalism* as a cultural study.[[25]](#cite_note-Edward_Said_1985,_p._96-25) In the Afterword to the 1995 edition of *Orientalism*, Said presented follow-up refutations of the criticisms that the Orientalist and historian [Bernard Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lewis "Bernard Lewis") made against the book's first edition (1978).[[5]](#cite_note-Orientalism-5): 329–54

### Literary criticism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Literary criticism")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Gayatri_Chakravorty_Spivak_at_Goldsmiths_College.jpg/250px-Gayatri_Chakravorty_Spivak_at_Goldsmiths_College.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gayatri_Chakravorty_Spivak_at_Goldsmiths_College.jpg)

The philosopher and theorist [Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayatri_Chakravorty_Spivak "Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak") wrote the essay "[Can the Subaltern Speak?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_the_Subaltern_Speak%3F "Can the Subaltern Speak?")" which also is a foundational post-colonialism document.

In the fields of [literary criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_criticism "Literary criticism") and of [cultural studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_studies "Cultural studies"), the notable Indian scholars of postcolonialism were [Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gayatri_Spivak "Gayatri Spivak") (*In Other Worlds: Essays in Cultural Politics*, 1987), whose essay "[Can the Subaltern Speak?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_the_Subaltern_Speak%3F "Can the Subaltern Speak?")" (1988) also became a foundational text of postcolonial culture studies;[[26]](#cite_note-26) [Homi K. Bhabha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homi_K._Bhabha "Homi K. Bhabha") (*Nation and Narration*, 1990);[[27]](#cite_note-27) [Ronald Inden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Inden "Ronald Inden") (*Imagining India*, 1990);[[28]](#cite_note-28) [Gyan Prakash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyan_Prakash "Gyan Prakash") ("Writing Post–Orientalist Histories of the Third World: Perspectives from Indian Historiography", 1990);[[29]](#cite_note-29) [Nicholas Dirks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Dirks "Nicholas Dirks") (*Castes of Mind*, 2001);[[30]](#cite_note-30) and [Hamid Dabashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamid_Dabashi "Hamid Dabashi") (*[Iran: A People Interrupted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran:_A_People_Interrupted "Iran: A People Interrupted")*, 2007).

In *White Mythologies: Writing History and the West* (1990), [Robert J. C. Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_J._C._Young "Robert J. C. Young") reports post-colonial explanations of the "How?" and the "Why?" of the nature of the post-colonial world, the peoples, and their discontents;[[31]](#cite_note-ryoung-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32) which verify the efficacy of the critical method applied in *Orientalism* (1978), especially in the field of [Middle Eastern studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Eastern_studies "Middle Eastern studies").[[2]](#cite_note-newhumanist-2)

In the late 1970s, the survey range of *Orientalism* (1978) did not include the genre of [Orientalist painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalist_painting "Orientalist painting") or any other visual arts, despite the book-cover featuring a detail-image of *[The Snake Charmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Snake_Charmer "The Snake Charmer")* (1880), a popular, 19th-century Orientalist painting—to which the writer [Linda Nochlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Nochlin "Linda Nochlin") applied Said's method of critical analysis "with uneven results."[[33]](#cite_note-33) In the field of [epistemological studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology"), *Orientalism* is an extended application of methods of critical analysis developed by the philosopher [Michel Foucault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Foucault "Michel Foucault").[[34]](#cite_note-34) Anthropologist [Talal Asad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talal_Asad "Talal Asad") said that the book *Orientalism* is:

> not only a catalogue of Western prejudices about and misrepresentations of Arabs and Muslims ... [but an investigation and analysis of the] authoritative structure of Orientalist discourse—the closed, self-evident, self-confirming character of that distinctive discourse, which is reproduced, again and again, through scholarly texts, travelogues, literary works of imagination, and the *obiter dicta* of public men-of-affairs.[[35]](#cite_note-Asad,_T_1980_p648-35)

Historian Gyan Prakash said that *Orientalism* describes how "the hallowed image of the Orientalist, as an austere figure, unconcerned with the world and immersed in the mystery of foreign scripts and languages, has acquired a dark hue as the murky business of [ruling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism") other [peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism"), now forms the essential and enabling background of his or her scholarship" about the Orient; without colonial imperialism, there would be no Orientalism.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

### Oriental Europe

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Oriental Europe")]

In [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe"), Milica Bakić-Hayden developed the concept of [Nesting Orientalisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesting_Orientalisms "Nesting Orientalisms") (1992), based upon and derived from the work of the historian Larry Wolff (*Inventing Eastern Europe: The Map of Civilization on the Mind of the Enlightenment*, 1994), and the ideas Said presents in *Orientalism* (1978).[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Bulgarian historian [Maria Todorova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Todorova "Maria Todorova") (*[Imagining the Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagining_the_Balkans "Imagining the Balkans")*, 1997) presented her [ethnologic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnology "Ethnology") concept of Nesting Balkanisms (*Ethnologia Balkanica*,1997), which is thematically extended and theoretically derived from Bakić-Hayden's Nesting Orientalisms.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Moreover, in "A Stereotype, Wrapped in a Cliché, Inside a Caricature: Russian Foreign Policy and Orientalism" (2010), James D. J. Brown says that Western stereotypes of Russia, Russianness, and things Russian are cultural representations derived from the literature of "[Russian studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_studies "Russian studies")," which is a field of enquiry little afflicted with the misconceptions of Russia-as-the-Other, but does display the characteristics of Orientalism—the exaggeration of difference, the presumption of Western cultural superiority, and the application of cliché in analytical models. That overcoming such intellectual malaise requires that area scholars choose to break their "mind-forg'd manacles" and deeply reflect upon the basic cultural assumptions of their area-studies scholarship.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

## Criticism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Criticism")]

Despite the book's wide-ranging influence, some have taken issue with the arguments and assumptions of *Orientalism*. Critics include [Albert Hourani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Hourani "Albert Hourani") (*[A History of the Arab Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_History_of_the_Arab_Peoples "A History of the Arab Peoples")*, 1991), [Robert Graham Irwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Graham_Irwin "Robert Graham Irwin") (*[For Lust of Knowing: The Orientalists and their Enemies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Lust_of_Knowing "For Lust of Knowing")*, 2006), [Nikki Keddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Keddie "Nikki Keddie") (*An Islamic Response to Imperialism, 1968)*, and [Bernard Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lewis "Bernard Lewis") ("The Question of Orientalism", *[Islam and the West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_and_the_West "Islam and the West")*, 1993).[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-42)

In a review of a book by [Ibn Warraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Warraq "Ibn Warraq"), American classicist [Bruce Thornton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Thornton_(classicist) "Bruce Thornton (classicist)") dismissed *Orientalism* as an "incoherent amalgam of dubious postmodern theory, sentimental [Third Worldism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-Worldism "Third-Worldism"), glaring historical errors, and Western guilt".[[43]](#cite_note-ThorntonGoldenThreads-43) Likewise, in the preface paragraphs of a book-review article "Enough Said" (2007), about *Dangerous Knowledge* (2007), which is the American title for British-published *[For Lust of Knowing: The Orientalists and Their Enemies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Lust_of_Knowing "For Lust of Knowing")* by [Robert Irwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Irwin_(writer) "Robert Irwin (writer)"), [Martin Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kramer "Martin Kramer") criticized what he said was the way Said turned the term "Orientalism" into a pejorative, saying "In a [semantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantics "Semantics") sleight of hand, Said appropriated the term "Orientalism", as a label for the ideological prejudice he described, thereby, neatly implicating the scholars who called themselves Orientalists."[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Nonetheless, the literary critic [Paul De Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_De_Man "Paul De Man") said that, as a literary critic, "Said took a step further than any other modern scholar of his time, something I dare not do. I remain in the safety of rhetorical analysis, where criticism is the second-best thing I do."[[45]](#cite_note-45)

### History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: History")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/OttomanEmpire1683.png/250px-OttomanEmpire1683.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OttomanEmpire1683.png)

[Ernest Gellner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Gellner "Ernest Gellner") argued that the political and military power of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") (pictured) as a threat to Europe undermined Said's argument that the West had dominated the East for 2,000 years.

[Ernest Gellner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Gellner "Ernest Gellner"), in his book review titled "The Mightier Pen? Edward Said and the Double Standards of Inside-out Colonialism: a review of *Culture and Imperialism*, by Edward Said" (1993), says that Said's contention of Western domination of the Eastern world for more than 2,000 years was unsupportable, because, until the late 17th century, the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") (1299–1923) was a realistic military, cultural, and religious threat to (Western) Europe.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

In "Disraeli as an Orientalist: The Polemical Errors of Edward Said" (2005), Mark Proudman noted incorrect 19th-century history in *Orientalism*, that the geographic extent of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") was not from Egypt to India in the 1880s, because the Ottoman Empire and the [Persian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qajar_Iran "Qajar Iran") in that time intervened between those poles of empire.[[47]](#cite_note-47) Moreover, at the zenith of the [imperial era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialism "Imperialism"), European colonial power in the Eastern world never was absolute, it was relative and much dependent upon [local collaborators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborationism "Collaborationism")—princes, rajahs, and warlords—who nonetheless often subverted the imperial and hegemonic aims of the colonialist power.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

In *[For Lust of Knowing: The Orientalists and Their Enemies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Lust_of_Knowing "For Lust of Knowing")* (2006), Robert Irwin says that Said's concentrating the scope of *Orientalism* to the Middle East, especially Palestine and Egypt, was a mistake, because the [Mandate of Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandatory_Palestine "Mandatory Palestine") (1920–1948) and [British Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Egypt_under_the_British "History of Egypt under the British") (1882–1956) were only under direct European control for a short time, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; thus they are poor examples for Said's theory of Western [cultural imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_imperialism "Cultural imperialism"). That *Orientalism* should have concentrated upon noteworthy examples of imperialism and [cultural hegemony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_hegemony "Cultural hegemony"), such as the [British colony of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") (1858–1947) and [Russian colonies in Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") (1721–1917), but he did not, because, as a [public intellectual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual "Intellectual"), Edward Said was more interested in making political points about the politics of the Middle East, in general, and of Palestine, in particular.[[49]](#cite_note-49) Moreover, that by unduly concentrating on British and French Orientalism, Said ignored the domination of 19th century Oriental studies by German and Hungarian academics and intellectuals, whose countries did not possess colonies in the East.[[50]](#cite_note-50) He frankly states that the "book seems to me to be a work of malignant charlatanry in which it is hard to distinguish honest mistakes from wilful misrepresentations."[[51]](#cite_note-51)

Irwin's book was later reviewed by [Amir Taheri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amir_Taheri "Amir Taheri"), writing in *[Asharq Al-Awsat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asharq_Al-Awsat "Asharq Al-Awsat")*. He listed certain factual and editing errors, and noted a number of prominent Orientalists were left unmentioned, but says that he believes it to be "the most complete account of Orientalism from the emergence of its modern version in the 19th century to the present day." He also describes it as "a highly enjoyable read both for the specialist and the broadly interested reader."[[52]](#cite_note-52)

American [scholar of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_studies "Religious studies") [Jason Ānanda Josephson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Ānanda_Josephson "Jason Ānanda Josephson") has argued that data from [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") complicates Said's thesis about Orientalism as a field linked to imperial power. Not only did Europeans study Japan without any hope of colonizing it, but Japanese academics played a prominent role as informants and interlocutors in this academic discipline, providing information both on their own practices and history and on the history of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China").[[53]](#cite_note-53) Moreover, Josephson has documented that European conferences on [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") predate European conferences on the Middle East described by Said, necessitating an alternative chronology of Western academic interest in the Orient.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

French orientalist [Maxime Rodinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Rodinson "Maxime Rodinson") was surprised by the popularity of the book in the United States, calling it a "polemic" and a "bit Stalinist".[[55]](#cite_note-55)

### Professional

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Orientalism_(book)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Professional")]

In the article "Said's Splash" (2001), [Martin Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kramer "Martin Kramer") says that, fifteen years after the publication of *Orientalism* (1978), UCLA historian [Nikki Keddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Keddie "Nikki Keddie") (whom Said praised in *[Covering Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covering_Islam "Covering Islam")*, 1981) who originally had praised *Orientalism* as an "important, and, in many ways, positive" book, had changed her mind. In *Approaches to the History of the Middle East* (1994), Keddie criticises Said's work on Orientalism, for the unfortunate consequences upon her profession as an historian:

> I think that there has been a tendency in the Middle East field to adopt the word "orientalism" as a generalized swear-word, essentially referring to people who take the "wrong" position on the [Arab–Israeli dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab–Israeli_conflict "Arab–Israeli conflict"), or to people who are judged too "conservative". It has nothing to do with whether they are good or not good in their disciplines. So, "orientalism", for many people, is a word that [substitutes for thought](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought-terminating_cliché "Thought-terminating cliché") and enables people to dismiss certain scholars and their works. I think that is too bad. It may not have been what Edward Said meant at all, but the term has become a kind of slogan.[[56]](#cite_note-56)

This webpage is a Wikipedia article about "Orientalism" (1978), the influential book by Edward W. Said, published by Pantheon Books (368 pages, ISBN 978-0-394-42814-7). The book established "Orientalism" as a critical concept describing the Western world's contemptuous depiction of the Eastern world (Asia and North Africa). Said argues that Western scholarship about the East is inextricably tied to imperialism, making Orientalist work inherently political and servile to power.

**Key Thesis:** Said distinguishes three interrelated meanings of Orientalism: (1) an academic tradition/field; (2) a worldview and "style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between 'the Orient' and 'the Occident'"; and (3) a powerful political instrument of domination. The book argues that Western cultural representations depict the Orient as primitive, irrational, violent, despotic, and inferior, serving as implicit justifications for colonial and imperial ambitions. Said contends that European literature carried and reinforced Orientalist notions, making possible the domination of Eastern peoples. He emphasizes the intimate relationship between knowledge and power, noting that "pure knowledge" is impossible as all knowledge is influenced by ideological standpoints.

**Geopolitics:** Said traces Western domination of the East for over 2,000 years since Classical antiquity, citing examples like Aeschylus's play The Persians (472 BC). The book's contemporary impact was in explaining imperial impotence in the wake of the 1973 Yom Kippur War and OPEC petroleum embargo.

**Influence:** Orientalism became a foundational text in post-colonial studies, influencing literary theory, cultural criticism, and Middle Eastern studies. Its method drew from post-structuralist analysis (Derrida and Foucault) and prior scholars including Abdul Latif Tibawi, Anouar Abdel-Malek, Maxime Rodinson, and R.W. Southern. Notable scholars influenced include Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak ("Can the Subaltern Speak?"), Homi K. Bhabha, Ronald Inden, Gyan Prakash, and Nicholas Dirks. Related concepts include Milica Bakić-Hayden's "Nesting Orientalisms" (1992) and Maria Todorova's "Nesting Balkanisms" (1997).

**Criticism:** Major critics include Albert Hourani, Robert Irwin (For Lust of Knowing, 2006), Nikki Keddie, and Bernard Lewis (who called the thesis "anti-Western"). Ernest Gellner argued Said's claim of 2,000 years of Western domination was unsupportable given Ottoman power until the late 17th century. Robert Irwin called the book "a work of malignant charlatanry." Martin Kramer criticized Said for turning "Orientalism" into a pejorative. Jason Ānanda Josephson argued Japanese data complicates Said's thesis. Critics also noted Said's disproportionate focus on British/French Orientalism while ignoring German/Hungarian scholarship. Nikki Keddie lamented that "orientalism" became a "generalized swear-word" in the Middle East field. Bruce Thornton dismissed the book as an "incoherent amalgam of dubious postmodern theory, sentimental Third Worldism, glaring historical errors, and Western guilt." Said responded to critics in an Afterword (1995) and Preface (2003) to later editions.

This is a YouTube video summary/explainer of Edward Said's seminal 1978 work "Orientalism," presented by Andrew Chapman, a philosophy professor, for the "Autodidact's Toolkit" channel (published 4 September 2024). The video provides an accessible breakdown of Said's groundbreaking postcolonial theory text.

Key concepts covered include:
- Said, a Palestinian-American scholar, critiques the Western academic study of Eastern societies, arguing that scholarship and artistic representations have perpetuated stereotypes and justified imperial domination.
- Orientalism is conceptualized as a "discourse" (drawing on Michel Foucault's theories)—a system of knowledge and power that constructs the Orient as fundamentally different, inferior, exotic, timeless, backward, and unchanging, contrasted with a supposedly dynamic and progressive West.
- Said argues that knowledge production about the Orient is intertwined with power relations, serving Western imperialist agendas—even well-intentioned scholarship can perpetuate stereotypes.
- Orientalist representations in literature, art, and academia create a "cultural hegemony" that shapes perceptions and justifies political and economic control.
- Said critiques Western scholars and writers (e.g., Bernard Lewis, Rudyard Kipling) for perpetuating orientalist tropes with real-world consequences for policy and attitudes.

The video situates the work within postcolonial and critical theory, noting Said's engagement with Foucault, Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, and other anti-colonial thinkers. It highlights the work's profound impact on literary studies, history, anthropology, political science, and its role in founding postcolonial studies. Practical implications include analyzing contemporary media, policy, international relations, cultural identity, and even AI ethics.

Major criticisms discussed include: (1) the analysis being overly deterministic and broad, implying all Western representations of the East are imperialist; (2) neglect of material and economic dimensions of colonialism due to focus on discourse; and (3) the framework's narrow focus on 19th- and 20th-century contexts, limiting applicability to non-Western contexts and other periods. Despite these critiques, the work remains a foundational framework for understanding cultural legacies of imperialism and power dynamics in representation.

[![David Kutz](https://davidkutz.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/WebLogo-190x29.png)](https://davidkutz.com/)

# Edward Said; Orientalism

[Anthropology](https://davidkutz.com/category/anthropology/), [Philosophy](https://davidkutz.com/category/philosophy/), [VCFA Visual Culture Papers](https://davidkutz.com/category/vcfa-visual-culture-papers/), [Writing](https://davidkutz.com/category/writing/)

This is my second paper written for the low-residency MFA program at the Vermont College of Fine Arts.

> Visual Studies Project  
>  An Annotation of:  
>  Said, Edward W. Orientalism. New York: Vintage Books, 1979. Print.  
>  By David Kutz  
>  Submitted to VCFA Faculty Adviser Humberto Ramirez on Tuesday October, 14, 2014

The “East” as differentiated from the “West”, which includes the Middle East, Near East, Central Asia, South Asia and the Far East, is today top of mind with news breaking in a stream of anxiety, fear, economic and political pressures, social conflict, unrest and war. When one does a WorldCat.Org search for the keyword “Orientalism” one is presented with over 16,000 entries, including over 7,000 peer-reviewed articles. A Google search returns over 870,000 listings. Clearly, Edward Said hit a worldwide nerve when he published Orientalism in 1979.

Born in Palestine in 1935, Said was educated first in Jerusalem and Cairo and then at Princeton and Harvard. He joined the faculty at Columbia University as a professor of English and comparative literature in 1981 where he continued to research, write and teach until his death in 2003.

As one might expect from an academic whose discipline is comparative literature, Orientalism is a text-based analysis with many literary and historical references and quotations, some in French or German without translation. However, Said’s text is so richly defined, detailed and clearly written that the reader does not loose the core message because of a paucity of knowledge about referenced authors or the inability to fully understand the occasional multi-lingual presentation.

Orientalism is widely considered a seminal and foundational text for postcolonial studies, a discipline that has expanded to consider not only political systems of hegemony and imperialism, but also power structures and relationships in philosophy, literature, the arts and other fields.

Although one can absorb and reflect on Said’s message it would require considerable time to evaluate the veracity of his sometimes bold statements, or the negative and positive responses this book has received.

Said opens by defining Orientalism as three interdependent ideas. First he states, “The most readily accepted designation for Orientalism is an academic one … Anyone who teaches, writes about, or researches the Orient – and this applies whether the person is an anthropologist, sociologist, historian, or philologist … is an Orientalist, and what he or she does is Orientalism.” (p. 2)

Second, “Orientalism is a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between “the Orient” and (most of the time) “the Occident.” (p. 3) Here he presents a key duopolistic theme repeated and expanded upon throughout the book. Said’s third meaning, “which is something more historically and materially defined than either of the other two. … Orientalism can be discussed and analyzed as the corporate institution for dealing with the Orient – dealing with it by making statements about it, authorizing views of it, describing it, by teaching it, settling it, ruling over it: in short, Orientalism as a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient.” (p. 3) And with this third definition, Said references Michel Foucault’s ideas about discourse as a source of power, and how one can reveal the hierarchies of power structures through the analysis of texts. Knowledge is power, or if you’d rather, textualized discourse is power.

Said then makes a distinction between “pure” and “political” knowledge,” stating: “For if it is true that no production of knowledge in the human sciences can ever ignore or disclaim its author’s involvement as a human subject in his own circumstances, then it must also be true that for a European or American studying the Orient there can be no disclaiming the main circumstances of his actuality: that he comes up against the Orient as a European or American first, as an individual second.” (p. 11) The core idea, that one can never escape one’s cultural baggage, is reiterated several times in Orientalism and in the closing chapter, Said states, “My principal operating assumptions were – and continue to be – that fields of learning, as much as the works of even the most eccentric artist, are constrained and acted upon by society, by cultural traditions, by worldly circumstances, and by stabilizing influences like schools, libraries, and governments; more over, that both learned and imaginative writings are never free, but are limited in their imagery, assumptions, and intentions.” (p. 202)

One can question Said’s position that one’s cultural background and the racial and social constructs they are raised with will always dominate how they experience or understand a foreign place or their perception of ‘others’, because Said fails to consider the possibility of a change in consciousness due to new experiences and knowledge. Surely one must always consider their own ‘position’ in life, their cultural baggage, but attitudes, relationships and policies do change both amongst individuals and societies. This change may be imperfect and have inconsistent results, but it does happen.

Said proceeds to outline his methodology for the book and adds a personal dimension, ending with a resonate statement, calling out his own secular humanism, “If this stimulates a new kind of dealing with the Orient, indeed if it eliminates the “Orient” and “Occidental” altogether, then we shall have advanced a little in the process of what Raymond Williams has called the “unlearning” of “the inherent dominative mode.” (p. 28) This aspirational desire that people can and should work to obliterate (or eliminate) the duopolistic and negative results of seeing the world as East or West, European or Asiatic, Oriental or Occidental, ‘us’ or ‘them’, is reiterated throughout Said’s text. It is a fundamentally important point, that one should keep in mind while reading his analysis, since it is a hopeful consideration that mitigates some of his harsher social criticisms.

Having established a definition of Orientalism, Said proceeds to provide a deeply detailed record of the development, evolution and impact of Orientalism. Although Said states early on that, “There still remained the problem … outlining something in the nature of an intellectual order within that group of texts without at the same time following a mindlessly chronological order” (p. 16) what follows, is indeed fundamentally a chronological review of Orientalist texts. However, each historical text is re-framed or oriented toward a discourse highlighting its impact on contemporary circumstances and understandings, and/or reiterating, emphasizing and expanding upon Said’s core definitions of Orientalism.

Before reverting to the origins of Orientalism during the European Enlightenment, Said presents excerpts from Arthur Balfour’s speech to the House of Commons in June 1910, defending Britain’s claims and obligations to remain as the colonizing power in Egypt. Balfour, a former Prime Minster of the United Kingdom (1902-1905), states, “Western nations as soon as they emerge into history show the beginnings of those capacities for self-government … having merits of their own. … You may look through the whole history of the Orientals in what is called, broadly speaking, the East, and you never find traces of self-government. All their great centuries — and they have been very great — have been passed under despotism, under absolute government. … Is it a good thing for these great nations – I admit their greatness – that this absolute government should be exercised by us? I think it is a good thing. I think that experience shows that they have got under it far better government than in the whole history of the world they ever had before, and which not only is a benefit to them, but is undoubtedly a benefit to the whole of civilized West. … We are in Egypt not merely for the sake of the Egyptian, though we are there for their sake; we are there also for the sake of Europe at large.” (p. 32-33) Said then makes the case that Lord Cromer, the British Consul-General in Egypt, utilized this Orientalist political, cultural and social framework of superiority to administer his rule over the Egyptians, and quotes from Cromer’s book, Modern Egypt, “Orientals or Arabs are thereafter shown to be gullible, ‘devoid of energy and initiative’ much given to ‘fulsome flattery,’ intrigue, cunning, and unkindness to animals … Orientals are inveterate liars, they are ‘lethargic and suspicious,’ and in everything oppose the clarity, directness, and mobility of the Anglo-Saxon race”. (p. 38)

Said provides a detailed analysis of Balfour and Cromer’s speeches and texts, framing this moment, the peak of British colonial and imperial rule, as “the apogee of Orientalist confidence. No merely asserted generality is denied the dignity of truth.” Westerners, see themselves as, “rational, peaceful, liberal, logical, capable of holding real values, without natural suspicion” and the Orientals are, “none of these things.” (p. 49) The introduction of Balfour and Cromer in Chapter One (The Scope of Orientalism) clearly shows how embedded Orientalism had become as the guiding principal and method for Europeans (and later Americans) in their relationship with the Orient. Said points out that in this period, the early twentieth century, Orientalism is a highly developed and powerful political vision that is the result of studies and texts, authored principally by white, European or American, Christian, Western men, that took several centuries to produce, to describe, define and suppress Eastern, Oriental, brown or black skinned, Arabic, Moslem populations.

An exceptionally interesting series of historic circumstances is presented as Said traces Napoleon’s incursion into Egypt in the late eighteenth century. Napoleon arrived on the shores of Egypt in his flag ship the Orient, with his Grande Armée and 167 Orientalist scholars (savants) in 1798. This may have been the first time the leader of an invading army deeply studied the foreign lands they were approaching through the work of scholars and their books, a primary characteristic of the Orientalist approach. Orientalism assumed that knowledge and control were gained not by direct or personal experience, but rather through the study of texts.

Napoleon, realizing that he did not have the military force to suppress the Egyptian people, used his Orientalist scholars (instead of his military officers) to not only negotiate with the local population but to assure that all his dictates were translated into Koranic Arabic. This was done to not only bolster Napoleon’s position that he respected Mohammed and Islam, but to further his claim that he was fighting for the Egyptians, as their liberator, not their conqueror. The Egyptian natives and of course Napoleon’s principal enemy, the Mamluk elite, did not accept this form of imperialism, which was informed by Orientalism. The French retained control of Egypt only until 1801. When Napoleon departed, he sent “strict instructions … to administer Egypt through the Orientalists and the religious Islamic leaders whom they could win over; any other politics was too expensive and foolish.” (p. 83) Although one might wonder if the America invasion of Iraq might have had a different result, if such a learned and respectful approach was used (instead of brute military force), it still presents as a continuation of the hegemony and the imperialist power defined by Orientalism.

A result of Napoleon’s campaign was that “everything said, seen, and studied was to be recorded, and indeed was recorded in that great collective appropriation of one country by another, the Description de l’Égypte, published in twenty-three enormous volumes between 1809 and 1828”. (p. 84)

The Description de l’Égypte is referenced through out Orientalism, along with the very many other consequential Orientalist texts, including the work of Silvestre de Sacy, Ernest Renan, Caussin, Carlyle, Flaubert, Disraeli, Kinglake, Lane, Chateaubriand, Curzon, Massignon, Gibb, T.E. Lawrence, Vico, Bernard Lewis and others. All were French, British or American white men.

In closing, Said raises and reiterates the critical questions presented in Orientalism. He says, “My project has been to describe a particular system of ideas, not by any means to displace the system with a new one. In addition, I have attempted to raise a whole set of questions that are relevant in discussing the problems of human experience: How does one represent other cultures? What is another culture? Is the notion of a distinct culture (or race, or religion, or civilization) a useful one, or does it always get involved either in self-congratulation (when one discusses one’s own) or hostility and aggression (when one discusses the “other”)? Do cultural, religious, and racial differences matter more than socio-economic categories, or politicohistorical ones? How do ideas acquire authority, “normality,” and even the status of “natural” truth? What is the role of the intellectual? ” (p. 325-326) These are all profoundly important and relevant questions and concerns for anyone living in today’s world to consider.

Since this paper is being written in the context of a graduate program in the visual arts, it seems necessary to remember that Orientalism is a text-based project. Said hardly mentions how the term has long been used in the study of art history. The Orientalist work of certain nineteenth century European painters runs fully parallel to Said’s analysis, as stated even in the dedication to the book where Said quotes Karl Marx, “They cannot represent themselves; they must be represented”. European paintings of Asiatic or Eastern or Arab or Moslem subject matter illustrate the same issues and concerns analyzed in Said’s book. However, the contention that Orientalist art is in the same framework as Said’s Orientalism, like many of his other interpretations, can be disputed. For example, John MacKenzie is quoted in Ali Behdad’s paper, Orientalism Matters, who states, “there is little evidence of a necessary coherence between the imposition of direct imperial rule and the visual arts. … Orientalism [in art history] celebrates cultural proximity, historical parallelism and religious familiarity [with the Middle East and North Africa] rather than true, ‘Otherness'”. (p. 51) Behdad further argues “that Orientalism should not be understood merely as an ideological discourse of power, nor as a natural art historical term, but rather as a network of aesthetic, economic, and political relationships that cross national and historical boundaries”. (p. 711)

 ////

**End Notes:**

 • Berkowitz, P. “Answering Edward Said Defending the West: a Critique of Edward Said’s Orientalism by Ibn Warraq.” Policy Review Washington. (2008): 75-81. Print.  
 • Trinh, T M.-H. Woman, Native, Other: Writing Postcoloniality and Feminism. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1989. Print.  
 • Trinh, T M.-H. When the Moon Waxes Red: Representation, Gender, and Cultural Politics. New York: Routledge, 1991. Print.

This webpage is a graduate student paper by David Kutz, written for the low-residency MFA program at Vermont College of Fine Arts (VCFA), submitted to faculty adviser Humberto Ramirez on October 14, 2014. The paper is an annotation and analysis of Edward Said's seminal 1979 book "Orientalism" (New York: Vintage Books).

The paper provides an overview of Said's background—born in Palestine in 1935, educated in Jerusalem, Cairo, Princeton, and Harvard, joining Columbia University as a professor of English and comparative literature in 1981 where he taught until his death in 2003.

Kutz outlines Said's three interdependent definitions of Orientalism: (1) an academic designation for anyone who teaches, writes about, or researches the Orient; (2) a style of thought based on an ontological and epistemological distinction between "the Orient" and "the Occident"; and (3) a corporate institution for dealing with the Orient—a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient, referencing Michel Foucault's ideas about discourse as a source of power.

The paper covers key themes including Said's argument that one can never escape one's cultural baggage, his analysis of Arthur Balfour's 1910 House of Commons speech defending Britain's colonization of Egypt, Lord Cromer's administration using Orientalist frameworks (describing Orientals as "gullible," "devoid of energy and initiative," "inveterate liars," and "lethargic and suspicious"), and Napoleon's 1798 incursion into Egypt with 167 Orientalist scholars (savants) aboard his flagship the Orient—a notable early example of an invading army using scholarly study of a foreign land, resulting in the 23-volume "Description de l'Égypte" published between 1809 and 1828.

Kutz also notes that Orientalism is widely considered a seminal and foundational text for postcolonial studies, cites critiques including John MacKenzie's argument (quoted in Ali Behdad's "Orientalism Matters") that there is little evidence of coherence between imperial rule and visual arts, and lists other referenced scholars including Silvestre de Sacy, Ernest Renan, Flaubert, Disraeli, T.E. Lawrence, and Bernard Lewis. The paper concludes with Said's critical questions about how one represents other cultures, the usefulness of distinct cultural categories, and the role of the intellectual.
args.key_excerpts: "The most readily accepted designation for Orientalism is an academic one … Anyone who teaches, writes about, or researches the Orient – and this applies whether the person is an anthropologist, sociologist, historian, or philologist … is an Orientalist, and what he or she does is Orientalism." (p. 2), "Orientalism can be discussed and analyzed as the corporate institution for dealing with the Orient – dealing with it by making statements about it, authorizing views of it, describing it, by teaching it, settling it, ruling over it: in short, Orientalism as a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient." (p. 3), "For if it is true that no production of knowledge in the human sciences can ever ignore or disclaim its author's involvement as a human subject in his own circumstances, then it must also be true that for a European or American studying the Orient there can be no disclaiming the main circumstances of his actuality: that he comes up against the Orient as a European or American first, as an individual second." (p. 11), "If this stimulates a new kind of dealing with the Orient, indeed if it eliminates the 'Orient' and 'Occidental' altogether, then we shall have advanced a little in the process of what Raymond Williams has called the 'unlearning' of 'the inherent dominative mode.'" This is a Threads post (by user @julian_chen5257) explaining the concept of "Orientalism" (東方主義) in Traditional Chinese. The post defines Orientalism as a knowledge system and power discourse developed by the West (particularly Europe and America) toward Eastern regions such as the Middle East and Asia, characterized by stereotypes and exoticism. It was systematically critiqued by Edward Said as a tool used by the West to consolidate its own superiority and colonial domination.

Key points covered:
- Said's 1978 critique established that Orientalism is not objective description but a Western-constructed "fantasy of the East" — a structural discourse that legitimized imperialism and colonial rule over the East.
- It essentializes diverse Eastern cultures, portraying them as backward, autocratic, or exotic "others."
- It establishes a binary opposition: "us" (West = advanced) vs. "them" (East = backward), cementing Western cultural centrality.
- Extended concept of "Self-Orientalism": Eastern nations (e.g., Japan, China) Orientalize themselves to accommodate Western perspectives and tourism demands, manufacturing stereotyped cultural traits.
- Power mechanism: Orientalism is not merely academic study ("Oriental studies") but a power practice that places the East under Western intellectual control.
- The post also describes how the Orient is "otherized" as stagnant, mysterious, irrational, passive, and feminine — in contrast to the West's civilization, rationality, and agency.

维基百科，自由的百科全书

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_-_Le_charmeur_de_serpents.jpg/330px-Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_-_Le_charmeur_de_serpents.jpg?utm_source=zh.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me_-_Le_charmeur_de_serpents.jpg)

由[尚-李奧·傑洛姆](/wiki/%E5%B0%9A-%E6%9D%8E%E5%A5%A7%C2%B7%E5%82%91%E6%B4%9B%E5%A7%86 "尚-李奧·傑洛姆")約1879年所繪的《弄蛇人（The Snake Charmer）》。收藏於美國[克拉克藝術中心](/wiki/%E5%85%8B%E6%8B%89%E5%85%8B%E8%89%BA%E6%9C%AF%E4%B8%AD%E5%BF%83 "克拉克艺术中心")。

在[藝術史](/wiki/%E8%97%9D%E8%A1%93%E5%8F%B2 "藝術史")、[文學](/wiki/%E6%96%87%E5%AD%B8 "文學")和[文化研究](/wiki/%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E7%A0%94%E7%A9%B6 "文化研究")中，**東方主義**（英語：Orientalism）指的是[西方世界](/wiki/%E8%A5%BF%E6%96%B9%E4%B8%96%E7%95%8C "西方世界")的作家、設計師和藝術家對[東方世界](/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E6%96%B9%E4%B8%96%E7%95%8C "東方世界")（或稱 "[東方文化](/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E6%96%B9%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96 "東方文化")"）各個方面的模仿或是描繪。在19世紀的[學院派藝術](/wiki/%E5%AD%B8%E9%99%A2%E8%97%9D%E8%A1%93 "學院藝術")中，東方主義繪畫是一門重要的專業領域，且特別盛行於描繪[西亞](/wiki/%E8%A5%BF%E4%BA%9E "西亞")與[北非](/wiki/%E5%8C%97%E9%9D%9E "北非")地區。[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)與此同時，西方文學也深受這股探索東方主題的風潮所影響。

自從[愛德華·薩依德](/wiki/%E6%84%9B%E5%BE%B7%E8%8F%AF%C2%B7%E8%96%A9%E4%BE%9D%E5%BE%B7 "愛德華·薩依德")撰寫的《[東方學](/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E6%96%B9%E5%AD%B8 "東方學")》於1978年出版以來，許多學術論述開始使用"東方主義"這個用語來指代西方對亞洲和北非社會普遍存在的傲慢態度。在薩依德的分析中，"西方"將這些社會[本質主義](/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%B4%A8%E4%B8%BB%E4%B9%89 "本质主义")視為靜態且不發達 - 而虛構出一種可為帝國權力服務，並加以研究、描繪和複製的東方文化視角。薩依德寫道，在這種虛構中隱含著一種觀念，即西方社會是發達、理性、靈活且優越的。[[3]](#cite_note-3)而使得"西方想像"，將"東方"文化和人民視為既迷人又對西方文明構成威脅的存在。[[4]](#cite_note-4)
