1 _Provincializing Europe: The Postcolonial World and Historical Difference_ (Chakrabarty 2000) turned 25 in 2025. I have been fortunate to be around these twenty-five years, and this moment affords me an opportunity to look back on the years that led me to write the book, however non-transparent they may feel today. I am enough of a historian, I hope, to know that one should not trust an author’s account of the genesis of their book any more than one trusts a piece of historical evidence. Weighing evidence, verifying evidence, said Marc Bloch (1954, 83-85), was the historian’s “method of doubt”. The attempt to write an explanatory account of how a book came to be written invariably entails the fabrication of a degree of coherence that cannot possibly be true to all the passions, confusions, and conflicts that rend our lives. A text is only a point, even if a nodal one, in a web of connections and conversations forged by arguments for and against that both preceded, attended, and followed its publication. Even the sniggers and off-hand dismissals that a text is sometimes subjected to play a role. _Provincializing Europe_ is no exception. It has survived criticisms so far, which does not mean the criticisms were necessarily wrong or that I have not benefited from them even when I have not agreed with them. Nor have criticisms ceased. Perhaps the questions the book asked and answers it provided still work to interest, engage, frustrate or even irritate its readers, warranting praise, criticism, modification, or refutation.

2 What I will undertake here is a two-step exercise: (a) explain what I see, in retrospect, as the intellectual origins of the book, and (b) share some thoughts on why I see the book as having a reflexive relationship to its own times, i.e. to the cultural-economic-medial-financial phenomenon that we call globalization. In other words, it was indeed the seemingly inexorable nature of late twentieth-century globalization of lives that made this book possible; and the book in turn was an attempt to use the theoretical resources of postcolonial studies and to explore the archives of the history of the modern in colonial Bengal in search of clues for how one might critically inhabit the global.

3 _Provincializing Europe_ (hereafter PE) is often read, not without reason, as a critique of Eurocentric thought. And it is that, no question. But it is also a book with its two parts organized under the signs of Karl Marx and Martin Heidegger and it ends, after all, with the acknowledgement of “an anticolonial debt of gratitude” to European thought. Clearly, this is also a book about a certain kind of self-conscious and postcolonial engagement/entanglement with a “Europe” of the mind. PE proceeds from the assumption that European thought, with all its inner richness, flaws, prejudices, and contradictions, is an indispensable heritage for every person who must inhabit or deal with modern institutions, practices, and technology from within the history of their colonial production. To this end, the book fundamentally seeks to think through a distinction it posits between the globalization and the universalization of capital by challenging some of the assumptions underlying the universalist claims that enabled European thought in the age of Kant, Hegel, Marx, and Mill to imagine a common and shared future of humanity, an increasingly unrealizable idea that still inspires.

## [1. The Intellectual Origins of Provincializing Europe](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#tocfrom2n1)

4 As any reader of PE would know, its roots go back to my involvement in the intellectually fecund project in South Asian history that was christened Subaltern Studies by its brilliant and inspiring founder Ranajit Guha (1923-2023). To remember those roots is to encounter, in imagination, a historical period that today seems as strange and remote as it once seemed familiar and completely our own. Consider the differences. My academic formation began in Calcutta in the early 1970s. The 1950s Cold-War paradigms of growth and development had been discredited in India and elsewhere by the 1970s with the rise of mass poverty, environmental problems, gender justice, and equality as critical global issues. But the question of transition to modernity, from pasts that we regarded as pre-capitalist, still retained a force that oriented much historical thinking in what was then called the Third World. This was also a period when, disappointed and disenchanted with the stultification of Marxism in the Soviet Union and its violent suppressions of dissident movements in Hungary (1956) and the-then Czechoslovakia (1968), many academics on the left invested politically in the idea of “the peasant as the modern, if not revolutionary, citizen”.

*   1 See his discussion of Mao’s “On Contradiction” in Althusser (1969).

5 There is no question that the political success of the peasant-based Chinese revolution, and the Vietnamese peasants’ heroic resistance to imperial aggressions – in short, the Vietnam War – acted as sources of inspiration for this intellectual turn to the peasant. It was in the nineteen seventies that academic and social-science interest in the “modern” political potential of peasants peaked. This was preceded, of course, by an international romance of Maoism and of even the Maoist (and destructive) Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution in the nineteen sixties and the seventies when the French philosopher and a very influential teacher of Étienne Balibar and Jacques Ranci è re and others, Louis Althusser – famous for making a distinction between the “young Marx” of the 1848 manuscripts and the more “mature Marx” of _Das Kapital_ – proclaimed Mao to be a greater dialectician than Hegel.[1](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn1)

6 Symptomatic of this growing interest in the peasant was the English-language magazine, _The Journal of Peasant Studies_, started in 1973. The journal emerged from the Peasant Studies Seminar that Terence Byres and Charles Curwen, two of the first three editors of the journal, ran from 1972 to 1989 at the University of London. They were joined in the first editorial board of _JPS_ by Teodor Shanin, the eminent Russian-British sociologist at the University of Manchester. Shanin, with his book _The Awkward Class_ (Shanin 1972) and his other writings on peasantry pioneered the field of “peasant studies”. It was no coincidence that Ranajit Guha (1974) published his first essay on a particular nineteenth-century peasant rebellion in colonial Bengal in the second issue of _JPS_. In the particular case of _Subaltern Studies,_ one has to remember the additional fact that many young Indians of my generation attempted through 1967 to 1971 to mount a violent and – in terms of lives – tragic revolution in India inspired by Mao. That movement was brutally crushed by the Indian state. But the young historians associated with _Subaltern Studies_ either came out of that movement or bore sympathies for it. Having emerged from that failed revolution, the puzzle of what made the idea of a peasant-based modern political revolution inoperative in India remained a fundamental question for these historians.

7 Globally speaking, _Subaltern Studies_(1982-2005) was a late, almost anachronistic, entrant into the field of “peasant studies”. Mao died in 1975, which is also when the Vietnamese war ended. The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution also ran out of steam. China would start its Four Modernizations program soon under the leadership of Deng Xiao Ping. The first volume of _Subaltern Studies_ came out in India in 1982. The discussion in the Anglophone academy had moved on by then. Two of the books shaping discussions in the humanities and the social sciences at that time, for instance, were Edward Said’s _Orientalism_ (1978) and Benedict Anderson’s _Imagined Communities_ (1983), though we did not engage with them until the publication of my colleague in _Subaltern Studies,_ Partha Chatterjee’s book, _Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World_ (1986). The foundational text for _Subaltern Studies_ was Ranajit Guha’s _Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India_(1983), a structural-historical analysis of what one might call the grammar of the “consciousness” of the insurgent peasant, made on the basis of a meticulous examination of more than a hundred instances of peasant rebellions in nineteenth-century India. Guha’s eclectic and imaginative use of Marx, Hegel, Mao, Gramsci, and the theoretical and conceptual tools of structuralism in this exercise was quite a heady mix for the young historians he had collected around him.

8 Why, of all things, “revolutionary consciousness” became the key question of Guha’s text and, by implication and influence, of _Subaltern Studies_ generally is an interesting problem I will not discuss here for reasons of space. Suffice it to say that in colonial contexts where organizing a revolution and/or mass forms of protest against imperial rule were imagined as a matter of creating a political will in a general condition of underdevelopment, “consciousness” seemed to be the key element over which both nationalists and revolutionaries felt they had some leverage. Guha’s theoretical reflections on peasant rebellions, however, left us with a political impasse in our imagination with respect to how a historiography that aimed to make the peasant or the subaltern the agents of their own history could actually make a contribution to the struggle for transition to a non-capitalist and just social order. For Guha’s meticulous research and brilliant analysis ended up demonstrating why the peasant could never on their own be the world-historical “revolutionary subject” that would take the place of the proletariat of classical Marxism to perform the role assigned to the latter, i.e. effect a “comprehensive reversal” of social hierarchies (Guha 1983, 337).

9 The consciousness of the insurgent peasant, Guha showed, had two fundamental limitations when looked at from a revolutionary point of view. Religious ideas and ideas derived from kinship constituted two of the most “elementary” ingredients of the peasant’s world and the peasant could never, as it were, think without those tools. With our incipient theory of a peasant-based revolution of which the peasants and not the elites or the Communist Party were the true heroes, we did not want the mediation of the Party either. The scrupulous historian that he was, Guha refrained from making any practical suggestions about how, in theory or practice, these limitations of the consciousness of the insurgent peasant could be overcome. As is well known, Guha later bade goodbye to his earlier project of subordinating historiography to the search for a revolutionary class in a later phase of _Subaltern Studies_ and of his own life. He went on to develop a humanist project that made “the small voice of history” that told the stories of everyday weal and woe the main staple of his thinking on subaltern histories.

10 _Provincializing Europe_, I now think, was my attempt to work a way out of this framework structuring _Subaltern Studies,_ a framework, once an inspiration, no doubt, but also that increasingly seemed too romantic as the years wore on: the problem of transition to modernity – either of a capitalist or socialist kind – in a situation where the insurgent peasant-subject necessarily and always fell short of the revolutionary subject demanded by the requirements of classical Marxism. This was the question we had inherited from Indian, and broadly third-world, Marxism. The influence of this vein of thinking and of the inspiration of _Elementary Aspects_ may be easily seen to be at work in my first book, _Rethinking Working-Class History_ (Chakrabarty 1989) that struggled, unsuccessfully, with the same problem of “class consciousness.”

11 Globally significant developments of the late twentieth century history rid us of this problematic of transition by shifting our intellectual goalposts. With the fall of the Soviet empire, of the Berlin wall, and with China, India, Vietnam and other nations decidedly joining the expansive neo-liberal global economy, the problematic of revolutionary transformation of peasant societies was replaced by the problem of globalization of capital. New questions arose. One of the key questions was about the relationship between the universalizing logic of capital and all the “anthropological differences” – differences of history, race, caste, gender, nationalisms, institutions, and practices – that mark human histories on the ground. Previously, to put it crudely, we used to think of capital (whether strictly conceived as a political-economic category within the Marxist tradition or loosely as “capitalism” or modernization) as having an innate capacity to overcome and absorb or mobilize into its logic of self-reproduction – somewhat in the manner of the operation of the Hegelian concept of _aufhebung_ or sublation– elements of history that pre-existed the advent of capital or modernity and that seemed opposed to the logic of the latter.

12 This may have been a vulgar version of Hegel circulating through the literature on modernization both on the left and the right, but the assumption was there all right. A prominent example would be, for instance, Suzanne and Lloyd Rudolphs’ celebrated book, _The Modernity of Tradition_ (1967), much praised for its argument that the caste associations formed in British India were only “traditional” in appearance but completely “modern” in their functions. This meta-narrative was shared by many strands of Marxism as well. Published in the same year as PE, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri’s imaginative and powerful book, _Empire_ (2000), argued, in direct opposition to difference philosophies (of Lacan, Derrida, and Foucault) that had led to theorizations of difference in post-structuralist and post-colonial texts, that all differences was mere grist to the mill of capital for the latter inevitably trumped them by converting them into so many sets of consumer preference! The politics of difference could never resist the sway of placeless or homelessness that global capital promoted. The immanent critique of capital that Marx’s “capital” was also stemmed, it was said, from this logic of placelessness. Critics had to argue by situating themselves in the “nowhere” land of theory. Or so ran the argument.

13 PE was a contribution to this debate, but it was also centrally concerned with aspects of religion that had been described in Guha’s text as inherent limitations of the peasant when measured by the standards of a world-historical revolutionary subject. PE did not deny the production of placelessness as _a_ tendency inherent in the universal logic of capital. That was indeed my History1. But I also sought to demonstrate that a close reading of Marx allowed for two kinds of histories of capital. History1’s tendency to destroy all sense of human belonging to specific times and places was always disrupted by the undertow of another logic that I called History2, a logic that allowed pasts different from History1 and not belonging to what Marx called the “life process” of capital to inhere in historical forms of capital and in the category itself. The negotiations between the two Histories ensured that even the globalization of capital – that fact anyone and everyone today live, however unevenly, under the sway of capital could not mean, in my terms, the universalization of the placeless logic of History1. Capital could not – thanks to the nature and the limitations of the marketplace – convert all differences into consumer preferences. Some differences constituted elements of loss, grief, pain, or even nostalgia but the marketplace could not make them into purchasable commodities.

14 The presence of History2 reflected thus the struggle for place and dwelling that was also internal to capital. This, I argued, was as true of capital’s career in Europe as it was of its career outside the so-called West. The very encounter of capital (in the process of its emergence) with very different ways of being in the world that, while not always hostile to capital, did not actually belong to what Marx called capital’s “life-process”, allowed us to live and experience both History1 and History2 (the latter necessarily plural as it represents plural ways of being in the world) as tendencies in our lives. The tensions, contradictions, frictions, and juxtapositions of History1 and the numerous History2 necessarily mark the life of capital. The porous opposition I set up between History1 and History2 allowed me to claim that every case of “transition” to capitalism also entail a process of “translation” – that is to say, every case of transition to capitalism is also a story of rough and ready, approximate translations of existing concepts and life-practices into the categories that sustained the grafting of the capitalist mode of production on preexisting historical relationships.

15 I was not the first scholar from within _Subaltern Studies_ to connect with some of the theorizations of difference that postcolonial theorists such as Edward Said, Gayatri Spivak, and Homi Bhabha were undertaking from the eighties of the last century. Partha Chatterjee’s _Nationalist Thought_(1986) was a key text here. It embodied our first engagement with the work of Edward Said in his book _Orientalism_(1978). The second key text of this transition was Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s “Can the Subaltern Speak?” first published in its fully developed form in 1988, soon after Chatterjee’s book – a fact that probably speaks to the emergent concerns of our time. The publication of _Selected Subaltern Studies_ in 1988 with an introduction by Spivak that described us as a group of unselfconscious deconstructionist historians, and a foreword by a person no other than Edward Said himself, was signal that our induction into the emergent field of postcolonial studies was nearly complete.

16 In my own case, last chapter of my first book, _Rethinking Working-Class History_ (1989) and some sections of the introduction of that book were really the places where, in hindsight, the problematic of PE seems to have begun to formulate itself, though the first time I used the expression “provincializing Europe” – riffing on a statement of Gadamer that Europe had already been provincialized by history – was when I published a programmatic essay titled “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” in the Berkeley journal _Representations_ (Chakrabarty 1992). This remaking of _Subaltern Studies_ internationally as a version of postcolonial-global historical studies was not easy. It generated dissent and denunciation within and outside the collective – Sumit Sarkar and David Hardiman famously and sternly criticized the transition in their different ways. However, Gyan Prakash’s publication of his _Another Reason_ (1999) put a seal of finality on this transition.

17 Our transition into postcolonial studies, ironically and eventually, forced on us the recognition that, whatever the extent of our commitment to “Indian society and history,” we were, to begin with, a dispersed, global, part-diasporic group of scholars. Our founder-guru Guha himself had been out of India more than two decades by the time _Subaltern Studies_ was born as a project. We had been in practical denial of this fact. But this fact had far-reaching implications for how we related to “national” histories or even to questions of memory. Guha himself would write a fascinating piece on the figure of the migrant for the Melbourne journal, _Meanjin,_ in the early 1990s, later reprinted in _Postcolonial Studies_ in 1998. Different members of the collective developed their own and personal strategies for coping with this fact whose cover was blown as the original historiographical project of _Subaltern Studies_ withered on the vine, leaving us with no other option but to face the glare of the rising sun of globalization/migrant studies.

18 To say this, I should add parenthetically, is not to deny either the uniqueness and global significance of the _Subaltern Studies_ project as it was originally conceived by Guha or of the long-lasting legacy of the aspiration articulated in its pages for non-elitist forms of history-writing and for critiques of the institutions of colonial archives and of history itself as a modern form of knowledge. My critique does not take away from these achievements. _Subaltern Studies_ was, in any case, a rare phenomenon in the global scene of history-writing. A group of young historians of South Asia, all of them in their thirties, led by an historian of an older generation, getting together and working collectively for the best part of a decade to write histories of socially subordinated groups – this was an exhilarating life-changing experience for all of us. That inspiring story remains to be told.

## [2. Global life as method](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#tocfrom2n2)

19 Ernst Cassirer asked a great question in his book on Kant’s life and thought. This was the question of the relation, if any, between form of thought and form of life:

> … with Kant the relationship between the form of thought and form of life cannot be understood to mean that the latter came to be only the basis and passive receptacle for the former. In Kant’s actual existence, as Goethe – doubtless correctly – says, thought, in its objective content and its objective ‘truth,’ not only rules life but also receives in return the characteristic stamp of the life to which it imparts its form. (Cassirer 1981, 6)

20 Goethe’s point that Cassier made his own was a general one: the relation between forms of thought and forms of life. Cassirer’s discussion helps me to see that the more my academic life got professionalized (in the American sense of the word), the more my work has borne the stamp of the life-form of someone displaced. But not of someone who inhabits a sense of placelessness. This should not be understood as a rejection of the value of professionalism. Professionalism lends a certain kind of rigor to your thought, for that thought must survive all the taxing and demanding questions fellow professionals ask of it. Living and working in the American university system and its institutional ecology have often given me a sense of intellectual exhilaration that I owe to my peers and colleagues here and in the global academia. But there is, to borrow a word from the lexicon of Karl Polanyi’s immortal book, _The Great Transformation_(2001), a concomitant sense of living a “disembedded” form of life as a migrant intellectual, a sense that I have negotiated again and again for fifty years by sometimes embracing abstraction itself as a form of thought and at other times by mobilizing, as archives, my memories of – or even my nostalgia for – another and a much more immersive form of life that I once knew in Calcutta in the way I imagine a worker-bee knows its own hive. The two parts of PE are indeed reflective of both strategies.

*   2 Cf. Barthes (1981, 21): “… I wanted to explore it [a photograph] not as a question (a theme) but as [(...)](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn2)

21 This is not a sentimental point, though sentiments are never absent from thought (see the chapter on widows in PE). Affect, as Antonio Damasio’s work (1994) explains, attends even our highest abstractions. Returning to a sense of loss has thus – over time – become a routine part of the first steps of my critical method. This is a move that also helps me to turn a critical eye on my own nostalgia and convert it into something that in its orientation remains no longer bound to the past but becomes inescapably futural. The migrant form of life gives me a method: a book begins – as Barthes came close to suggesting a long time ago in his book _Camera Lucida_– when a loss or wound or injury has turned into a question.[2](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn2)

22 To illustrate my methodological point, however, please allow me to refer to my recent work on climate change (Chakrabarty 2021 and 2023) to say a little more on this question of migrancy as method. Australia was my first experience of “the West”. I was very much a formed individual by then. I was 27. The country came into my life through the capital city of Canberra, a city that had the Australian “bush” running all through it. The Australia I came to love was also the place I found in that city. There were things that I had never known to be possible in Calcutta. I had not known what it meant to study in serene, bucolic surroundings. Nature in Calcutta often meant looking up at the sky. You barely saw the horizon. In Canberra, the sky was all around you – a bright deep blue you felt you could drink. But it was not always an ‘Australian nature’ that I discovered in Canberra and its environs. I often found the nature I had read about in Bengali literature and sometimes seen in Bengali films. A creek, called Sullivan’s Creek, ran through my university campus and joined the Lake Burley Griffin created out of the Molonglo river and named after the main architect of Canberra, Walter Burley Griffin, a student of Frank Lloyd Wright, a US-Midwest connection that came into my life long before my move to Chicago. There was a dirt track that followed the creek as it made its way to the lake. If you walked along that path towards the lake, the land on your right would quickly fall away into the creek, into a long line of reeds that skirted the bank, among which wild ducks and geese would paddle with their fuzzy little families. The scene always reminded me of lines written by the immortal Bengali poet Jibanananda Das (translated – ironically, for my argument here, as if it had been foretold that I would one day move to the University of Chicago! – by my former University of Chicago colleague, Clinton B. Seely):

> If I were a wild duck,
> 
> If you were my mate,
> 
> On some faraway Jalsiri river bank 
> 
> Beside a paddy field 
> 
> Among the slender reeds 
> 
> In a secluded nest.

*   3 In writing this paragraph I have drawn on Chakrabarty (2018, xxv-xxvi).

23 I knew intellectually that the Bangladeshi district of Barisal celebrated in Das’s poetry had nothing in common with the landscape of Canberra, but the creek comforted me by giving me an illusion of being somewhere near a home that I had never even had, for I had not yet been to Bangladesh (formerly East Pakistan) from where my parents’ families migrated. My nostalgia was really nostalgia for Das’s nostalgia for another time. But that is perhaps how nostalgia works. I fell in love with the bush in and around Canberra through the mediation of Bengali literature. This was to prove rather important for my historical work in the long run. For it was my intensely personal sense of grief at the loss of this ‘nature’ when devastating fires broke out in Canberra in 2003 that eventually led me to think about the implications of climate change for historical thinking.[3](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn3)

24 The first book I wrote from within my Australian life was _Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890-1940_(Chakrabarty 1989, hereafter RWH)_,_ a not-so-revised version of my doctoral thesis. RWH was an in-between book. Half a continuation of arguments within Indian Marxism I had grown up with, and half arguments with and about a new Marx I discovered in Australia as I began to devour – in reading groups, in discussions with the brilliant and creative Ranjit Guha who relocated to Australia in 1980 – a burgeoning Western Marxology that we were dimly aware of in Calcutta from the odd publications some bibliophile professor would bring in from an occasional trip to the West or from the small number of Western publications that happened to hit the inadequate bookstands of Calcutta. The inspiration of _Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India_ (Guha 1983), and the work of colleagues in _Subaltern Studies_ were, of course, another strong source of influence as were discussions with my cohorts at ANU and my liberal-minded gentle supervisor, D. A. Low, a historian of East Africa and Southern Asia.

25 This second round of exposure to Marx allowed me to see the historical difference that separated my Bengali past from the European assumptions of Marx’s thought. My relationship to Marx himself was changing. If I may cite myself once again on my Calcutta background and how the separation from Calcutta came to matter, this is how I put it elsewhere:

> [In my life in Calcutta] I was a Marxist but was also vaguely aware of having been born in a poor Brahmin family that valued education above all. My friends in India and I argued about Indian history, but we were all insiders. Our passions about our histories came out of the literature we read, the soccer teams we supported, the songs we sang, [the plays we patronized,] and the films we watched. Nothing was separated from the immediacy of life. The plane that brought me to Canberra as a student broke my connection to that immediacy in a matter of hours. (Chakrabarty 2018, xxxvii-xxxviii)

26 The question of Marx’s Europeanness as a thinker never bothered us in Calcutta. But, now, being in a society that was aware of its own European settler-colonial heritage, Marx became for me much more of a white, European, even Jewish, and male thinker than before, and I could not help asking myself why it was with his European ideas that I was trying to find a key to unlock some mysteries of my Bengali life, society, and history. I did not ask this question explicitly until I wrote PE, but you can see the question stirring below the surface of the text of RWH. Unsurprisingly, therefore, as I was completing my thesis (later RWH), I began to have glimmers of the project that became PE. Did the European story have to be a model for us? Was the future of a country like India already anticipated – as Marx once said – in the history of the developed West? Was the main task of the historian to enable India to find its own _sonderweg_ to capitalism and modernity? You can hear the rumblings of these questions, still somewhat inchoate, in the first and last chapters of RWH. It took me almost twenty years to develop my own answer to the transition-to-capitalism problem. European thought, I later concluded, was both indispensable and inadequate. RWH took shape over a decade. Subsequently, I worked on materials that produced two books in the end: _Provincializing Europe_(Chakrabarty 2000) and _Habitations of Modernity_ (Chakrabarty 2002). They were companion volumes and perhaps need to be read together.

*   4 See the discussion in Chakrabarty (2000, 246).

27 Ironically, then, what we may call – in a Heideggerian vein – “the question of Europe” became more pressing as I began to live in countries much more self-consciously Europeanized (Australia, the United States) than my native India. After all, it is to the eyes of those who feel out of place – a stranger, a migrant, a refugee, an asylum seeker – that a place reveals its prejudices. I use the word “prejudice” in a Gadamerian sense, pre-judice, the judgment you make of someone before consciously judging them; prejudice thus speaks of the always-already interpreted world that grown-ups usher us into in our childhood and youth. “Provincializing Europe” could not have been my project while I was still based in India, for I was at home in whatever “Europe” meant there. There was no need there to ask about the meanings of Europe in non-Western lives – some nationalist philosophers used to ask such questions but usually to answer them in nativist and/or nationalist terms. But here, in Australia or the US, finding myself in a state of migrancy, enjoying, if that is the right word, my having become a member of an ethnic, religious, and linguistic minority, the question of my unassimilable sense of difference from whatever was assumed to be “universal” or “normal” about being modern in Australia or the US (granting many subtle and coarse differences separating them as well) – the unassimilable figure of the minor in, say, the eyes of Hannah Arendt or Deleuze – became the key question of PE. But there was, at the same time, no question of denying reason, modernity, and the aspiration to emancipatory politics, for had not B. R. Ambedkar, the leader of one of the most oppressed groups in India – the Dalits – declared in the middle of an intensely bitter polemic with Gandhi in the late 1930s that Indian society ought to be rebuilt on the basis of the three principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity?[4](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn4)

*   5 See, for instance, Jensen Suther’s somewhat familiar (mis)reading of History 2 as “the particular h [(...)](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn5)

28 The second part of _Provincializing Europe_ – called “Histories of Belonging” – is made up of a mobilization of facts and memories of middle-class Hindu-Bengali life and history before globalization. I mobilized them to combat and break out of the relentless and unbearable logic of History1. But I also went back to Marx to find a way of discussing how these memories of plural ways of belonging could be seen – within his theory – as cleaving to, functioning within, and yet interrupting that logic of placelessness. That for me was History2. Not something one could programmatically write as concrete, determinate histories.[5](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn5) It was more something you could retrospectively glimpse _within_ the history of capital only when certain ways of being human seemingly aligned with the profit-making drive of capital got dislodged – for whatever reasons – from that alignment. I could have, in a more self-conscious gesture, embracing an incongruence, called this section of the book “Dwelling in/on Capital”. For what that section and the book did was to search through the archives of being a Bengali of a certain kind in colonial and pre-global times to find answers to how one might inhabit – in a Heideggerian sense, dwell in and be in strife with – the relentless sense of homelessness that global capital tends produce and promote.

## [3. Reception, criticism, and the afterlife of Provincializing Europe](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#tocfrom2n3)

29 PE has been subject to much criticism. It would be tedious to go over all the criticism (and encouragement) that PE has so far received. As I said in the beginning, I am grateful for both. Let me simply just say that most early reviews were critical, the first ones in India being damning, their criticisms ranging from the allegedly jargon-ridden quality of my prose to pointing to the utter unoriginality or vacuity of what I had to say. When the French publishers of the book brought out a second edition of the French translation with a new preface, Thomas Brisson, its author, gave an interesting account of the difficult passage the book has had in France in getting to a point where the issuance of a second edition seemed justified, at least to the publishers. On its first publication in French, the book was denounced for “essentializing” India and the West and their differences; it was also judged to have been a part of the “academic carnival” that the field of postcolonial studies was, with nothing much to contribute to existing discussions of colonialism (Brisson 2020, 9-10). Arvind Elangovan, a US-based professor of history, has recently published an essay on PE where, among other things, there is an informative and detailed discussion of the major criticisms that the book has received since its publication. Interested readers may look up this essay (Elangovan 2025). As for myself, I would like to think that if a book, for all its faults, has survived for twenty-five years, it must have had something to say.

30 Let me end by sharing my own sense of the limitations and possibilities for PE as it goes forward in the twenty-first century. PE, as I have said, was heavily indebted to all the difference philosophers – Lacan, Derrida, Foucault, Deleuze and Guattari, Lyotard, Balibar, Irigaray, Ranci è re, and others – that France produced at the end of the last century. Hayden White’s _Metahistory_(1973) was also an inspiration. But the models and metaphors these philosophers worked with had to do with text and language (however broadly and abstractly conceived). They were part of the so-called “linguistic turn” in the humanities and the social sciences. It was working within these language-based paradigms that Gayatri Spivak (1988) could ask her famous question “Can the Subaltern Speak?” I now wonder how our methods of thinking would have had to be tweaked if the question, for instance, were: “Can the Subaltern Speak if the Subaltern is nonhuman?” Would “listening” and “speaking” be still the relevant terms to use if the subaltern were hills, rivers, microbes or something as large as what scientists call the earth system? The question of the nonhuman, a critical question of this century, forces us to look beyond the resources that difference-philosophy could provide.

*   6 For a beginning, see my “Questions Concerning Longevity”, forthcoming in _Critical Inquiry,_ Summer 2 [(...)](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn6)

31 But the idea of the “minor” as a position to think from – an idea I developed (with obvious debts to Deleuze) in the context of explaining what I called “subaltern pasts” in PE – does travel into my more recent work on our planetary environmental crisis. Humans are a minor form of life on this planet while the majority forms of life are invisible, microbial. Yet humans and their cities and technologies dominate all other forms of life, producing a crisis of biodiversity that threatens all life including ours. I sometimes think of my new project as one of “provincializing humans” in our own understanding of what we are when we have become a planetary force – and maybe in the process provincialize the planet-destroying consumerist conceptions of abundance and growth that the US has produced and promoted throughout the Cold War years and since.[6](https://journals.openedition.org/lerhistoria/16293#ftn6) Maybe the idea of “provincializing” will have another life, after all?

This webpage is the full-text article "Provincializing Europe, Twenty-five Years On: Retrospect and Reconsideration" by Dipesh Chakrabarty, published in the journal Ler História (Issue 88, 2026, pp. 9-24), as part of its "Magna Opera" section. The article revisits Chakrabarty's landmark book "Provincializing Europe" (2000) twenty-five years after its publication, reflecting on its intellectual origins, theoretical interventions, and critical reception.

KEY CONTENT:

**Intellectual Origins:** Chakrabarty traces the book's roots to his involvement with the Subaltern Studies collective (1982-2005), founded by Ranajit Guha (1923-2023). He describes the intellectual context of the 1970s, when interest in "the peasant as the modern revolutionary citizen" peaked, inspired by the Chinese and Vietnamese revolutions. He discusses Guha's foundational text "Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India" (1983) and the theoretical impasse it created—demonstrating that peasants could never be world-historical revolutionary subjects due to the limitations of their consciousness (grounded in religion and kinship). Chakrabarty explains that his own first book, "Rethinking Working-Class History" (1989), struggled with the same problem of class consciousness. The fall of the Soviet empire and the rise of neoliberal globalization in the late 1980s shifted the intellectual problematic from revolutionary transition to the globalization of capital.

**Core Theoretical Framework:** The essay clarifies the central distinction between History1 and History2. History1 represents the universalizing, placeless logic of capital that destroys human belonging to specific times and places. History2 represents plural ways of being in the world that inhere in and interrupt capital's logic—pasts that do not belong to capital's "life process" but cleave to it. Chakrabarty argues that capital cannot convert all differences into consumer preferences; some differences constitute loss, grief, and nostalgia that the marketplace cannot commodify. Every transition to capitalism also entails a process of "translation."

**Global Life as Method:** Chakrabarty reflects on migrancy as both a form of life and a critical method. He discusses how his move from Calcutta to Canberra, Australia (at age 27) and later to the United States shaped his thinking. The migrant's perspective reveals a place's prejudices (in a Gadamerian sense). He describes how his personal grief at the loss of Australian "nature" during the 2003 Canberra fires led him to think about climate change's implications for historical thinking. He explains that "the question of Europe" became more pressing as he lived in more self-consciously Europeanized countries than India.

**Reception and Criticism:** Early reviews of PE were largely critical, with the first Indian reviews being "damning." French reception denounced the book for "essentializing" India and the West. Arvind Elangovan published a detailed essay (2025) on the book's major criticisms. Despite this, Chakrabarty suggests the book's 25-year survival indicates it had something to say.

**Contemporary Relevance:** The essay concludes by considering the book's limits and its relevance for contemporary planetary and environmental thought. Chakrabarty notes that PE was indebted to French difference philosophers (Lacan, Derrida, Foucault, Deleuze, etc.) and the "linguistic turn." He now asks whether methods would need adjustment if the subaltern were nonhuman—hills, rivers, microbes, or the earth system itself. He frames his new project as one of "provincializing humans" in understanding ourselves as a planetary force, and potentially provincializing the planet-destroying consumerist conceptions of abundance promoted by the US.
args.key_excerpts: "PE proceeds from the assumption that European thought, with all its inner richness, flaws, prejudices, and contradictions, is an indispensable heritage for every person who must inhabit or deal with modern institutions, practices, and technology from within the history of their colonial production."

# Revisiting the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and its legacy

Read more Share this publication on

**The Bandung conference of 1955 was the result of political vision and meticulous planning. It marked the first ever summit-level meeting of independence leaders. It had an extremely important legacy, sparking organisations of developing countries like the NAM and the G77.**

---

**By Adriano José Timossi**

On April 18-24, 1955, leaders of Asian and African countries gathered in a historic meeting in Bandung, Indonesia. They included Premiers Chou En-Lai of China, Jawaharlal Nehru of India, U Nu of Burma, President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt besides President Sukarno of Indonesia, and leaders from Liberia, Sudan, Gold Coast, Jordan, Iran, Ceylon, Nepal, Pakistan and Philippines. The meeting of these leaders was a key point in the history of developing countries that gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) and the concept of the Third World or the South. At the start of the Cold War between the West and the former Soviet Union, the leaders of the developing countries gathered in Bandung asked for an alternative way of just global governance and global justice, to achieve greater social and economic development for their people, and to continue the process of political and economic decolonization.

**Sukarno’s Opening Speech**

In his opening speech at the first Asian-African Conference, President Sukarno of Indonesia recognized that the gathering of the leaders of the 29 Asian-African independent countries was a result of the sacrifices made by their forefathers and by the people of their own and younger generations. “The hall was filled not only by the leaders of the nations of Asia and Africa but also contained within its walls the undying, the indomitable, the invincible spirit of those who went before them”, he said. Their struggle and sacrifice paved the way for this meeting of the highest representatives of independent and sovereign nations from two of the biggest continents of the globe. In a historic event, Asian and African peoples were meeting together to discuss and deliberate upon matters of common concern to them.

Sukarno stated that the burden of the delegates attending the Conference was not a light one. “For many generations our peoples have been the voiceless ones in the world. We have been the unregarded, the peoples for whom decisions were made by others whose interests were paramount, the peoples who lived in poverty and humiliation. Then our nations demanded, nay fought for independence, and achieved independence, and with that independence came responsibility. We have heavy responsibilities to ourselves, and to the world, and to the yet unborn generations. But we do not regret them”.

Below are some extracts of his speech:

“We are often told ‘Colonialism is dead’. Let us not be deceived or even soothed by that. I say to you, colonialism is not yet dead. How can we say it is dead, so long as vast areas of Asia and Africa are unfree. And, I beg of you do not think of colonialism only in the classic form which we of Indonesia, and our brothers in different parts of Asia and Africa, knew. Colonialism has also its modern dress, in the form of economic control, intellectual control, actual physical control by a small but alien community within a nation. It is a skilful and determined enemy, and it appears in many guises. It does not give up its loot easily. Wherever, whenever and however it appears, colonialism is an evil thing, and one which must be eradicated from the earth.

“If this Conference succeeds in making the peoples of the East whose representatives are gathered here understand each other a little more, appreciate each other a little more, sympathise with each other’s problems a little more – if those things happen, then this Conference, of course, will have been worthwhile, whatever else it may achieve. But I hope that this Conference will give more than understanding only and goodwill only – I hope that it will falsify and give the lie to the saying of one diplomat from far abroad: “We will turn this Asian-African Conference into an afternoon-tea meeting”.

“I hope that it will give evidence of the fact that we Asian and African leaders understand that Asia and Africa can prosper only when they are united, and that even the safety of the World at large cannot be safeguarded without a united Asia-Africa. I hope that this Conference will give guidance to mankind, will point out to mankind the way which it must take to attain safety and peace. I hope that it will give evidence that Asia and Africa have been reborn, nay, that a New Asia and a New Africa have been born!

“Our task is first to seek an understanding of each other, and out of that understanding will come a greater appreciation of each other, and out of that appreciation will come collective action. Bear in mind the words of one of Asia’s greatest sons: “To speak is easy. To act is hard. To understand is hardest. Once one understands, action is easy”. Let us remember that the highest purpose of man is the liberation of man from his bonds of fear, his bonds of human degradation, his bonds of poverty – the liberation of man from the physical, spiritual and intellectual bonds which have for too long stunted the development of humanity’s majority.”

The other 28 leaders also spoke eloquently in calling for unity among Asian and African countries and for greater solidarity, self-determination, mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, and equality.

**The Bandung Final Communiqué 1955**

The Final Communiqué of the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference provided the basis for South-South cooperation with concrete proposals for promoting economic, political, technological, cultural spheres. It declared full support of the fundamental principles of human rights as set forth in the Charter of the United Nations and took note of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations in a moment in history when many South nations were still under Western colonial rule.

The communiqué deplored all forms of racial segregation and discrimination. In declaring support for the cause of freedom and independence for all peoples it also deplored colonialism, in all its manifestations.

The communiqué took note that several States had still not been admitted to the United Nations, and that for effective cooperation and world peace, membership in the United Nations should be universal. The leaders also considered that representation of Asian and African countries in the UN Security Council, in relation to the principle of equitable and geographical distribution, was inadequate, as it is today. The right to self-determination, stated the communiqué, should be enjoyed by all peoples.

The Ten Bandung Principles enunciated in 1955 continue to be as relevant today as it was 60 years ago and in the decades since. These are as follows:

“Free from   mistrust     and   fear,   and   with   confidence and   goodwill   towards   each other,   nations   should   practice   tolerance   and   live   together     in peace   with   one another   as good   neighbours and develop   friendly   cooperation on the basis of the following   principles:

“1. Respect for fundamental human rights and for the purposes and the principles of the Charter of the United Nations.

“2. Respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations.

“3. Recognition of the equality of all races and of the equality of all nations large and small.

“4. Abstention from intervention or interference in the internal affairs of another country.

“5. Respect for the right of each nation to defend itself singly or collectively, in conformity with the Charter of the United Nations.

“6. (a) Abstention from the use of arrangements of collective defense to serve the particular interests of any of the big powers,

(b) Abstention by any country from exerting pressures on other countries.

“7. Refraining from acts or threats of aggression or the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any country.

“8. Settlement of all international disputes by peaceful means, such as negotiation, conciliation, arbitration or judicial settlement as well as other peaceful means of the parties’ own choice, in conformity with the Charter of the United Nations.

“9. Promotion of mutual interests and cooperation.

“10. Respect for justice and international obligation.”

The 1955 Bandung communiqué concluded by expressing its conviction that friendly cooperation in accordance with the 10 Principles of Bandung would effectively   contribute to the maintenance and promotion of international peace and security,   while cooperation in the economic, social and   cultural   fields would   help   bring   about   the common prosperity and well-being of all.

**What has the Bandung spirit achieved in 60 years?**

In the six decades after the 1955 Bandung Conference that gave rise to the “Bandung Spirit” of South-South cooperation, decolonization has for the most part taken place, with most developing countries now independent. The basic principles of Bandung, namely, mutual interest, solidarity and respect for national sovereignty, continue to play important roles in shaping and guiding the relations of developing countries with each other. Developing countries have also joined the United Nations and actively developed different regional and multilateral South-South institutions to defend and promote their common interests in the various multilateral negotiating processes. The “Bandung Spirit” continues to animate and motivate the spirit of South-South cooperation, as can be seen in the fact that the recent 60th anniversary commemoration of the 1955 Bandung Conference saw over 100 developing countries from Asia, Africa, and Latin America participating.

More importantly, the 1955 Bandung Conference led to the establishment in 1961 of the **Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)**. This was followed by the establishment of the **Group of 77 (G77)** in 1964. These two multilateral groupings of the South together enable developing countries to actively voice and articulate their views and perspectives on political and economic issues, respectively, in the United Nations and other international arenas and to promote the unity and solidarity among the developing countries of the South in their common struggle for a fairer world. Other multilateral Southern institutions such as the South Centre (and its precursor the South Commission) can also trace their intellectual and political lineage to the 1955 Bandung Conference and the South-South spirit that it engendered.

Several regional initiatives which have taken shape in Africa, Asia, and Latin America in the past decades are also concrete reflections of the ideals of South-South cooperation and solidarity discussed in Bandung and adopted by leaders in the Final Communiqué. These include the African Union, the African continent’s primary vehicle for greater continental integration. In Latin America and the Caribbean, the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR) and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) are two newly established initiatives that are contributing to open a new era of integration among the countries of the regions and their representation in global affairs with greater independence. It is also the case of Asia, with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) among many other initiatives. The emergence of the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa) grouping itself, as well as recent projects such as the BRICS Development Bank and the Bank of the South are important examples of the vision of South-South cooperation from Bandung. These and many other developments that have taken place, and which continue to take place, in the developing world are all examples that point to the continuing relevance of the intellectual and political legacy of the 1955 Bandung Conference.

An international conference held in Bandung, Indonesia, on 18-24 April 1955, including representatives from 29 Asian and African countries. The purpose of the conference was to promote anti-colonialism and to discuss policies in light of the Cold War. Israel was not invited to the conference, due to the threat of boycott from Arab countries. The conference adopted a 10-point resolution echoing the UN Charter, resolved to support the Arabs in the Arab-Israeli conflict, and called on Israel to withdraw to the borders envisioned in the [Partition Plan](/issues/issue/102). The conference is considered a milestone in the creation of the Non-Aligned Movement.

args.summary: This webpage is a video description and transcript from the Research Society of International Law (RSIL) commemorating the 70th anniversary of the Bandung Conference of 1955. Held from 18-24 April 1955 in Bandung, Indonesia, the conference brought together leaders from 29 Asian and African nations in what was the largest gathering of its kind on Asian or African soil at the time. The conference took place against the backdrop of the Cold War and the surging post-war national liberation movements in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement, the concept of the "third world," and the Global South, advocating for an alternative form of just global governance and countering colonialism in all its forms. The conference produced the "Ten Principles of Bandung," a political statement outlining guiding principles for developing countries to promote peace and cooperation. These principles include: (1) respect for fundamental human rights and UN Charter purposes; (2) respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations; (3) recognition of equality of all races and nations, large and small; (4) abstention from intervention or interference in internal affairs of other countries; (5) respect for the right of each nation to defend itself in conformity with the UN Charter; (6) abstention from using collective defense arrangements for big power interests and from exerting pressures on other countries; (7) refraining from aggression or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence; (8) peaceful settlement of all disputes; (9) promotion of mutual interests and cooperation; and (10) respect for justice and international obligations. The video notes that in the decades following Bandung, friction among conference members increased as decolonization progressed, making the concept of Asian-African solidarity less meaningful. On its 70th anniversary, the content asks whether the principles remain relevant today, noting that while they are deeply under threat, their observance is needed more than ever amid rising global tensions. The video was posted on 25 February 2025 and has received 8,247 views.
args.key_excerpts: "The Bandung Conference set the stage for the Non-Aligned Movement and the rise of the Global South, advocating for self-determination, sovereignty, and global cooperation outside the influence of major powers."

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Gedung.Merdeka.jpg/250px-Gedung.Merdeka.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gedung.Merdeka.jpg)

The first large-scale **Asian–African** or **Afro–Asian Conference** ([Indonesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_language "Indonesian language"): *Konferensi Asia–Afrika*), also known as the **Bandung Conference**, was a meeting of Asian and African states, most of which were newly independent, which took place on 18–24 April 1955 in [Bandung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandung "Bandung"), [West Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Java "West Java"), Indonesia.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The twenty-nine countries that participated represented a total population of 1.5 billion people, 54% of the world's population.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The conference was organized by Indonesia, [Burma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-independence_Burma_(1948–1962) "Post-independence Burma (1948–1962)") (Myanmar), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Ceylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_Ceylon "Dominion of Ceylon") (Sri Lanka), and [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan "Dominion of Pakistan") and was coordinated by [Ruslan Abdulgani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruslan_Abdulgani "Ruslan Abdulgani"), secretary general of the [Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Indonesia) "Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Indonesia)").

The conference's stated aims were to promote [Afro-Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Asia "Afro-Asia") economic and cultural cooperation and to oppose [colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism") or [neocolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neocolonialism "Neocolonialism") by any nation. The conference was a step towards the eventual creation of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement") (NAM) yet the two initiatives ran in parallel during the 1960s, even coming in confrontation with one another prior to the [2nd Cairo NAM Conference in 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Summit_of_the_Non-Aligned_Movement "2nd Summit of the Non-Aligned Movement").[[3]](#cite_note-Bogetić-3)

In 2005, on the 50th anniversary of the original conference, leaders from Asian and African countries met in Jakarta and Bandung to launch the New Asian–African Strategic Partnership (NAASP). They pledged to promote political, economic, and cultural cooperation between the two continents.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

## Background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bandung_Conference&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

Indonesian President [Sukarno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukarno "Sukarno") and Indian Prime Minister [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru") were key organizers in their quest to build a nonaligned movement that would win the support of the newly emerging nations of Asia and Africa. Nehru first got the idea at the [Asian Relations Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Relations_Conference "Asian Relations Conference"), held in India in March 1947, on the eve of India's independence. There was a second 19-nation conference regarding the status of Indonesia, held in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi"), India, in January 1949. Although Nehru initially attached relatively little importance to Indonesia's calls to convene the Bandung Conference, he showed increasing interest during and after late 1954 due to his concern about American foreign policy as it applied to Asia, his belief that he could secure a guarantee of peaceful coexistence with China, and his desire to avoid embarrassing Indonesia.[[4]](#cite_note-4) [Decolonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization "Decolonization") was underway and an increasing number of new nations in Africa or Asia were emerging with, for the first time, their own diplomatic corps and need to integrate into the international system.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

[Chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party") [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") was also a key organizer, backed by his influential right-hand man, [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_China "Premier of China") and Foreign Minister [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai"). Mao believed that an anti-colonial nationalist and anti-imperialist agenda was underway in Africa and Asia, and he wanted to make China the leader of these forces.[[5]](#cite_note-maounknown-5) In his efforts to present China as a model, Mao publicly maintained a friendly, conciliatory tone towards newly independent Asian nations,[[6]](#cite_note-ShuGuangZhangColdWarHistory-6) while simultaneously denouncing the Western colonial empires.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

At the Colombo Powers conference in April 1954, Indonesia proposed a global conference. A planning group with the leaders of Indonesia, India, Pakistan, Burma, and Ceylon met in [Bogor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogor "Bogor"), West Java in late December 1954[[8]](#cite_note-8) and formally decided to hold the conference in April 1955. They had a series of goals in mind: to promote goodwill and cooperation among the new nations, to advance their mutual interests, to examine social economic and cultural problems, to focus on problems of special interest to their peoples such as racism and colonialism, and to enhance the international visibility of Asia and Africa in world affairs. As many of the participating countries were countries the USA and Soviet Union wanted to influence, they sought to establish a unified non-aligned identity and promote political solidarity independent of both Western and Soviet influence.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The Bandung Conference reflected what the organizers regarded as a reluctance by the Western powers to consult with them on decisions affecting Asia in a setting of [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") tensions: their concern over tension between the People's Republic of China and the United States, their desire to lay firmer foundations for China's peace relations with themselves and the West, their opposition to colonialism (especially [France's neocolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France's_neocolonialism "France's neocolonialism") in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa") and its colonial rule in [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria")), and Indonesia's desire to promote its case in the [West New Guinea dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_New_Guinea_dispute "West New Guinea dispute") with the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] One of Sukarno's primary goals with the conference was to build support for Indonesia's claim to West Papua and to prevent the Netherlands from transferring sovereignty of West Papua to indigenous Papuans.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Sukarno portrayed himself as the leader of this group of states, which he later described as "NEFOS" (Newly Emerging Forces).[[11]](#cite_note-11)

On 4 December 1954, the United Nations announced that Indonesia had successfully placed the issue of West New Guinea on the agenda of the 1955 General Assembly.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[*[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*] Plans for the Bandung conference were announced in December 1954.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

## Discussion

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Bandung_Conference&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Discussion")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Delegations_held_a_Plenary_Meeting_of_the_Economic_Section_during_the_A-A_Conference_in_Merdeka_Building%2C_Bandung%2C_on_April_20th_1955.jpg/250px-Delegations_held_a_Plenary_Meeting_of_the_Economic_Section_during_the_A-A_Conference_in_Merdeka_Building%2C_Bandung%2C_on_April_20th_1955.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Delegations_held_a_Plenary_Meeting_of_the_Economic_Section_during_the_A-A_Conference_in_Merdeka_Building,_Bandung,_on_April_20th_1955.jpg)

Delegations held a Plenary Meeting of the Economic Section during the Bandung Conference, April 1955.

Major debate centered on the question of whether [Soviet policies in Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_occupations "Soviet occupations") and Central Asia should be censured along with Western colonialism. A memo was submitted by 'The Moslem Nations under Soviet Imperialism', accusing the Soviet authorities of massacres and mass deportations in Muslim regions, but it was never debated.[[14]](#cite_note-Schindler-14) A consensus was reached in which "colonialism in all of its manifestations" was condemned, implicitly censuring the Soviet Union, as well as the West.[[15]](#cite_note-15) China played an important role in the conference and strengthened its relations with other Asian nations. Having survived [an assassination attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir_Princess "Kashmir Princess") on the way to the conference, the Chinese premier, [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai"), displayed a moderate and conciliatory attitude that tended to quiet fears of some anticommunist delegates concerning China's intentions.[*[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*]

Later in the conference, Zhou Enlai signed an [agreement on dual nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indonesian_Dual_Nationality_Treaty "Sino-Indonesian Dual Nationality Treaty") with Indonesian foreign minister [Sunario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunario "Sunario"). World observers closely watched Zhou. He downplayed revolutionary communism and strongly endorsed the right of all nations to choose their own economic and political systems, including even capitalism. His moderation and reasonableness made a very powerful impression for his own diplomatic reputation and for China.[*[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*] By contrast, Nehru was bitterly disappointed at the generally negative reception he received. Nehru mainly advocated for non-alignment, The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and cautioned against military alliances with either side of the Cold War. Senior diplomats called him arrogant.[*[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*] Zhou said privately, "I have never met a more arrogant man than Mr. Nehru."[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)

China began voicing [support for Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China–Palestine_relations "China–Palestine relations") at Bandung, with Zhou stating, "[T]here was a parallel between the problems of Palestine and Formosa; neither could be solved peacefully unless intervention by outside forces was excluded; China was suffering from the same problem as the Arab countries."[[20]](#cite_note-:02-20): 61
