# 2. Coloniality and Decoloniality in the Global South Higher-Education Context

© 2022 Carmen Martinez-Vargas, CC BY-NC-ND <https://doi.org/10.11647/OBP.0273.02>

> Universities have embraced or preached transformation and integration policies. These are unseen or even unheard of for many students within universities. They feel prejudiced because of certain actions portrayed by universities and other students different from them.

> In January 2012, Thabang Makhoang from North-West University in Potchefstroom drowned in the campus swimming pool in what was alleged to be initiation activities. Instructions were in Afrikaans and it is said that he did not understand them well. The university claims that he had the option of saying yes or no to the activity, he might have agreed or not but the fear of isolation after not agreeing to the group activities was much higher than the fear of being unable to swim.

> Keith Arlow of St John’s College was alleged to have made racist remarks to pupils over an extended period of time. Despite being found guilty of serious misconduct, he was said to have remained, as the school stated that it is a result of mitigating factors.

> This problem has also occurred at the University of the Free State where students and workers were harassed, violated and arrested for seeking the implementation of a presidential commission on in-sourcing.

> The alleged victim of racism at the University of Pretoria is a Kenyan national. In 2012, a black parent was killed in a stampede at the gates of the University of Johannesburg, where crowds of students had gathered in the quest to gain admission into this university.

> These are just a few of many incidents that have occurred and they have had huge impacts on people’s lives. It all goes back to the issue of racism, which occurs within South African universities. It simply shows how much has not changed as much as people say things have changed.

> Excerpt from *Narratives on Social Injustices: Undergraduate Voices*, the collaborative book by DCR members, 2018

## 2.1 Coloniality in the Global South

There is a significant body of knowledge highlighting the social, political and epistemological transition that old colonies need to overcome in order to liberate their communities and cultures (Mbembe 2001). Nowadays this process seems to be central for many scholars and grassroots movements, as many countries in the Global South, while having overcome territorial or political domination, have, however, not succeeded in some other important aspects, such as the social, economic or epistemological areas. This includes processes of knowledge generation as well as higher-education institutions in general (De Sousa Santos 2014; Dussel 2007; Mignolo 2007).

In brief, since the fifteenth century, colonialism and imperialism have played a major role in the Western conquest of other nations and the expansion of Western power across the world (Parra-Romero 2016). Mignolo (2010; 2007) conceptualises this Western idea as the North Atlantic block, arguing that the Western space has been historically repositioned to the geographical point of the North Atlantic, which represents the domination of a European-American system. Furthermore, for post-colonial scholars, this phenomenon, as stated above, goes beyond the initial colonial aim of conquering territory; it is a political and intellectual invasion and exploitation of other cultures (Chilisa 2012; Wa Thiong’o 1986). Chilisa (2012, 29) states that colonialism was ‘a brutal process through which two-thirds of the world experienced invasion and loss of territory accompanied by the distribution of political, social, and economic systems, leading to external political control and economic dependence on the West’. For Chilisa, this power over territories accelerated not only the loss of territory but the loss of local knowledge systems, cosmovisions,[1](ch2.xhtml#footnote-004) and beliefs. Further, Wa Thiong’o (1986) supports a similar perspective, stating that it was a psychic and mental conquest, appropriating the wealth of other societies, their territories, and goods, thus establishing a colonised universe in which culture, institutions, languages and social and political systems are imposed as a unique and hegemonic world paradigm.

For post-colonial scholars, the colonial question remains a present and urgent issue. Wa Thiong’o (1986) uses the term ‘neocolonies’ to refer to the current situation of domination and injustices maintained through cultural and political constraints, such as colonial language and identity formation in the Global South. On the other hand, Mbembe (2001; 2015) names this state of affairs ‘postcolony’, referring to present colonial spaces which continue to sustain identity assimilation under a ‘regime of violence’ (1992, 3). Appiah (1993) and Wa Thiong’o (1986) use the term ‘neocolonial territory’, where identities are constructed through the codes of the coloniser, using their languages and admiring their historical figures as tools to construct a single, exceptional, valid history.

In brief, for many of these scholars, what is currently problematic is the maintenance of this system of domination, which is not colonial per se, but preserves dominant colonial elements across the world, especially in the academic field and the ways in which scholars produce knowledge and understand reality (Smith 1999). This Eurocentric domination is related to the onto-epistemological challenges highlighting the need to understand and critically analyse epistemic inequalities, which dominate in present-day higher-education institutions.

## 2.2 Deciphering the Global North Codes

The onto-epistemological challenges can be summed up by two demands: the universal ontological claim of Western sciences by Castro-Gomez (cited in Soldatenko 2015) and epistemic killing—epistemicide—by De Sousa Santos (De Sousa Santos 2014). Both critiques are substantial in order to understand the decolonial debate and the proposals for social justice and democratisation of knowledge in higher-education institutions. Firstly, these two colonial challenges perpetuate colonisation as a way to sustain hegemony (Escobar 2007). Hegemony is here conceptualised as a dominant system that establishes and balances two dimensions—‘the good life’ and ‘the valid life’—inadvertently imposing them on everyone (Dussel 2007; Joseph 2002). These two dimensions represent a normative position, which is culturally related and attached to a clear Western colonial, and subsequently capitalist, tradition that conceptualises reality (the ontological position), whilst understanding knowledge creation and its use in a particular way (the epistemic system).

Firstly, the ontological narrowness is based on a Western conceptualisation of reality as universal, which is incapable of understanding its own positionality. This idea is called ‘zero-point’ by Castro-Gomez and explained by Soldatenko (2015) as an ‘imaginary position of objective neutrality that enlightenment science took for itself by displacing other epistemic frameworks in the colonial world as primitive, irrational and religious’ (Soldatenko 2015, 140). To a certain extent, this Western tradition conceptualises nature as detached from individuals and assumes a universal, disembodied reality (Mignolo 2007). This stands in contrast with other perspectives such as, for instance, those of Indigenous communities who regard nature and human beings as deeply interconnected (Smith 1999). Hence, the problem itself is not this particular positionality, which is as valid as any other, but its imposition on others due to its self-proclaimed status as the only objective perception and investigations of our reality as human beings, despite our cultural and cosmological differences. Therefore, this critique is based on the influence of the unquestioned universality and superiority of Western ontological positions. Further, as Mignolo and Walsh (2018) recently argued, this ontology is, in itself, a Western and Eurocentric term, as it assumes that objects and subjects create reality instead of knowledge. Mignolo and Walsh (2018) clarify that in order to find a more accurate terminology, we will need to think about cosmologies instead of ontologies, as the former are able to overcome the limitation of meaning to objects, despite having other cultures that attach meaning to relationalities.

On the other hand, ontological or cosmological domination is linked to the epistemological challenge because, as Mignolo and Walsh confirm, ‘ontology is an epistemological concept’ (2018, 135). Hence, the imposition of Western ontology as superior also sustains a particular way of understanding the nature of knowledge and the processes in which it is produced, thus maintaining a hegemonic epistemological system. This issue has been named ‘epistemological blindness’ by Hlela (2018) or ‘epistemicide’ by De Sousa Santos (2014). Both terms refer to the destruction or invisibility of other knowledge systems due to the ‘universal’ perception of the Western epistemological canon as superior (De Sousa Santos 2014) or the inability to recognise other knowledge systems as valid (Hlela 2018). For instance, one example broadly referred to in the literature is the fact that Indigenous people need to validate their knowledge as rigorous, and therefore universal, by means of scientific procedures (Cooper & Morrell 2014). As Berenstain (2016, 571) clearly states:

> This creates a burden on the marginalised to educate and enlighten. Though the privileged demand the epistemic labour of the marginalised, they often perpetuate epistemic oppression by dismissing the knowledge produced. The marginalised are excluded from the realm of recognised knowledge creators despite contributing novel conceptual resources and epistemic frameworks.

Hence, epistemic oppressions highlight how hegemonic epistemic perspectives have narrowed the richness of human knowledge and wisdom beyond the Western epistemic system (Zibechi 2015).

Furthermore, these scholars do not deny the importance of Western thought or its philosophical tradition, conversely; they believe that this tradition is rich and has generated valuable knowledge, from other cultures and civilisations too (Dussel 2007; Mignolo 2007). Their issue lies in the fact that this system does not understand its own superior positionality and does not allow for a space in which knowledge could be considered or produced differently (De Sousa Santos 2014). Therefore, these cosmological and epistemological gaps provide the foundation for alternative pathways towards decoloniality, from a Global South perspective, that these scholars articulate.[2](ch2.xhtml#footnote-003) Moreover, as higher education is the central interest of this book, the following section will explore universities with a particular decolonial project for social justice through the use of participatory research practices and its role in these debates.

## 2.3 Transforming Our ‘Uni-Versity’ into a ‘Pluri-Versity’

In light of the complexity outlined above, what the universal project, the hegemonic project, ignores is the diversity of perspectives (cosmologies) and knowledges (epistemic systems) beyond itself. Therefore, a group of scholars (Boidin, Cohen & Grosfoguel 2012; Dussel 2007; Mignolo 2007; Escobar 2018) have developed a perspective that provides the heterogeneous foundation needed to reverse these colonial challenges; this is called the ‘pluriverse’ project. This project aims to transform a uni-verse into a pluri-verse better capable of accommodating the diversity that has historically been excluded due to structures of domination. Although the pluriversal project is extensive and fertile, I will focus here on its educational derivative, the ‘pluriversity’, in order to understand the foundational ideas.

In this pluriversity model, the idea is to transform a monolithic university institution into a less provincial one (Boidin et al. 2012). In addition, in this project, the fight against epistemic coloniality is substantial for the transition to an academic model which is capable of challenging academic knowledge production and practice (Tamdgidi 2012).

In this matter, the concept of an ‘ecology of knowledges’—epistemic multiplicity—coined by De Sousa Santos (2014) is helpful for understanding the equal relevance of different knowledge systems and the possibility of bringing them together as a way of cooperation. De Sousa Santos (2010; 2014) asserts that every knowledge system is incomplete, due to its own internal and external limitations. Therefore, the incompleteness of all knowledge systems—including the Western epistemic system—necessitates an epistemological dialogue between them, which is called an ecology of knowledges. When scholars are able to interrogate their knowledge system and bring it into conversation with others, an ecology of knowledges is stimulated, and this is a necessary condition in promoting a pluriversity. Thus, this is a way to include Southern perspectives long ignored by the Global North.

The pertinent questions are: what are universities currently doing to challenge these colonial issues, and how can these strategies be improved or reformulated, if necessary? Do we decide to propose a solution ‘within’ or ‘outside’ our higher-education institutions? Is it even possible to achieve a decolonial project in the Western higher-education system?

This book seeks to conduct an internal analysis of what higher-education institutions are doing so far, and how these practices, specifically participatory practices, can be improved and stimulated by new theoretical insights, bringing methodological plurality into our research processes from a Southern perspective. However, before analysing and assessing different participatory practices, it is necessary to investigate how, if at all, participatory approaches are aligned with decolonial debates.

## 2.4 Participatory Approaches in the Twenty-First Century: A Decolonial Intention

Certainly, participatory approaches are related to certain values of togetherness, democracy, inclusion, heterogeneity and social justice, which are strongly represented in many categories such as Participatory Action Research, Participatory Research, Educational Action Research or Community Based Action Research, among others. These discourses are especially visible within the Action Research family, which, despite being part of the industrial strand, and the more conventional line of practices, nowadays embraces all participatory typologies. Hence, scholars tend to refer to many participatory practices as Action Research. For example, we may consider the many handbooks exploring different participatory practices that use Action Research in their titles, such as *The Palgrave International Handbook of Action Research* (2017). Further, these handbooks tend to claim decolonial aims in different ways and among different families of participatory approaches. One of the latest compilations about the diverse practices of AR claims in its preface:

> We believe Action Research has a crucial role to play in the work of creating, an ‘alternative globalisation’ that counters the standard view being propagated by those whose interest lies in maintaining the status quo of colonial domination largely by the global North at the expense of the peoples, cultures, resources, and epistemologies of the global South. (Rowell et al. 2017, xii)

Equally, they state that ‘[they] represent efforts to push against various forms of colonisation of hearts and minds’ (Rowell et al. 2017, xii). *The SAGE Handbook of* *Action Research* (2008), another reference for AR practitioners, states:

> Most of us educated within the Western paradigm have inherited a broadly ‘Cartesian’ worldview, which channels our thinking in significant ways. It tells us the world is made of separate things […] and it tells us that mind and physical reality are separate […] This split between humanity and nature, and the abrogation of all mind to humans, is what Weber meant by the disenchantment of the world. As Fals Borda has put it, participation is one way through which we may ‘re-enchant’ our plural world. (Reason & Bradbury 2008, 8)

These works incisively expose the Western worldview, calling for a shift towards a more plural world. This is especially relevant for many of the decolonial arguments, which acknowledge the colonial imposition of reason over tradition in modern Cartesian thinking as a Western creation, and emphasise its perpetuation through imperialism. This is why they confirm that:

> Action Research without its liberating and emancipatory dimension is a shadow of its full possibility and will be in danger of being co-opted by the status quo. (Reason & Bradbury 2008, 5)

Thus, despite the diversity of practice within participatory approaches, current discourses of AR sustain and support the use of these practices as a way to move towards decoloniality. Further, the role of epistemic justice is central to this debate. These AR-focused handbooks expose the invisibility of other knowledge systems that are dominated by the technocratic and objectivist perspectives sustained by a hegemonic academic system. Additionally, the same book, in its most recent edition published in 2015 (Bradbury 2015), maintains similar ideas:

> While our theoretical groundings are informed by the post-modernist deconstructing of classical theorising, which privileged the objective observer with his ostensibly value-free language and logical deduction/generalisation, we also know that criticism is not enough. (Bradbury 2015, 3)

Hence:

> When action researchers think of epistemology, we understand the impoverishment of having only the objective voice of conventional social science. We are called to consider how multiple epistemological voices can be better integrated to serve our inquiry and our co-inquirers. (Bradbury 2015, 4)

And finally, the Educational Action Research Family pursues these critiques eloquently, expressing that AR aims to:

> Promote decolonisation of lifeworld that has become saturated with bureaucratic discourses, routinised practices and institutionalised forms of social relationships. (Kemmis, McTaggart & Nixon 2013, 12)

Therefore, the democratisation of knowledge, epistemic justice, and the promotion of a pluriversal world, or justice as a whole, are all examples of the challenges that the diverse and extended family of participatory approaches is aiming to overcome. Nevertheless, to critically engage with these practices, we need to analyse them and understand that not all practices and approaches might be directed to decolonise or democratise research in the way this book defends. Thus, [the following chapter](ch3.xhtml#_idTextAnchor009) aims to clarify different traditions and goals within participatory research to uncover Western homogenising tendencies and their consequences. Doing so, we are able to highlight the pitfalls and shortcomings and advance towards decolonisation and social justice more broadly, whilst also defining an innovative participatory practice.

<webpage_content>
# Decolonization: Rethinking the coloniality of power, knowledge and being｜Webinar
## University of Calgary
13100 subscribers
56 likes

### Description
3559 views
Posted: 22 Oct 2021
The Courageous Conversations Speaker Series hosted by the Office of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion presents: 

Decolonization: Rethinking the coloniality of power, knowledge and being. This second event in the Decolonization and Questions of Justice in the University series featured Dr. Ndlovu-Gatsheni and Dr. Altamirano-Jiménez who explored theories and practices of decolonization, knowledge production in the contemporary university, and the rhetorics of liberation and freedom across time and space.

Beginning with the contemporary politics of knowledge, Dr. Ndlovu-Gatsheni examined several interrelated themes: the need for a critical reflection on the grammars of liberation; decolonial “turns” in a long struggle for liberation; the African experience with decolonization of knowledge; and, finally, conclude with a focus on the resurgent and insurgent decolonization of the 21st century. In examining decolonization beyond the English-speaking world, Dr. Altamirano-Jiménez explored knowledge production, thinking feeling and interculturality; decoloniality and its discontents; decolonization in relation to land, body and Indigenous freedom; and, finally, concluded with a discussion of thinking-feeling-doing Indigenous futures.

Dr. Malinda Smith, vice-provost (Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion) hosted and moderated the questions from the audience. 

About the Speakers

Dr. Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni is Professor and Chair of Epistemologies of the Global South at the University of Bayreuth in Germany. His various publications include: Decolonizing the University: Knowledge Systems and Disciplines in Africa, coedited with Siphamandla Zondi (2016), Decolonization, Development and Knowledge in Africa: Turning Over A New Leaf (2020). 

Isabel Altamirano-Jiménez is Binizaá (Zapotec) from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico and Professor of Political Science. She was appointed Canada Research Chair in Comparative Indigenous Feminist Studies in 2017. Among her books are Indigenous Encounters with Neoliberalism. Place, Women and the Environment (2013), Living on the Land. Indigenous Women’s Understandings of Place edited with Kermoal (2016).

This webpage documents a webinar from the University of Calgary's "Courageous Conversations Speaker Series" (2020-2021-2022 theme: "Decolonization and Questions of Justice in the Academy"), hosted by the Office of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion. The second event, "Decolonization: Rethinking the coloniality of power, knowledge and being," was posted on 22 Oct 2021 and featured two internationally renowned scholars.

**Host and Moderator:** Dr. Malinda Smith, Vice-Provost and Associate Vice President Research for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion at the University of Calgary.

**Speakers:**
1. **Dr. Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni** – Professor and Chair of Epistemologies of the Global South at the University of Bayreuth, Germany. His publications include *Decolonizing the University: Knowledge Systems and Disciplines in Africa* (coedited with Siphamandla Zondi, 2016) and *Decolonization, Development and Knowledge in Africa: Turning Over A New Leaf* (2020). He previously worked as a research professor at the University of South Africa.
2. **Dr. Isabel Altamirano-Jiménez** – Binizaá (Zapotec) from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico; Professor of Political Science and Canada Research Chair in Comparative Indigenous Feminist Studies at the University of Alberta. Her books include *Indigenous Encounters with Neoliberalism* (2013) and *Living on the Land: Indigenous Women's Understandings of Place* (coedited with Kermoal, 2016).

**Key Themes from Dr. Ndlovu-Gatsheni's presentation:**
- We are living in a moment of "epistemological turbulence" and "uncertainties of knowledges" where certitudes from the colonizer's model of the world are being exposed.
- Basic epistemological questions have been reopened: the relationship between identity and knowledge, whether knowledge has a geography (geopolitics of knowledge), and the biography/body politics of knowledge.
- The "cognitive empire" is responsible for most problems of the modern world—it invades people's mental universes and makes them think against themselves, their knowledges, histories, and cultures.
- Coloniality operates on three interconnected levels: coloniality of being (social/racial/gender classification creating an "invisible social pyramid" that determines who is considered fully human), coloniality of power (governing through modern colonial power structures that hierarchize languages, gender, beauty), and coloniality of knowledge (a "global economy of knowledge" underpinned by an uneven intellectual division of labor where "international" journals mean North American or European ones).
- Various "grammars of liberation" have been attempted: deracialization (critiqued for often only changing demographics, not structures), Africanization (1960s, enabling Africans to assume positions of authority, but often lacking structural/institutional change), indigenization (economy-related in Africa), plus social inclusion, diversification, abolition, and reparations.
- Decolonial "turns" include nationalistic, Marxist, post-colonial, and gender turns; the language of decolonization emerges from "the battlefields of history" (e.g., Amilcar Cabral, Frantz Fanon, Kwame Nkrumah), not classrooms, and its "imperfection is its power."
- Decolonization is embraced by Indigenous peoples' movements, feminist movements, ecological struggles, students, and academics, and is not a singular concept.

**Key Themes from Dr. Altamirano-Jiménez's presentation:**
- Approached from an Indigenous (specifically Zapotec) perspective, asking what it means to include experiences of dispossessed bodies "without centering land itself."
- Distinguished between colonialism (historical phenomenon) and coloniality (the ongoing context/outcome in which we all reside despite decolonization movements).
- Coloniality and Western domination have silenced Indigenous and local knowledges, instituting a theological reading of history that assumes Western civilization is the pinnacle of progress.
- Decoloniality is a political project challenging Eurocentric epistemological foundations, reclaiming non-Western ontologies, and imagining "that other worlds are possible" (Subcomandante Marcos, Zapatista movement).
- Introduced the concept of "internal colonialism" (following Mexican sociologist Pablo González Casanova), showing that Indigenous peoples in newly independent Latin American states remained in the same or worse colonial relations of domination.
- Argued that ongoing Indigenous dispossession must be central to any post-colonial accounts; decolonization is an "embodied movement," not just cognitive or semantic.
- Emphasized *sentir y pensar* ("thinking from the heart"), a way of knowing that is practical, not just theoretical.
- Connected the Zapotec concepts of *ombligo* (belly button) and *obligación* (obligation): obligation is a course of responsible action arising from being interconnected with each other and the non-human world. Knowledge requires "making relatives" and relationality that includes water, land, wind, and animals (expanding beyond human-centric relations per Melanie Yazzie).
- Warned against appropriation in academic settings when engaging colonized knowledge systems without obligation, and against reproducing Eurocentric hierarchies in citation and writing practices.
- Described the "University of Communality" project in Oaxaca/Tehuantepec isthmus, which enacts higher education as a communal responsibility, honoring communal practices, languages, values, and governance structures of Indigenous communities.
- Expressed concern about universities moving toward commercialization of knowledge where "objective" knowledge is valued by its ability to make profits.

**Opening segments:**
- Elder Colleen Sitting Eagle (Sipiyana'tokumiyaki), a Siksika language instructor and elder for the series, opened with a blessing in her language, sharing about the power of Indigenous people to fight battles (residential schools, current addictions crisis in Siksika), and promoting language and cultural preservation. She noted the Indigenous bishop for Canada is Bishop Sydney Black from Six Nations.
- Dr. Smith highlighted two inspirations: Violet King (Calgary-born first Black woman lawyer in Canada, who refused limits placed on her) and Maya Angelou ("courage is the most important of all virtues, because without courage, we can't practice any other virtue consistently").
- The session cited Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's idea that "decolonization is not a metaphor," and discussed prefixes (post-, neo-, decolonial), knowledge production in universities, curriculum and citational practices, and shifting from university to "pluri-university."

**Discussion:**
- Q&A addressed that decolonial thinking comes from battlefields, not classrooms, and that knowledge production is disconnected from land, place, and territories; the connection between degradation of a people's humanity and inability to achieve epistemic freedom was emphasized.
args.key_excerpts: "We are living at a moment when there is actually turmoil in the contestation in the world of knowledge... This turmoil and contestation in the world of knowledge has implications for our lives as human beings and before our survival." — Dr. Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni

Idea

# Towards an epistemological alliance for the decolonization of knowledge of the global South and the global North

"The future of education and human and planetary sustainability are inconceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the global North and those of the global South"

12 April 2021

Last update:7 July 2023

![Diversity and work inclusion](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2023-07/iStock.jpg.webp?itok=AfT624fy)

© iStock / Angelina Bambina

by **Obrillant Damus**

Social, cultural and scientific practices in the twenty-first century should not be areas where local knowledge is sacrificed on the altar of Western scientific rigour, but rather spaces that encourage a respectful and fruitful dialogue between knowledge holders from the global North and knowledge holders from the global South (with a mutually emancipatory aim). Learning to be or to become means opening up to epistemological diversity in order to develop our human potential in a sustainable and multidirectional way. It is essential to think, within the limits of a transgressive and emancipatory pedagogy, about the practical modalities of an alliance between the epistemologies of the global North and those of the global South to promote the futures of education.   
  
  
  
The monocultural educational paradigm is like a steamroller that crushes local knowledge in its multiple dimensions (technical, symbolic, magical, religious, relational, rational...) that appear irrational or residual, while much of this knowledge plays a very important role in human and planetary sustainability. If schools and societies of the future are to diminish the conscious and unconscious practices of destruction of local and indigenous knowledge in the global South and global North, they must invite the holders of this knowledge to teach and use it without constraint, in order to strengthen its resilience and optimize its transmission to present and future generations. Valuing the diversity of knowledge, ontologies, historical paths, temporalities, human cultures, languages, world views, ways of thinking and acting will allow the education of the future to confront monocultural violence. The education systems of the future should be based on an ecology of knowledge, in the sense that they are called upon to link the knowledge of the global South and the knowledge of the global North with a view to producing allocentric, place-centric and planet-centric humans capable of grasping dialectical units in the kaleidoscopic flow of human and natural facts.   
  
  
  
The products of Western and Western-centric education systems generally view the poor lacking in revenue in the global North and global South as also lacking in thought. Based on the dichotomy between knowers and non-knowers or between scholars and believers, these educational systems consciously and unconsciously promote socio-epistemic separation to the detriment of the epistemological mutual aid necessary for human survival. This age-old attitude is a hindrance to the hybridization of knowledge, which better reflects the complexity of human life. By excluding the language (symbolic linguicide ) of local knowledge holders and modes of knowledge production that do not coincide with the epistemology of the global North, formal educational processes, of which the monoculture of scientific knowledge is the substratum, lead to immeasurable cognitive losses in all fields of activity. The integration of local knowledge holders into formal education will lead to the co-construction of new knowledge and mutual correction between the knowledge of the global South and the knowledge of the global North, which will undoubtedly enrich science as a work of humanity.  
  
  
  
The integration of local and indigenous knowledge holders into mainstream education will not be achieved without the use of local idioms. The use of ancestral languages in formerly colonized countries as the main vehicles of instruction will bring about intellectual liberation and autonomy, critical thinking, a sense of linguistic security, and the development of cognitive and metacognitive skills, all of which are essential to the process of knowledge production. Inequalities in the mastery of one or more "world" languages create an abyssal line between the global South and the global North in the field of knowledge production. Despite efforts to reform and develop many of them, local languages are still considered within many States as instruments unsuited to abstraction or modern science. However, it is necessary to make these languages teaching vehicles for an emancipating multicultural education and sustainable development.   
  
  
  
Local and indigenous knowledge systems are not only associated with human sustainability but also with planetary sustainability by enabling communities to participate in conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity and ecosystems. The integration of local knowledge into primary, secondary and university curricula will enable educational institutions of the future to reduce auto-epistemicide (local knowledge disappears on its own because it is not valued or used, especially by young people), endo-epistemic practices (many actors from Western-centred education systems, as well as several holders of ancestral knowledge such as Haitian midwives and African and Andean-Amazonian traditional doctors, cease to use some local knowledge) and exo-epistemic practices (Western-centred intervention is causing the rapid disappearance of much local knowledge and know-how that was previously effective, both consciously and unconsciously; the destruction of traditional technical knowledge can be referred to as technocide).

The future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South.

One of the main aims of the education of the future is to remove unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational...), on the human and planetary level, by forming cosmocentric (versus egocentric) beings capable of grasping dialectical units, human and natural occurrences through the filter of an interdisciplinary language. They will be able to harmonise their interests with those of others, giving more meaning to the idea of living together and connected living (relational universalism; universal brotherhood) than to living for oneself (destructive egocentrism). If we want the current model of economic and social development to become less antinomic with human and planetary sustainability, we need to base the future of education on systems of knowledge, know-how and savoir-être derived from multiple anthropic practices between which all relations of scientific subordination and oppression must be excluded (ecology of paradigms, ontologies, temporalities and practices). If the educational institutions of the future cease to be places where local and indigenous knowledge is sacrificed on the altar of Western scientific rigour, but rather spaces that encourage a respectful and fruitful dialogue between the holders of knowledge from the North and the possessors of knowledge from the South (co-emancipatory aim), exo and endo-epistemic practices will be reduced in the southern hemisphere. The future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South.

The ideas expressed here are those of the authors; they are not necessarily the official position of UNESCO and do not commit the Organization.

**Obrillant Damus** is a socio-anthropologist, linguist, educator and professor at the Université d'État d'Haiti and the Université Quisqueya. He is also an associate professor at the University of Shebrooke (Centre d’études du religieux contemporain). Additional note: This article is based on a [background paper](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000374047) prepared for the International Commission on the Futures of Education.

args.summary: This UNESCO "Idea" article, written by Obrillant Damus (socio-anthropologist, linguist, educator, and professor at the Université d'État d'Haiti, Université Quisqueya, and the University of Shebrooke), was published on 12 April 2021 and argues for a constructive epistemological alliance between the global North and global South to decolonize knowledge and shape the future of education. Damus contends that the monocultural educational paradigm "crushes local knowledge" in its multiple dimensions and promotes socio-epistemic separation that hinders the hybridization of knowledge essential for human survival. He advocates for integrating local and indigenous knowledge holders into formal education systems, using ancestral/local languages as vehicles of instruction in formerly colonized countries to achieve "intellectual liberation and autonomy," and building education on an "ecology of knowledge" that links Southern and Northern epistemologies. The article describes three harmful phenomena to address: auto-epistemicide (local knowledge disappearing because it is not valued, especially by youth), endo-epistemic practices (actors abandoning local knowledge), and exo-epistemic practices (Western-centred intervention causing disappearance of local knowledge, with destruction of traditional technical knowledge termed "technocide"). Damus argues that local and indigenous knowledge systems are crucial not only for human sustainability but also for planetary sustainability through biodiversity conservation. He calls for education that forms "cosmocentric (versus egocentric)" beings capable of overcoming unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational) and emphasizes that "the future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South." The article is based on a background paper prepared for the International Commission on the Futures of Education, and the ideas expressed are those of the author, not necessarily the official position of UNESCO.
args.key_excerpts: "The future of education and human and planetary sustainability are inconceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the global North and those of the global South", "The monocultural educational paradigm is like a steamroller that crushes local knowledge in its multiple dimensions (technical, symbolic, magical, religious, relational, rational...) that appear irrational or residual, while much of this knowledge plays a very important role in human and planetary sustainability.", "The use of ancestral languages in formerly colonized countries as the main vehicles of instruction will bring about intellectual liberation and autonomy, critical thinking, a sense of linguistic security, and the development of cognitive and metacognitive skills, all of which are essential to the process of knowledge production.", "One of the main aims of the education of the future is to remove unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational...), on the human and planetary level, by forming cosmocentric (versus egocentric) beings capable of grasping dialectical units.", "The future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South."

This is a Facebook post from the page "Black HistoryStudies" (dated April 16, likely 2026), which presents an educational graphic explaining the concept of "Coloniality of Knowledge." The post defines this concept as first introduced by Aníbal Quijano and expanded by scholars including Walter Mignolo and Dr. Sabelo Ndlovu-Gatsheni, describing how Eurocentric worldviews continue to dominate global knowledge systems.

The graphic highlights five interwoven mechanisms of Eurocentric Hegemony:
1. **Epistemicide** – the killing, destruction, and erasure of non-Western knowledge systems, replaced by colonial knowledge systems (attributed to Boaventura de Sousa Santos).
2. **Linguicide** – the killing or suppression of languages, popularized by Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and expanded by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o in "Decolonising the Mind," showing how linguistic domination serves cultural erasure.
3. **Cognitive Imperialism** – the imposition of Western thought as the universal standard (attributed to Marie Battiste).
4. **Hermeneutical Injustice** – structural gaps in interpretive resources that disadvantage marginalized groups (attributed to Miranda Fricker).
5. **Cultural Imperialism** – the domination of culture and imagination through language and power (attributed to Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o).

The post argues that together these forces uphold the Coloniality of Knowledge, and that decolonization involves reclaiming suppressed epistemologies and centering Africentric and Indigenous ways of knowing. It is described as rooted in Africentric and decolonial scholarship, shared to educate and invite critical reflection, with the statement that "truth precedes reconciliation." The post is credited to @ubuntucentredpractice and wellnessEmpowered.com. One commenter (Amanda Sutton) noted the utility of having words to describe these concepts.

--- SOURCE 1: Latin American Dependency Theory | Global South Studies ---
URL: https://www.globalsouthstudies.org/keyword-essay/latin-american-dependency-theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This essay by Steven Schmidt (January 21, 2018, Global South Studies) traces the intellectual history of Latin American Dependency Theory, a political-economic school of thought that emerged from the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) shortly after World War II. Key scholars include Raúl Prebisch, Fernando Cardoso, Enrique Faletto, and Andre Gunder Frank, with later influence on world-systems analysis by Immanuel Wallerstein, Giovanni Arrighi, and Christopher Chase-Dunn.

Dependency theory argues that under-development in Latin America is the direct result of capital intervention and global economic forces, not a "lack" of development. It emerged as a response to modernization theory (associated with economist William Rostow's five stages of economic growth), which dependency theorists rejected as a false dichotomy between "traditional" and "modern" societies.

Central to the theory is the Prebisch-Singer thesis, developed by Prebisch (former Argentine chief trade diplomat) and UN economist Hans Singer, which demonstrated through trade data that an imbalance in terms of trade caused a constant flow of capital out of Latin America—as the region exported primary goods (food, lumber, minerals) while re-importing higher-value manufactured products from the Global North, creating a perpetual trade deficit.

The theory split into two camps: (1) liberal reformers like Prebisch, Cardoso, and Faletto, who advocated for import-substitution industrialization (ISI) and protectionist policies to develop domestic markets; and (2) neo-Marxists like Gunder Frank, who argued dependency could only be escaped through socialism and challenging the capitalist mode of production. A further offshoot was world-systems analysis (Wallerstein, Amin, Frank).

During the 1940s-1950s, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile adopted ISI policies, but debt crises in the 1980s led the World Bank and IMF to impose structural adjustment programs (SAPs), which dismantled these protections. While dependency theory is no longer widely applied as policy, its core insights remain valuable: understanding how global capital flows structure development disparities, challenging assumptions that Latin American economies are "feudal and backwards," that modernity equals industrialization, and that all nations can equally pass through development "stages." The theory laid groundwork for research on the international division of labor, commodity chains, and global cities (Sassen 1991).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory argues that under-development as experienced in Latin America and elsewhere is the direct result of capital intervention, rather than a condition of 'lacking' development or investment."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Dependency theory - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependency_theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikipedia article on Dependency theory, an international relations theory within the broader frameworks of imperialism studies and Marxist international relations theory. 

**Core concept:** Dependency theory posits that resources flow from a "periphery" of poor, exploited states to a "core" of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. The central contention is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by how poor states are integrated into the "world system." The theory was formally developed in the late 1940s following World War II as scholars sought to explain the lack of development in Latin America.

**Origins and History:** The theory arose as a reaction to modernization theory, which held that all societies progress through similar development stages. Dependency theory rejected this, arguing underdeveloped countries are not primitive versions of developed ones but have unique structures and are weaker members of the world market economy. The theory originated with two 1949 papers by Hans Singer and Raúl Prebisch, who observed deteriorating terms of trade for underdeveloped countries (the Prebisch–Singer thesis). Prebisch, an Argentine economist at the UN Commission for Latin America, advocated import-substitution industrialization (ISI) over export orientation. Paul A. Baran developed it from a Marxian perspective in 1957 with *The Political Economy of Growth*. Two main streams emerged: Latin American Structuralist (Prebisch, Celso Furtado, Aníbal Pinto) and American Marxist (Baran, Paul Sweezy, Andre Gunder Frank). The theory was popular in the 1960s-1970s as criticism of modernization theory. Walter Rodney's 1972 book *How Europe Underdeveloped Africa* applied it to Africa. Ruy Mauro Marini developed a specifically Marxist dependency theory focused on super-exploitation and unequal exchange. Fernando Henrique Cardoso (later Brazilian President 1995-2002) wrote extensively on dependency theory, developing the concept of "dependent development."

**Basic premises:** (1) Poor nations provide natural resources, cheap labor, destinations for obsolete technology, and markets for developed nations, without which the latter couldn't enjoy their standard of living; (2) Wealthy nations actively perpetuate dependence through economics, media control, politics, banking, finance, education, culture, and sport.

**Key concepts:** Baran placed surplus extraction and capital accumulation at the center of analysis, arguing that surplus in poor countries goes to luxury consumption rather than development investment. Latin American Structuralists argued for "dependent development" - partial development still controlled by outside decision-makers. Some argue the sine qua non of dependency is not technological difference but financial strength - particularly the inability of peripheral countries to borrow in their own currency, and US control of the international reserve currency (the dollar). Theotonio dos Santos described a "new dependency" based on Marxian analysis. The theory influenced world-systems theory developed by Immanuel Wallerstein, which added a third category of "semi-periphery" countries.

**Examples:** European colonization (1650-1900) of the Americas, Africa, and Asia, where wealth was transferred from colonized regions to Europe through control of materials, production, and distribution.

**Criticism:** India's economic improvement after moving to open trade is cited as evidence against the theory (though Indian economists Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik argue this may reflect a globalized reserve workforce). Import-substitution economies in Africa like Zimbabwe have performed poorly while trade-based economies like Egypt, South Africa, and Tunisia have succeeded. Economic historian Robert C. Allen argues dependency theory's claims are "debatable" because protectionism in Latin America failed, leading to excessive debt and recession, partly because national markets were too small to efficiently produce complex industrial goods.

**Other details:** The article also covers aid dependency, including instilling aid dependency, stunted economic growth, political dependency, corruption, and efforts to end aid dependency. Dependency theorists divide into liberal reformists (advocating targeted policy interventions) and neo-Marxists (proposing planned economies). The theory has lost influence with the growth of India and East Asian economies but still influences NGO campaigns like Make Poverty History and the fair trade movement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory is the idea that resources flow from a 'periphery' of poor and exploited states to a 'core' of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. A central contention of dependency theory is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by the way poor states are integrated into the 'world system.'"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Remembering Dependency Theory - New Politics ---
URL: https://newpol.org/issue_post/remembering-dependency-theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Marxist-Humanist review article by Edward L. Tapia, published in New Politics (Summer 2017, Vol. XVI No. 3, Whole Number 63), titled "Remembering Dependency Theory." The article argues that dependency theory—a set of anti-colonial and anti-imperialist theoretical schemas that emerged after World War II—failed to properly grasp Marx's concept of value because it remained fixated on exchange value rather than penetrating into the social relations of production and abstract labor, which Tapia identifies as the defining principle of capitalism.

Key arguments and content:

1. **Origins and schools of dependency theory**: The theory emerged from anti-colonial/anti-imperialist struggles in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It argued that global capitalist expansion generated development in core locations (Western Europe, North America, Japan) and underdevelopment in peripheral locations (Africa, Asia, Latin America). It spanned from the revolutionary socialist school (Andre Gunder Frank, Samir Amin, Theotonio dos Santos) to the bourgeois nationalist/social-democratic school (Arghiri Emmanuel, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Enzo Faletto).

2. **Unequal exchange theory**: Dependency theorists relied on the Prebisch-Singer thesis, arguing primary commodity prices secularly fall relative to manufactured goods. They followed Ricardian theory of value, assuming commodities exchange at value and international equalization of profit rates, whereas Marx showed prices of production deviate from value due to abstract/socially necessary labor-time.

3. **Marx's counter-argument**: Marx demonstrated that advanced countries with higher organic composition of capital sell at prices of production above their value, exploiting less-advanced countries. Key quotes from Theories of Surplus Value, Grundrisse, and Capital Vol. III illustrate this—including Marx's statement that "three days of labor of one country can be exchanged against one of another country" and that "the richer country exploits the poorer one, even where the latter gains by the exchange."

4. **Industrialization and delinking strategies**: Two divergent theses emerged: "associated dependent development" (Cardoso and Faletto, involving semi-peripheral industrialization with international/local capital alliances) and "development of underdevelopment" (Frank). Both advocated "delinking"—either as mercantilist strategy to re-enter the world market later, or as disassociation toward socialism.

5. **Critique of delinking**: Tapia argues delinking fails because it addresses distribution rather than abstract value production, and socially necessary labor-time continues operating in national contexts. He cites Raya Dunayevskaya's Philosophy and Revolution on the whole human being and the persistence of the law of value.

6. **Failure of dependency theory**: It failed to anticipate the "new industrial division of labor" exemplified by the East Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan) in the 1970s. The article discusses John Smith's Imperialism in the 21st Century on globalization of production (foreign direct investment and "arm's length outsourcing"), noting the global economically active population grew from 1.9 billion (1980) to 3.1 billion (2006), a 63% increase. Tapia criticizes Smith's "super-exploitation" theory as an inadequate basis for understanding imperialism, siding with Michael Roberts that exploitation is determined by the ratio of surplus value to the value of labor power.

7. **Conclusion**: Tapia calls on today's revolutionary activists to choose between building freely associated human relations that negate the law of value, or repeating the "old illusions of past socialist experiments." He cites the fates of dependency theorists—Cardoso became a neoliberal Brazilian president, Amin remained a self-declared Maoist, and Frank argued capitalism and socialism never existed.

The article includes a substantial bibliography of works by Amin, Anderson, Birkan, Carchedi, Roberts, Cardoso/Faletto, Dunayevskaya, Evans, Frank, Grossman, Hudis, Marx, Pieterse, Pradella, and Smith.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Three days of labor of one country can be exchanged against one of another country. … Here the law of value undergoes essential modification. … The relationship between labor days of different countries may be similar to that existing between skilled, complex labor and unskilled, simple labor within a country. In this case, the richer country exploits the poorer one, even where the latter gains by the exchange." — Marx, Theories of Surplus Value
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Key Arguments of Dependency Theory: Understanding Economic Exploitation • PolSci Institute ---
URL: https://polsci.institute/international-relations/key-arguments-dependency-theory-economic-exploitation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from PolSci Institute provides a comprehensive explanation of dependency theory (theory of dependencia) and its key arguments regarding economic exploitation in the global system.

**Definition and Origins:** Dependency theory explains the underdevelopment of certain nations by emphasizing constraints imposed by the global economic and political order. It emerged in Latin America in the 1950s-1960s and gained influence through the 1970s. Its intellectual roots trace to Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch, executive director of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA/CEPAL) in 1950, whose work with Hans Singer produced the Prebisch-Singer thesis.

**Core-Periphery Structure:** The world economy is divided into core countries (wealthy, industrialised) and peripheral countries (poorer, raw material exporters). Theotonio Dos Santos defined dependence as a situation where some economies can expand and be self-sustaining while others only grow as a reflection of that expansion. Immanuel Wallerstein later added the semi-periphery category in his world-systems theory.

**Key Arguments:**
1. Underdevelopment is produced, not inherited—André Gunder Frank's "development of underdevelopment" concept (1966 essay, 1967 book) argues poor countries are poor because of how capitalism reached them, using a "metropolis and satellite" chain of exploitation. Frank noted that periods of less global integration (e.g., world wars) coincided with stronger local growth.
2. Unequal exchange and deteriorating terms of trade—prices of primary goods fall relative to manufactured goods, forcing peripheral economies to export ever-larger quantities to afford imports, making trade a mechanism of impoverishment.
3. Mechanisms of extraction include unequal trade relationships, foreign investment with repatriated profits, and brain drain.
4. Dependent development—Fernando Henrique Cardoso (with Enzo Faletto) argued peripheral nations could achieve some growth within the system, though lopsided and dependent on the core. Domestic elites often benefit from and maintain dependent relationships.

**Indian Experience:** British colonial rule exemplified dependency—raw materials (cotton, tea, minerals) were extracted and exported to Britain, then sold back as finished goods at higher prices. This resonates with the older "drain of wealth" theory by Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. Post-independence import substitution industrialisation was an attempt to break dependency.

**Criticisms:** The theory is criticized as overly deterministic and simplistic, neglecting internal factors (governance, institutions, human capital). The East Asian success stories (South Korea, Taiwan) challenge it—these countries achieved growth through export-oriented strategies and deep integration into the world economy. Samir Amin noted Frank's analysis was too generalised and failed to capture uneven development among peripheral states.

Despite criticisms, dependency theory retains explanatory value for debates on fair trade, debt relief, technology transfer, and Global South supply chains.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory is an approach that explains the underdevelopment of certain nations by emphasising the constraints imposed on them by the global economic and political order."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: World-systems theory ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World-systems_theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikipedia article on **World-systems theory** (also known as world-systems analysis or the world-systems perspective), a multidisciplinary approach to world history and social change that emphasizes the world-system—rather than nation-states—as the primary unit of social analysis. The theory explains the rise and fall of states, income inequality, social unrest, and imperialism.

**Key Concept:** The "world-system" refers to the inter-regional and transnational division of labor that divides the world into core countries (higher-skill, capital-intensive industries), semi-periphery countries, and periphery countries (low-skill, labor-intensive industries and raw material extraction). This structure constantly reinforces the dominance of core countries. The world-economy is rooted in capitalism, and historical hegemony has passed from the Netherlands to the United Kingdom and most recently to the United States.

**Main Proponent:** Immanuel Wallerstein developed the best-known version of the theory beginning in the 1970s, tracing the rise of the capitalist world-economy from the "long" 16th century (c. 1450–1640) as an accidental outcome of the crisis of feudalism (c. 1290–1450). Wallerstein rejects the term "theory," calling it a "knowledge movement" that transcends 19th-century divisions within the social sciences and between social sciences and history.

**Origins and Influences:** World-systems theory emerged in the 1970s to replace modernization theory, which Wallerstein criticized for (1) focusing on the nation-state as the only unit of analysis, (2) assuming a single path of evolutionary development, and (3) disregarding transnational structures. Three major predecessors: the Annales School (Fernand Braudel's longue durée concept), the Marxist tradition, and dependency theory. It builds upon but differs from dependency theory—Wallerstein argues core countries do not simply exploit poor countries because capitalism is organized around an inter-regional and transnational division of labor, not an international one.

**Wallerstein's Definitions:** A world-system is "a unit with a single division of labor and multiple cultural systems." He distinguishes between world-empires (e.g., Roman Empire, Han China—large bureaucratic structures with a single political center) and world-economies (large axial division of labor with multiple political centers and multiple cultures). The modern world-system emerged around 1450-1550 and expanded geographically across the entire planet by about 1900. Wallerstein defines four temporal features: cyclical rhythms, secular trends, contradiction, and crisis.

**Characteristics:** Core states are the most economically diversified, wealthy, and powerful; have strong central governments; are highly industrialized; produce manufactured goods; and increasingly specialize in information, finance, and service industries. Periphery states own very little of the world's means of production and provide less-skilled labor. Chirot (1986) lists five benefits core states gain from domination: (1) access to raw materials, (2) cheap labor, (3) profits from direct capital investments, (4) a market for exports, and (5) skilled professional labor through migration. Wallerstein identifies three forms of economic dominance: productivity dominance, trade dominance, and financial dominance.

**Applications and Importance:** The theory is applied to understanding world history, core countries' imperialization motives, climate change (e.g., the G-77 coalition of peripheral and semi-peripheral states), CO2 emissions analysis, global obesity from processed food dumping, and the knowledge economy shift. It has also influenced Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), which critiques international law as a hierarchical tool of global capital rather than a neutral framework of horizontal equality.

**Other Contributors:** Samir Amin, Giovanni Arrighi, Andre Gunder Frank, Oliver Cox, Christopher Chase-Dunn, Beverly Silver, Janet Abu Lughod, Li Minqi, and Kunibert Raffer.
</summary>

"a system is defined as a unit with a single division of labor and multiple cultural systems." — Immanuel Wallerstein (1974), "a social system, one that has boundaries, structures, member groups, rules of legitimation, and coherence. Its life is made up of the conflicting forces which hold it together by tension and tear it apart as each group seeks eternally to remold it to its advantage." — Immanuel Wallerstein, "not the system of the world, but a system that is a world and which can be, most often has been, located in an area less than the entire globe." — Immanuel Wallerstein (1987), "Exploitation and the refusal to accept exploitation as either inevitable or just constitute the continuing antinomy of the modern era" — Immanuel Wallerstein, "We must invent a new language" to transcend the illusions of the "three supposedly distinctive arenas" of society, economy and politics — Immanuel Wallerstein

--- SOURCE 7: Immanuel Wallerstein's World-System Theory: Core, Periphery, and Semi-Periphery • PolSci Institute ---
URL: https://polsci.institute/international-relations/world-system-theory-core-periphery-semi-periphery

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from PolSci Institute explains Immanuel Wallerstein's world-system theory, a framework for understanding global inequality. Wallerstein, an American sociologist and historian, developed this theory in the 1970s with his major work "The Modern World-System" published in 1974. He drew on Marxism, dependency theory, and the French Annales school of history, particularly Fernand Braudel's idea of studying long historical timespans.

The theory argues that the modern world is best understood as a single capitalist world economy based on an international division of labour, deliberately breaking from modernization theory which assumed all countries pass through the same stages of growth. Instead, Wallerstein argued that "underdevelopment" of poor nations is actively produced by their position within the global economy.

The world-system is divided into three zones:
- **Core countries**: Economically developed, politically stable, technologically advanced nations (e.g., US, Germany, Japan) that dominate global trade and finance and exploit poorer regions. Historically first developed in northwestern Europe (England, France, Holland).
- **Peripheral countries**: At the bottom of the hierarchy, these nations supply raw materials, agricultural goods, and cheap labour. They are exploited by the core and kept poor because their role is to be drained of resources. Examples include parts of Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and Asia.
- **Semi-peripheral countries**: Wallerstein's signature addition to the older centre-periphery model. These nations (e.g., Brazil, China, India, Mexico, South Africa) both exploit the periphery and are exploited by the core. Wallerstein argued this intermediate zone performs a vital political function by stabilizing the entire system and absorbing discontent, preventing stark polarization between rich and poor nations that would make revolution more likely. However, sociologist Christopher Chase-Dunn has argued the semi-periphery is less a stabilizing force and more a likely source of social change and resistance.

Wallerstein traced the origins of the system to the "long sixteenth century" (roughly 1450-1640), when the feudal order collapsed in Europe. Unlike earlier empires that were single political units, the modern world-system was a world-economy spanning many separate states. European maritime expansion, colonialism, and the Atlantic slave trade were central to creating the periphery that fed the emerging European core.

The engine driving this system is "unequal exchange"—wealth is systematically drained from the periphery to the core through trade structures where peripheral regions export low-value raw materials and import high-value manufactured goods. In the modern era, this drainage operates through global institutions like the World Bank and IMF, whose structural adjustment programmes and loan conditions reinforce existing hierarchies.

While Wallerstein accepted that individual countries can move up or down (South Korea rose from periphery toward core; Spain and Portugal declined into the semi-periphery), he maintained that the structure itself never changes—there will always be a core, semi-periphery, and periphery, and some regions must remain poor to be exploited.

Criticisms of the theory include: (1) it is too economically deterministic, neglecting the independent role of culture, politics, and social dynamics; (2) it is Eurocentric, downplaying the agency and histories of non-European societies; (3) it may struggle to capture 21st-century realities like digital industries and complex supply chains; and (4) its categories, especially the semi-periphery, can be vague and hard to define. Despite these limitations, the theory remains a powerful holistic analytical tool that offers a corrective to the optimistic assumption that development is simply a matter of good policy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"He argued that the 'underdevelopment' of poor nations is not a starting point they will leave behind, but a condition actively produced by their position within the global economy."

--- SOURCE 9: World Systems Theory (Definition & Easiest Explanation) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0HejgWVaExE

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This content is an educational video transcript from Helpful Professor Explains (published 17 May 2025) that provides an accessible overview of World Systems Theory, a sociological and economic framework developed by Immanuel Wallerstein in the 1970s. The theory divides the world into three groups within the global capitalist system: (1) Core countries, which are wealthy, powerful, and have advanced industries; (2) Periphery countries, which are poorer and provide raw materials or cheap labor to core countries; and (3) Semi-periphery countries, which fall in between with moderate development. The theory explains how resources, money, and labor flow between countries, often benefiting the core the most.

The video provides examples: core countries import raw materials (e.g., oil, cotton) from periphery countries and turn them into finished products (e.g., gasoline, clothing) sold at higher prices, while semi-periphery countries build cars or electronics using parts from periphery countries and technology from core countries.

Key strengths of the theory: it shows economic problems are global rather than just local, explains why some countries remain poor despite hard work (stuck in a system favoring wealthier nations), highlights the role of history and long-term patterns (trade, colonization, development over hundreds of years), and encourages thinking beyond individual countries to the global system.

Key weaknesses: it divides countries into fixed categories that may not reflect real-life changes (countries grow or decline), focuses mostly on economics while overlooking culture, environment, or local politics, and can be too general as not every country fits neatly into the model.

Alternatives discussed: (1) Modernization theory, which suggests all countries can develop the same way by following steps such as building industries, improving education, and using new technology; and (2) Dependency theory, which focuses on how richer countries keep poorer ones dependent through trade and finance, whereas World Systems Theory examines the global structure as a whole.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"World systems theory is a sociological and economic framework that examines the global capitalist system and its impacts on nations and societies. Developed by Immanuel Wallerstein in the 1970s, the theory posits that the world is divided into a core, semi-periphery, and periphery, each playing distinct roles in the global economy."

--- SOURCE 10: World-System Theory. ---
URL: https://irows.ucr.edu/papers/irows133/irows133.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Oxford Bibliography entry on World-System Theory in International Relations, authored by Christopher Chase-Dunn and Marilyn Grell-Brisk (v. 7-30-19; 9,200 words). It provides a comprehensive overview of the world-systems perspective, its intellectual origins, key elaborations, critiques, and applications across multiple domains.

**Core Concepts and Origins:**
The world-systems perspective emerged during the world revolution of 1968, developed by Immanuel Wallerstein, Terence Hopkins, Samir Amin, Andre Gunder Frank, and Giovanni Arrighi. The central idea is that the global system has a stratified structure of inequality based on institutionalized exploitation, making the whole system the proper unit of analysis rather than national societies. Development and underdevelopment have been structured by global power relations for centuries. The modern world-system is a self-contained entity based on a geographically differentiated division of labor bound together by a world market.

Wallerstein's version held that capitalism became predominant in Europe and its peripheries during the long 16th century, with core states concentrating the most profitable economic activities and exploiting semiperipheral and peripheral regions through colonialism and an international division of labor relying on unequal exchange. Wallerstein proposed a 3-tiered structure with an intermediate "semiperiphery" between core and periphery. Current terminology refers to the Global North (core) and Global South (periphery and semiperiphery).

**Intellectual Foundations:**
The perspective builds on Karl Marx's 1867 theory of capitalist contradictions (expanded to global scale), Lenin's 1916 theory of imperialism, Bukharin's work on imperialism and world economy, Kondratieff's long waves (40-60 year economic cycles), Schumpeter's business cycles, Polanyi's cycles of marketization and reregulation, and Braudel's focus on long-term historical structures. The world-system theorists argued that modern slavery and serfdom were forms of peripheral capitalism necessary for the reproduction and deepening of capitalism.

**Dependency Theory Roots:**
The world-systems perspective grew directly out of dependency theory, which criticized modernization theory's linear trajectory from backwardness to modernization. Dependency theory emerged from the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (UN ECLAC) led by Raúl Prebisch (1950). Key figures include Samir Amin (unequal exchange), Andre Gunder Frank (the "development of underdevelopment," 1966), Paul Baran (monopoly capitalism), Theotonio dos Santos, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso and Enzo Faletto (dependent capitalist development). Cardoso later became president of Brazil.

**Emergence and Elaboration:**
Wallerstein realized Poland had been peripheralized in the long 16th century by Western European core states. The semiperiphery—a stabilizing fixture engaging in both core and peripheral activities—is one of Wallerstein's most important analytic contributions. Elaborators I include Christopher Chase-Dunn, who developed structural models; Arrighi and Jessica Drangel (1986), who empirically confirmed a stable trimodal distribution of wealth using GNI per capita; Arrighi (1994) on systemic cycles of accumulation tied to hegemony transitions; and Hopkins and Wallerstein on cyclical rhythms. Elaborators II placed the system's emergence earlier or elsewhere: Janet Abu-Lughod (13th century multicore Eurasian system), Gunder Frank and Barry Gills (capitalist imperialism since Mesopotamia), and Gunder Frank (China as original center). Chase-Dunn and Thomas Hall developed a comparative evolutionary world-systems approach based on interpolity systemic interaction networks.

**Critiques:**
Aristide Zolberg charged circular economic reductionism; Theda Skocpol critiqued Wallerstein's teleological arguments about capitalism's emergence; Robert Brenner (the "neo-Smithian" critique) argued Wallerstein ignored internal class struggles; Stanley Aronowitz charged that race, gender, and environment were neglected; Anievas and Nişancıoğlu critiqued Eurocentrism; Leslie Sklair noted state-centrism and neglect of transnational processes; Sing Chew critiqued limited incorporation of ecology. Wallerstein responded in the 2011 Prologue of The Modern World System; Arrighi (1998) and Jason Moore (2003) also responded.

**Commodity and Value Chains:**
Hopkins and Wallerstein (1986) launched commodity chain analysis—forward and backward linkages of production and consumption processes crossing national boundaries. Gary Gereffi developed buyer-driven vs. producer-driven commodity chains. Case studies include coffee (Derudder and Witlox 2010; John Talbot 2004) and the apparel industry (Jane Collins 2003).

**International Relations Theory:**
Significant overlap exists with long cycle theory (George Modelski and William R. Thompson), particularly on rise and fall of hegemonic powers, though world-system scholars are less functionalist, more critical of global capitalism, and pay more attention to the non-core.

**Women and Gender:**
Feminist scholars (Maria Mies 1986, Claudia von Werlhof, Kathryn Ward, Joan Smith, Valentine Moghadam, Wilma Dunaway) demonstrated how capitalist accumulation relies on unwaged labor of women and the systematic reproduction of non-wage forms of labor, and argued that racism and sexism are part and parcel of the capitalist world-economy.

**Racism, Ethnogenesis, and Slavery:**
Wallerstein contended racism is structurally connected to the core/periphery hierarchy. Thomas Hall studied ethnogenesis through world-system processes. Dale Tomich studied slavery in the sugar circuit of Martinique and slavery's role in capitalist development. Arrighi (1990) distinguished voluntary vs. involuntary (slave) unilateral transfers of labor as significant as unequal exchange in reproducing the core/periphery hierarchy.

**Hegemonic Rise and Fall and Global Social Movements:**
The world-system perspective depicts three modern periods of hegemony: Dutch (17th century), British (19th century), and United States (20th century). Beverly Silver (2003) linked labor-capital conflict to cycles of hegemony; Arrighi and Silver (1999) discussed U.S. hegemonic decline; Jackie Smith linked social movements and global resistance to capitalist conflicts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The big idea was that the global system had a stratified structure on inequality based on institutionalized exploitation. This implied that the whole system was the proper unit of analysis, not national societies and that development and underdevelopment had been structured by global power relations for centuries."
</key_excerpts>

Eisenstadt critiqued the theory of structural differentiation as the main process underlying socio-structural evolution, as well as convergence theories of modernization.
