--- SOURCE 15: Decolonising epistemologies - Alana Lentin ---
URL: https://www.alanalentin.net/2017/02/10/decolonising-epistemologies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the second post in Alana Lentin's "Race Critical and Decolonial Sociology" blog series, published February 10, 2017, focusing on decolonising epistemologies. The post examines the interconnections between postcolonial theory and decolonial approaches, exploring epistemological implications and possibilities for transformative social and political action.

**Postcolonial Theory**: Postcolonialism grew out of anti-colonial movements and theorizes both the legacy of European colonization and the aspiration for emancipation. Key thinkers discussed include Couze Venn (who frames postcolonialism as both postcolonial and post-occidental), Ella Shohat (questioning when the "post-colonial" begins), Gyan Prakash (arguing that both nationalism and Marxism reproduced colonial master narratives, and that postcolonial critique must "undo the Eurocentrism produced by the institution of the west's trajectory"), and Homi Bhabha (the postcolonial subject as hybrid, occupying an in-between position). The postcolonial is relational rather than territorial, with the Third World subject seen as deterritorialised and politics understood as a "politics of positionality."

**Dirlik's Critique**: Arif Dirlik offers a scathing critique of postcolonial theory, arguing it only became significant once Third World academics succeeded in the western academy. He contends that postcolonial discourse is "an expression not so much of agony over identity... but of newfound power," and that postcolonial critics generalize from local contexts to the global while denying global forces' impact on the local. Critics like O'Hanlon and Washbrook argue the focus on hybridity leads to a "depoliticising insulation of social from material domains," making postcolonialism conservative. David Macey's critique of the "post-colonial Fanon" is quoted at length—that the angry Third Worldist Fanon was replaced by one "worried about identity politics" who "is no longer angry."

**Historicism and Modernity**: Dipesh Chakrabarty's "Provincializing Europe" problematises history as a narrative of transition, showing how Indian nationalists internalised western universal presumptions. Gurminder Bhambra critiques modernisation theory as a "theory of convergence" and the multiple modernities approach for remaining Eurocentric, arguing instead that "colonisation was not simply an outcome of modernity, but, rather, modernity itself, the modern world, developed out of colonial encounters." Bhambra emphasises interrelatedness and "connected and entangled histories," exemplified by how cotton milling in Manchester depended on cotton from India.

**The Decolonial Approach**: Decolonial thinking originates mainly with Latin American scholars (Ramon Grosfoguel, Walter Mignolo, Enrique Dussel, Arturo Escobar, Gloria Anzaldua) and traces its genealogy through liberation theology, dependency theory, and Latin American autonomous social science. Unlike postcolonialism, decolonial thinkers call for "delinking" from modern colonial epistemology rather than merely deconstructing it. Mignolo states: "the rhetoric of modernity is that of salvation, whereas the logic of coloniality is a logic of imperial oppression... you cannot have modernity without coloniality."

**The Modernity/Coloniality Research Programme**: Escobar outlines five key points: (1) the conquest of the Americas as the starting point of modernity (Dussel's "first modernity"), not the Enlightenment; (2) colonialism as constitutive of modernity (Quijano's "coloniality of power"—colonial logics persisting after colonialism); (3) modernity as a worldwide process (Dussel's "transmodernity," giving voice to negated Others); (4) domination of non-Europeans as integral to modernity, with silenced knowledges; and (5) Eurocentrism as the knowledge form of modernity/coloniality.

**Impacts on the Academy**: Boaventura de Sousa Santos's "abyssal thinking" is discussed—modern knowledge and law divide social reality into visible and invisible realms, rendering indigenous and plebian knowledges nonexistent. Mignolo's "border thinking" (drawing on Gloria Anzaldua) rejects both Eurocentrism and anti-western fundamentalism, redefining concepts like citizenship, democracy, and human rights for non-western contexts, with the Zapatista movement as an example. Gender is introduced as a further power divide through Anzaldua and Maria Lugones.

A comment from Erik Ljungberg (April 19, 2019) challenges the claim that the Industrial Revolution depended on Indian cotton, noting England sourced cotton from America (citing "Empire of Cotton" by Sven Beckert), though acknowledging this doesn't change the overall argument about interconnectedness.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"the rhetoric of modernity is that of salvation, whereas the logic of coloniality is a logic of imperial oppression. They go hand in hand, and you cannot have modernity without coloniality; the unfinished project of modernity carries over its shoulders the unfinished project of coloniality." — Walter Mignolo
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: The South Centre | Revisiting the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and its legacy ---
URL: https://www.southcentre.int/question/revisiting-the-1955-bandung-asian-african-conference-and-its-legacy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the South Centre presents an article by Adriano José Timossi titled "Revisiting the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and its legacy," published in South Bulletin 85 (15 May 2015). The article examines the historic Bandung Conference held April 18-24, 1955, in Bandung, Indonesia, which marked the first-ever summit-level meeting of independence leaders from 29 Asian and African countries. Key leaders included Chou En-Lai (China), Jawaharlal Nehru (India), U Nu (Burma), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), President Sukarno (Indonesia), and leaders from Liberia, Sudan, Gold Coast, Jordan, Iran, Ceylon, Nepal, Pakistan, and Philippines.

The article highlights Sukarno's opening speech, in which he declared that "colonialism is not yet dead" and warned of its "modern dress" in the form of economic, intellectual, and physical control. He called for Asian-African unity as essential for prosperity and world safety, emphasizing the conference's purpose to foster understanding, appreciation, and collective action among developing nations.

The Bandung Final Communiqué established the foundation for South-South cooperation, supporting UN human rights principles, deploring racial segregation, opposing colonialism in all forms, and advocating for universal UN membership and equitable Asian-African representation in the Security Council. The communiqué also established the Ten Bandung Principles, which include respect for fundamental human rights, sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of all races and nations, abstention from intervention in internal affairs, peaceful dispute settlement, and promotion of mutual interests and cooperation.

In the 60 years following the conference, the "Bandung Spirit" led to significant achievements: decolonization of most developing countries, establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) in 1961, the Group of 77 (G77) in 1964, and other Southern institutions including the South Centre and South Commission. Regional initiatives reflecting Bandung ideals include the African Union, UNASUR, CELAC, ASEAN, and SAARC. The article also cites the emergence of BRICS, the BRICS Development Bank, and the Bank of the South as continuing examples of Bandung's vision for South-South cooperation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are often told 'Colonialism is dead'. Let us not be deceived or even soothed by that. I say to you, colonialism is not yet dead... Colonialism has also its modern dress, in the form of economic control, intellectual control, actual physical control by a small but alien community within a nation." - President Sukarno, opening speech, 1955 Bandung Conference, "Our task is first to seek an understanding of each other, and out of that understanding will come a greater appreciation of each other, and out of that appreciation will come collective action." - President Sukarno, "The 1955 Bandung Conference led to the establishment in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). This was followed by the establishment of the Group of 77 (G77) in 1964." - Adriano José Timossi, "For many generations our peoples have been the voiceless ones in the world. We have been the unregarded, the peoples for whom decisions were made by others whose interests were paramount, the peoples who lived in poverty and humiliation." - President Sukarno
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Bandung Conference 1955 ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g5UQ7Z3C2QQ

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a video description and transcript from the Research Society of International Law (RSIL) commemorating the 70th anniversary of the Bandung Conference of 1955. Held from 18-24 April 1955 in Bandung, Indonesia, the conference brought together leaders from 29 Asian and African nations in what was the largest gathering of its kind on Asian or African soil at the time. The conference took place against the backdrop of the Cold War and the surging post-war national liberation movements in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement, the concept of the "third world," and the Global South, advocating for an alternative form of just global governance and countering colonialism in all its forms. The conference produced the "Ten Principles of Bandung," a political statement outlining guiding principles for developing countries to promote peace and cooperation. These principles include: (1) respect for fundamental human rights and UN Charter purposes; (2) respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations; (3) recognition of equality of all races and nations, large and small; (4) abstention from intervention or interference in internal affairs of other countries; (5) respect for the right of each nation to defend itself in conformity with the UN Charter; (6) abstention from using collective defense arrangements for big power interests and from exerting pressures on other countries; (7) refraining from aggression or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence; (8) peaceful settlement of all disputes; (9) promotion of mutual interests and cooperation; and (10) respect for justice and international obligations. The video notes that in the decades following Bandung, friction among conference members increased as decolonization progressed, making the concept of Asian-African solidarity less meaningful. On its 70th anniversary, the content asks whether the principles remain relevant today, noting that while they are deeply under threat, their observance is needed more than ever amid rising global tensions. The video was posted on 25 February 2025 and has received 8,247 views.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Bandung Conference set the stage for the Non-Aligned Movement and the rise of the Global South, advocating for self-determination, sovereignty, and global cooperation outside the influence of major powers."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Bandung Conference - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandung_Conference

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Bandung Conference (also known as the Asian–African or Afro–Asian Conference) was a landmark meeting of Asian and African states held from April 18–24, 1955, in Bandung, West Java, Indonesia. Twenty-nine countries participated, representing approximately 1.5 billion people (54% of the world's population). The conference was organized by Indonesia, Burma (Myanmar), India, Ceylon (Sri Lanka), and Pakistan, and was coordinated by Ruslan Abdulgani, secretary general of Indonesia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Its stated aims were to promote Afro-Asian economic and cultural cooperation and to oppose colonialism or neocolonialism by any nation.

Key organizers included Indonesian President Sukarno, Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, and Chinese leaders Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. The conference was motivated by the desire to create a unified non-aligned identity independent of both Western and Soviet influence during the Cold War, as well as concerns over Western reluctance to consult Asian nations on decisions affecting the region. Sukarno sought support for Indonesia's claim to West New Guinea (West Papua).

Major debate centered on whether Soviet policies should be censured alongside Western colonialism; a consensus was reached condemning "colonialism in all of its manifestations," implicitly censuring both the Soviet Union and the West. Zhou Enlai, who survived an assassination attempt (the Kashmir Princess incident) en route to the conference, displayed a moderate and conciliatory attitude, signing an agreement on dual nationality with Indonesia and endorsing the right of all nations to choose their own systems. Nehru, who advocated for non-alignment and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, received a generally negative reception and was criticized as arrogant. China also voiced support for Palestine at the conference.

The conference produced the Dasasila Bandung (Bandung's Ten Principles), a 10-point declaration on the promotion of world peace and cooperation, incorporating principles of the UN Charter and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. These principles covered respect for human rights, sovereignty, territorial integrity, equality of races and nations, non-interference in internal affairs, self-defense rights, abstention from collective defense arrangements serving big power interests, refraining from aggression, peaceful dispute settlement, promotion of mutual interests, and respect for justice and international obligations.

The United States was not officially represented (at the urging of Secretary of State John Foster Dulles), but formed a "Working Group on the Afro-Asian Conference" involving multiple agencies for propaganda and "Image Management." Representative Adam Clayton Powell Jr. attended unofficially, sponsored by Ebony and Jet magazines, and spoke in favor of American foreign policy. African American author Richard Wright also attended and later published "The Color Curtain: A Report on the Bandung Conference."

The conference was a step toward the eventual creation of the Non-Aligned Movement (formed at the Belgrade Summit in 1961), though the two initiatives ran in parallel and sometimes in confrontation during the 1960s. A proposed second Bandung Conference in Algiers failed due to events including the 1965 Algerian coup, the ouster of Sukarno, and the 1966 Ghanaian coup. A 50th anniversary Asian-African Summit was held in 2005 in Jakarta and Bandung, launching the New Asian–African Strategic Partnership (NAASP). A 60th anniversary summit was held in 2015 with delegates from 109 Asian and African countries. A 70th anniversary "Bharat Summit" was organized by the Telangana government in Hyderabad, India, in April 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The twenty-nine countries that participated represented a total population of 1.5 billion people, 54% of the world's population."

This is Chapter 2 of the open-access book "Democratising Participatory Research" (© 2022 Carmen Martinez-Vargas, CC BY-NC-ND), titled "Coloniality and Decoloniality in the Global South Higher-Education Context." The chapter examines how colonial systems of domination persist in higher education across the Global South, focusing on ontological and epistemological challenges, and argues for transforming universities from "uni-versities" into "pluri-versities" through decolonial and participatory approaches.

The chapter begins with an excerpt from "Narratives on Social Injustices: Undergraduate Voices" (2018) documenting racism and injustice in South African universities, including the 2012 drowning death of Thabang Makhoang at North-West University in Potchefstroom during alleged initiation activities conducted in Afrikaans, racist remarks by Keith Arlow of St John's College, harassment of students at the University of the Free State, and the killing of a black parent in a stampede at the University of Johannesburg.

Key sections covered:
1. **Coloniality in the Global South**: Post-colonial scholars (Chilisa, Wa Thiong'o, Mbembe, Appiah, Mignolo) argue that despite overcoming territorial and political domination, Global South countries still face social, economic, and epistemological domination. Wa Thiong'o (1986) uses "neocolonies" and Mbembe (2001) "postcolony" to describe ongoing cultural and political constraints.

2. **Deciphering Global North Codes**: The chapter analyzes two onto-epistemological challenges: (a) the "zero-point" universal ontological claim of Western sciences (Castro-Gomez), which positions Western reality as universally objective while displacing other epistemic frameworks; and (b) "epistemicide" (De Sousa Santos) or "epistemological blindness" (Hlela)—the destruction or invisibility of non-Western knowledge systems. The authors argue Western ontology is an imposed, Eurocentric concept and suggest "cosmologies" as a more accurate alternative to "ontologies."

3. **Transforming Uni-versity into Pluri-versity**: The "pluriverse" project (Boidin, Cohen, Grosfoguel, Dussel, Mignolo, Escobar) aims to transform monolithic universities into less provincial institutions. De Sousa Santos's "ecology of knowledges" concept asserts all knowledge systems are incomplete, requiring epistemological dialogue among them as a necessary condition for promoting a pluriversity.

4. **Participatory Approaches as Decolonial Intention**: Participatory approaches (Participatory Action Research, Community-Based Action Research) claim decolonial aims. Major handbooks (The Palgrave International Handbook of Action Research 2017; The SAGE Handbook of Action Research 2008 and 2015) position Action Research as a tool for "alternative globalisation," re-enchanting a plural world (Fals Borda), and promoting decolonisation of lifeworlds (Kemmis, McTaggart & Nixon 2013).

The chapter concludes that while participatory approaches are broadly aligned with decolonial intentions, not all practices necessarily decolonise or democratise research. The following chapter (Chapter 3) aims to clarify different traditions and goals within participatory research to uncover Western homogenising tendencies and advance toward decolonisation and social justice. The chapter includes an extensive reference list of decolonial scholarship.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This creates a burden on the marginalised to educate and enlighten. Though the privileged demand the epistemic labour of the marginalised, they often perpetuate epistemic oppression by dismissing the knowledge produced. The marginalised are excluded from the realm of recognised knowledge creators despite contributing novel conceptual resources and epistemic frameworks." (Berenstain 2016, 571)
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage documents a webinar from the University of Calgary's "Courageous Conversations Speaker Series" (2020-2021-2022 theme: "Decolonization and Questions of Justice in the Academy"), hosted by the Office of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion. The second event, "Decolonization: Rethinking the coloniality of power, knowledge and being," was posted on 22 Oct 2021 and featured two internationally renowned scholars.

**Host and Moderator:** Dr. Malinda Smith, Vice-Provost and Associate Vice President Research for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion at the University of Calgary.

**Speakers:**
1. **Dr. Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni** – Professor and Chair of Epistemologies of the Global South at the University of Bayreuth, Germany. His publications include *Decolonizing the University: Knowledge Systems and Disciplines in Africa* (coedited with Siphamandla Zondi, 2016) and *Decolonization, Development and Knowledge in Africa: Turning Over A New Leaf* (2020). He previously worked as a research professor at the University of South Africa.
2. **Dr. Isabel Altamirano-Jiménez** – Binizaá (Zapotec) from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico; Professor of Political Science and Canada Research Chair in Comparative Indigenous Feminist Studies at the University of Alberta. Her books include *Indigenous Encounters with Neoliberalism* (2013) and *Living on the Land: Indigenous Women's Understandings of Place* (coedited with Kermoal, 2016).

**Key Themes from Dr. Ndlovu-Gatsheni's presentation:**
- We are living in a moment of "epistemological turbulence" and "uncertainties of knowledges" where certitudes from the colonizer's model of the world are being exposed.
- Basic epistemological questions have been reopened: the relationship between identity and knowledge, whether knowledge has a geography (geopolitics of knowledge), and the biography/body politics of knowledge.
- The "cognitive empire" is responsible for most problems of the modern world—it invades people's mental universes and makes them think against themselves, their knowledges, histories, and cultures.
- Coloniality operates on three interconnected levels: coloniality of being (social/racial/gender classification creating an "invisible social pyramid" that determines who is considered fully human), coloniality of power (governing through modern colonial power structures that hierarchize languages, gender, beauty), and coloniality of knowledge (a "global economy of knowledge" underpinned by an uneven intellectual division of labor where "international" journals mean North American or European ones).
- Various "grammars of liberation" have been attempted: deracialization (critiqued for often only changing demographics, not structures), Africanization (1960s, enabling Africans to assume positions of authority, but often lacking structural/institutional change), indigenization (economy-related in Africa), plus social inclusion, diversification, abolition, and reparations.
- Decolonial "turns" include nationalistic, Marxist, post-colonial, and gender turns; the language of decolonization emerges from "the battlefields of history" (e.g., Amilcar Cabral, Frantz Fanon, Kwame Nkrumah), not classrooms, and its "imperfection is its power."
- Decolonization is embraced by Indigenous peoples' movements, feminist movements, ecological struggles, students, and academics, and is not a singular concept.

**Key Themes from Dr. Altamirano-Jiménez's presentation:**
- Approached from an Indigenous (specifically Zapotec) perspective, asking what it means to include experiences of dispossessed bodies "without centering land itself."
- Distinguished between colonialism (historical phenomenon) and coloniality (the ongoing context/outcome in which we all reside despite decolonization movements).
- Coloniality and Western domination have silenced Indigenous and local knowledges, instituting a theological reading of history that assumes Western civilization is the pinnacle of progress.
- Decoloniality is a political project challenging Eurocentric epistemological foundations, reclaiming non-Western ontologies, and imagining "that other worlds are possible" (Subcomandante Marcos, Zapatista movement).
- Introduced the concept of "internal colonialism" (following Mexican sociologist Pablo González Casanova), showing that Indigenous peoples in newly independent Latin American states remained in the same or worse colonial relations of domination.
- Argued that ongoing Indigenous dispossession must be central to any post-colonial accounts; decolonization is an "embodied movement," not just cognitive or semantic.
- Emphasized *sentir y pensar* ("thinking from the heart"), a way of knowing that is practical, not just theoretical.
- Connected the Zapotec concepts of *ombligo* (belly button) and *obligación* (obligation): obligation is a course of responsible action arising from being interconnected with each other and the non-human world. Knowledge requires "making relatives" and relationality that includes water, land, wind, and animals (expanding beyond human-centric relations per Melanie Yazzie).
- Warned against appropriation in academic settings when engaging colonized knowledge systems without obligation, and against reproducing Eurocentric hierarchies in citation and writing practices.
- Described the "University of Communality" project in Oaxaca/Tehuantepec isthmus, which enacts higher education as a communal responsibility, honoring communal practices, languages, values, and governance structures of Indigenous communities.
- Expressed concern about universities moving toward commercialization of knowledge where "objective" knowledge is valued by its ability to make profits.

**Opening segments:**
- Elder Colleen Sitting Eagle (Sipiyana'tokumiyaki), a Siksika language instructor and elder for the series, opened with a blessing in her language, sharing about the power of Indigenous people to fight battles (residential schools, current addictions crisis in Siksika), and promoting language and cultural preservation. She noted the Indigenous bishop for Canada is Bishop Sydney Black from Six Nations.
- Dr. Smith highlighted two inspirations: Violet King (Calgary-born first Black woman lawyer in Canada, who refused limits placed on her) and Maya Angelou ("courage is the most important of all virtues, because without courage, we can't practice any other virtue consistently").
- The session cited Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's idea that "decolonization is not a metaphor," and discussed prefixes (post-, neo-, decolonial), knowledge production in universities, curriculum and citational practices, and shifting from university to "pluri-university."

**Discussion:**
- Q&A addressed that decolonial thinking comes from battlefields, not classrooms, and that knowledge production is disconnected from land, place, and territories; the connection between degradation of a people's humanity and inability to achieve epistemic freedom was emphasized.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are living at a moment when there is actually turmoil in the contestation in the world of knowledge... This turmoil and contestation in the world of knowledge has implications for our lives as human beings and before our survival." — Dr. Sabelo J. Ndlovu-Gatsheni
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 19: Towards an epistemological alliance for the decolonization of ---
URL: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/towards-epistemological-alliance-decolonization-knowledge-global-south-and-global-north

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This UNESCO "Idea" article, written by Obrillant Damus (socio-anthropologist, linguist, educator, and professor at the Université d'État d'Haiti, Université Quisqueya, and the University of Shebrooke), was published on 12 April 2021 and argues for a constructive epistemological alliance between the global North and global South to decolonize knowledge and shape the future of education. Damus contends that the monocultural educational paradigm "crushes local knowledge" in its multiple dimensions and promotes socio-epistemic separation that hinders the hybridization of knowledge essential for human survival. He advocates for integrating local and indigenous knowledge holders into formal education systems, using ancestral/local languages as vehicles of instruction in formerly colonized countries to achieve "intellectual liberation and autonomy," and building education on an "ecology of knowledge" that links Southern and Northern epistemologies. The article describes three harmful phenomena to address: auto-epistemicide (local knowledge disappearing because it is not valued, especially by youth), endo-epistemic practices (actors abandoning local knowledge), and exo-epistemic practices (Western-centred intervention causing disappearance of local knowledge, with destruction of traditional technical knowledge termed "technocide"). Damus argues that local and indigenous knowledge systems are crucial not only for human sustainability but also for planetary sustainability through biodiversity conservation. He calls for education that forms "cosmocentric (versus egocentric)" beings capable of overcoming unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational) and emphasizes that "the future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South." The article is based on a background paper prepared for the International Commission on the Futures of Education, and the ideas expressed are those of the author, not necessarily the official position of UNESCO.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The future of education and human and planetary sustainability are inconceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the global North and those of the global South", "The monocultural educational paradigm is like a steamroller that crushes local knowledge in its multiple dimensions (technical, symbolic, magical, religious, relational, rational...) that appear irrational or residual, while much of this knowledge plays a very important role in human and planetary sustainability.", "The use of ancestral languages in formerly colonized countries as the main vehicles of instruction will bring about intellectual liberation and autonomy, critical thinking, a sense of linguistic security, and the development of cognitive and metacognitive skills, all of which are essential to the process of knowledge production.", "One of the main aims of the education of the future is to remove unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational...), on the human and planetary level, by forming cosmocentric (versus egocentric) beings capable of grasping dialectical units.", "The future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 20: The #ColonialityofKnowledge: first introduced by Aníbal Quijano and ... ---
URL: https://www.facebook.com/black.historystudies/posts/the-colonialityofknowledge-first-introduced-by-an%C3%ADbal-quijano-and-expanded-by-sc/1418846460272997

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Facebook post from the page "Black HistoryStudies" (dated April 16, likely 2026), which presents an educational graphic explaining the concept of "Coloniality of Knowledge." The post defines this concept as first introduced by Aníbal Quijano and expanded by scholars including Walter Mignolo and Dr. Sabelo Ndlovu-Gatsheni, describing how Eurocentric worldviews continue to dominate global knowledge systems.

The graphic highlights five interwoven mechanisms of Eurocentric Hegemony:
1. **Epistemicide** – the killing, destruction, and erasure of non-Western knowledge systems, replaced by colonial knowledge systems (attributed to Boaventura de Sousa Santos).
2. **Linguicide** – the killing or suppression of languages, popularized by Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and expanded by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o in "Decolonising the Mind," showing how linguistic domination serves cultural erasure.
3. **Cognitive Imperialism** – the imposition of Western thought as the universal standard (attributed to Marie Battiste).
4. **Hermeneutical Injustice** – structural gaps in interpretive resources that disadvantage marginalized groups (attributed to Miranda Fricker).
5. **Cultural Imperialism** – the domination of culture and imagination through language and power (attributed to Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o).

The post argues that together these forces uphold the Coloniality of Knowledge, and that decolonization involves reclaiming suppressed epistemologies and centering Africentric and Indigenous ways of knowing. It is described as rooted in Africentric and decolonial scholarship, shared to educate and invite critical reflection, with the statement that "truth precedes reconciliation." The post is credited to @ubuntucentredpractice and wellnessEmpowered.com. One commenter (Amanda Sutton) noted the utility of having words to describe these concepts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The #ColonialityofKnowledge: first introduced by Aníbal Quijano and expanded by scholars like Walter Mignolo and Dr. Sabelo Ndlovu-Gatsheni, describes how Eurocentric worldviews continue to dominate global knowledge systems.
</key_excerpts>

This webpage is the Internet Archive (archive.org) item page for the book "Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America: Historical Studies of Chile and Brazil" by Andre Gunder Frank (1929-2005), published in 1969 by Monthly Review Press (New York). The book is 344 pages (xxiii, 344 pages; 22 cm) plus front matter, totaling 374 pages, and includes bibliographical references (pages 319-333) and an index. The item size is 971.2 MB with 1,310 views and 10 favorites.

The book is organized into five sections: (I) Capitalist development of underdevelopment in Chile, (II) On the "Indian problem" in Latin America, (III) Capitalist development of underdevelopment in Brazil, (IV) Capitalism and the myth of feudalism in Brazilian agriculture, and (V) Foreign investment in Latin American underdevelopment.

It is an access-restricted item (printdisabled collection) digitized from the Internet Archive Books collection on 2022-03-16. Subjects covered include economic history, capitalism in Latin America, economic conditions in Brazil and Chile, traditional tenure types, underdeveloped areas, and the "Indian problem" in Latin America.

Robarts Centre Research Papers The Post-Washington Consensus: The market disconnect and the public reconnect Daniel Drache, Senior Research Fellow and Associate Director Robarts Centre for Canadian Studies York University, Toronto www.robarts.yorku.ca 2 The post-Washington Consensus: The market disconnect and the public reconnect Daniel Drache* Introduction After the protests in Seattle, Prague, Washington and Windsor, popular and national sovereignty have once again become powerful forces on the global stage. These agenda-setting fundamentals challenge the Washington Consensus goals and objectives of zero inflation, broadening market access and promoting privatization. The mood swing today is away from reliance on narrow market-led strategies and one of the casualties of this move is that the Washington Consensus is no longer a ‘framework agreement’ supported unqualifiedly by policy makers everywhere. Significantly, even John Williamson, who first coined the term, has criticized this neo-liberal framework of public policy-making as inappropriate and too rigid for developing countries. Its largest failure is that it has not produced the growth and jobs expected (1999). Williamson is not alone. Other mainstream economists, such as Joseph Stiglitz, Dany Rodrik, Sylvia Ostry, John Helliwell and Paul Krugman, have also questioned the appropriateness of market fundamentalism as the developmental strategy for southern countries. After close to two decades of triumphant market policies, new economic and social fundamentals for a different kind of consensus are needed to manage the global economy (World Bank 2000). So far, two contending reform-minded agendas have emerged. The first is not all that different from what currently exists and could be called simply the Washington Consensus with a human face (World Bank 1997). Its goals include poverty reduction, improving equity and building socially inclusive societies in the developing world rather than narrowly market oriented ones. Adding hot-button words, such as civil society, capacity building and transparency, is 3 important but the basic problems remain unaddressed. There is no recognition of the basic incompatibility between the old policy instruments of structural reform and the new equity outcomes espoused by the Washington Consensus reformers. In their rush to give the Washington Consensus a human face, the reform-minded elites have not absorbed the lessons of the past decade, which suggest that poverty is part of a low growth cycle. When markets underperform, public authority does not have the resources at its command to ensure sufficient growth levels. Higher levels of growth require massive capital inflows but when interest rates remain in the doubt digit range, the first casualty is domestic growth. A good example of developing countries trapped in a long-term poverty cycle are the Latin American countries that cannot attract the foreign capital that they badly need and do not have the domestic resources to finance their own development (ECLAC 2000). As long as zero inflation goals define the macro-economic framework of good governance as laid out in the original, if now dated Washington Consensus, the rules and norms that underpin the present order are largely unchanged (Drache 2001). Paradoxically, the onslaught against the triumph of markets comes at a time when the triumph of market liberalism has converted the boardrooms and economic ministries around the world to its singularity of focus. Yet the free trade gospel no longer appears to be winning public opinion to its side. The new agenda pushed by civil society’s social activists is that globalization requires a new model of governance without which international civil society lacks a defensive shield against market intrusiveness (Higgott and Phillips 2000). The beginnings of change in public policy discourse is marked but still uneven, compared to the clear-headed if not simplistic goals espoused by the Washington Consensus benchmark. At present, the second agenda starts with the compelling view that global governance requires bar-raising standards of all kinds. These demands are front and centre on civil society’s agenda, 4 including environmental and human rights, and labour and financial standards, such as closing off-shore tax shelters and holding corporations accountable for their investment decisions. The new expectations are that global public goods must be provided adequately and social protection must be accorded to the most vulnerable members of the world economy. If the line between the market and public domain is to be effectively redrawn to include these bar-raising standards, a large-scale reform of the institutions of global governance is required (Picciotto and Mayne (1999). This paper responds to two compelling concerns: why have the zero inflation goals entrenched in the Washington Consensus framework proved to be counterproductive, if not self-defeating, even when the world’s economy is more open than ever and trade barriers of all kinds have fallen? Once we see how the fundamentals of the Consensus are being challenged by new research about the asymmetrical effects of trade as a motor of growth and prosperity, a second concern emerges. With the crisis of markets, new trade rules, which provide collective goods and social protection as well as recognition of the critical place of the public domain in a modern notion of governance, are needed. The world’s trading system requires a larger framework in order to provide an adequate level of access to the collective entitlements of society—to the resources shared in common. In Charles Taylor’s term, the global politics of mutual recognition requires a strong public sphere as an essential element of democratic governance. The difficult but relevant question is, can the world’s trade system be uncoupled from the programmatic reforms of the Washington Consensus so as to redraw the line between trade, investment and human development in an adequate fashion? This is a large and complex issue but the paper suggests some grounds for optimism are in order. 5 Table 1 The Elusive Goal of Trade Convergence in the World Economy The Degree of Openness For Select Countries in % Countries Degree of Openness of Economy Import Penetration of Internal Market Exports as a % of GDP 1980 1990 1998 1980 1990 1998 1980 1990 1998 Germany 28.7 30.8 25.7 28.7 32.1 25.6 28.5 36.4 25.8 Argentina 8.0 7.5 11.7 9.0 10.6 12.7 6.7 19.7 10.4 Australia 17.4 17.1 20.7 13.7 14.8 21.1 17.0 16.3 19.8 Brazil 10.0 6.8 8.9 10.8 5.6 9.9 8.9 7.2 7.6 Canada 27.4 25.4 40.6 26.9 24.9 40.4 28.3 25.2 41.3 China n.d. 15.7 20.1 n.d. 18.0 18.6 n.d. 20.1 22.3 United States 10.4 10.4 12.2 10.7 11.1 12.8 10.2 9.9 11.3 France 22.1 22.5 24.7 22.5 22.7 24.0 21.5 22.6 26.0 India 8.3 8.4 11.9 9.7 9.1 13.0 6.6 7.5 10.4 Indonesia 26.1 26.3 46.9 24.2 25.2 44.2 29.7 25.9 40.6 Italy 21.9 18.8 23.1 23.0 19.6 22.2 19.8 19.2 24.7 Japan 15.3 10.3 10.1 15.6 9.4 9.3 14.9 10.7 11.1 Mexico 13.0 16.1 32.2 13.4 13.5 32.5 12.6 19.7 31.3 United Kingdom 26.1 25.5 27.3 25.6 26.5 27.5 27.2 24.8 26.9 Thailand 27.2 37.7 45.4 28.3 40.8 45.2 24.5 36.8 46.9 Source: OECD 2000; WTO 2000; Simao Davi Silber, 2000. 6 The contradictory effects of competitive markets Contrary to conventional wisdom, the Washington Consensus has failed to create a one-size-fits-all policy model. It was never meant to be the Ten Commandments of public policy. It was only the beginning point for change, not a final goal. The Washington Consensus was a set of principles used by the elites as an authoritative benchmark but was without a clear definition of priorities (Naim 2000). It was intended to be a moving consensus that could be adapted to different conditions. Countries were free to choose how to implement its different goals and priorities in the same way Keynesian goals were adapted to sharply contrasting national realities. Few countries embraced full employment objectives as a rigid rule of policy-making. Similarly, zero inflation targets were interpreted with marked variation. The US goal was a three-percent inflation rate, while the Bank of Canada fixed on zero-percent resulting in an unemployment rate nearly twice the US target level. While the Consensus defined benchmark goals of macro-economic management for all governments, few anticipated the increasingly divergent outcomes, which resulted when national needs and institutional practices asserted themselves. In Latin America structural adjustment programs became the norm of the Washington Consensus (Ramonet 2001). In Canada, while there was no need for structural adjustment of finances the government did embark on a program of sharp and prolonged deficit reduction between 1993 and 1998. Canada reduced its rather middle of the road deficit of seven percent of GDP more sharply and quickly than any other G-7 country did. Compared to other jurisdictions such as the UK, New Zealand and Australia there was no wholesale privatization movement in Canada, but there was a massive sell-off of state enterprises provincially and federally. Canada was not subject to the worst kinds of IMF conditionality that many developing countries faced when seeking badly needed loans to reduce 7 their debt burden. Still without being forced to do so, Ottawa retrenched social and health transfer payments cutting deeply into the social safety net. In the absence of agreement on goals and outcomes, the hollowing out of public authority has been dramatic with state authority being diffused downwards, sideways and upwards, and the leakage of power pronounced. So, even though there has been no wholesale convergence to the ‘less state less tax model,’ as predicted a decade ago, the benchmark of good governance has been redefined by the exigencies of trade openness (TD Economics 2001). Despite acceptance of the broad framework of the Washington Consensus, integration into the world economy and the benchmark of competitive markets has produced not less but more contradictory effects, even amongst industrialized countries with highly developed economies. Even the simplest idea that economic integration is the universal trend line is wrong. Economic integration, despite the formation of trade blocs, remains partial and uneven. Many countries are less integrated than previously, according to conventional measures. Germany’s degree of trade openness, measured by the standard economic criteria of imports plus exports, actually declined from 1980 to 1998—28% to 25.7%. Argentina’s economy shared little in the competitive drive to acquire new markets during the same period yet rose from 8% to 11.7%. The United States, the defender of global free trade, saw its trade openness rise minimally from 10.4% to 12.2%, hardly the success story of global forces at work. To make matters more complex, Japan was more trade dependent in 1980 at 15.3% than in 1998 at 10.1%. If globalization is such a universal force, why is Japan, one of the world’s leading trade nations, seemingly moving backwards? (See Table 1: The Elusive Goal of Trade Convergence in an Open Economy). By conventional measures, the Canada-US model has been a commercial success. 8 Canada has been a leader in embracing global free trade, first with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1988. Five years later, the far-reaching North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) with Mexico and the US created the largest free trade area in the world. Yet Canada’s core competitiveness has been eroded directly and indirectly by the general framework of the Washington Consensus and the Canadian economic recovery, post-94, was driven by the US business cycle, rising commodity prices for Canada’s energy products and a devalued dollar. Living standards in Canada declined sharply, as trade liberalization gained momentum. Canada’s real GDP per capita income in 1980 was almost 90% of GDP in the US, by 1999 it had dropped twenty points to 70%. This is an impressive statistic because it attempts to measure living standards converted at 1995 purchasing parity exchange rates and there is little evidence that opening Canada’s economy and relying on exports has transformed the economy in ways that global free trade predicted (Helliwell 2000). Significantly, among OECD countries, Canada achieved its best ranking in real GDP product per capita prior to 1990. Since the two trade agreements have come into effect, Canada has fallen from 4th to 7th place among OECD countries. What no free trade theorist can explain is why Canada made its greatest strides when the economy was less open and its trade was less concentrated on the US. Over the past fifteen years, Canada’s economic performance measured by percentage change in real GDP per capita growth has been 4th last among OECD countries. Canada ranks just behind Greece but ahead of Sweden, New Zealand and Switzerland. Canada’s fifteen year compound annual growth rate was only 1.61% and its fifteen year cumulative growth rate was 27.0%, compared to the US, its best trading partner, with a 39.7% cumulative growth rate and a 2.25% compound annual growth rate. This evidence raises troubling questions about the adequacy of free trade theory, 9 particularly its belief in the automatic benefits that accrue from integration into the world economy. Many of the gains appear to be ideological rather than structural, as the promise of dynamic efficiency gains, cheaper goods and job creation have not materialized as trade theory predicted. Certainly there is no template operating at the international level (Gilpin 2000). New Zealand’s Labour government, a flag-bearer for neo-liberalism, carried out the most radical reforms of state-market relations, yet had the lowest compound annual growth rates of the last fifteen years at 1.1%. Sweden did not do much better than New Zealand at 1.3% but maintained most of its social market welfare state programs with a full commitment to an export-led economy. These numbers raise troubling questions about the framework of the Washington Consensus that its vigorous supporters cannot answer with credible data.
