Her research focuses on the club governance (G8/G7, G20, BRICS), new (digital) technologies and internet governance, sustainable development, global governance and security, and humanitarian cooperation. Dr. Panova holds her PhD in History of International Relations from the Moscow State University of International Relations (MGIMO-University, MFA of Russia). She was a visiting fellow (now a life member) at the University of Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Political Sciences (LSE), BRICS Policy Centre in Brazil (PUC-Rio). Dr. Panova is also an alumna of the Asian Forum on Global Governance organized by ORF, India and Bucerius School/Zeit Stiftung, Germany. Since the Russian BRICS Chairship in 2015, Dr. Panova has been Co-Founder of the BRICS Civil Forum and Co-Chair for the Civil BRICS process initiated by the Russian civil society. Since 2015, Dr. Panova is a member of the Council of the Eurasian Women’s Forum.

As ORF’s President and member of the Foundation’s Board, he provides strategic direction and leadership to the foundation’s multiple centres on fundraising, research projects, platform design and outreach initiatives including stakeholder engagement. He curates the Raisina Dialogue, India’s annual flagship platform on geopolitics and geo-economics, and is the founder of CyFy, India’s annual conference on cybersecurity and internet governance. He spearheads the foundation’s efforts to foster new international partnerships and incubate young leaders networks and youth led conversations globally.

South Africa: SABTT

He currently serves as Dean of the Faculty of the Humanities at the University of the Free State, providing strategic leadership to 23 departments and advancing engaged, decolonial scholarship within the sector.

An NRF C1-rated researcher, Prof Masoga holds a PhD from the University of the Free State as well as multiple postgraduate qualifications in the humanities and musicology. His career spans senior roles in academia, research councils, and development institutions, including the National Research Foundation, the Development Bank of Southern Africa, the CRL Rights Commission, the University of Venda, the University of Limpopo, and the University of Zululand. Prof Masoga has published extensively in accredited journals and edited volumes on Indigenous Knowledge Systems, African thought, religion, climate change, and community-engaged scholarship. He is Series Editor of the Knowledge Pathing: Multi-, Inter- and Trans-Disciplining in Social Sciences book series, and has supervised numerous master’s and doctoral candidates across disciplines. A respected sector leader, he served as President of the South African Humanities Deans Association (SAHUDA) and sits on multiple national and international boards, editorial committees, and scientific bodies, contributing to debates on curriculum transformation, language policy, and the future of the Humanities and Social Sciences in Africa.

The BRICS Think Tanks Council (BTTC) website serves as the official platform for the council, which was proposed in March 2013 at a meeting of BRICS countries' think tanks and confirmed by BRICS Leaders at the eThekwini Summit (Durban, South Africa) that same month. The Council's purpose, as defined in its Declaration, is to form a platform for exchanging ideas among researchers, academia, and think tanks, convene the BRICS Academic Forum, and present policy recommendations to BRICS Leaders. BRICS cooperation is built on principles of collaborations & partnerships, equal sovereignty, and mutual respect.

The Council's research focuses on five key areas: BRICS Currencies (studying national currencies in trade, swap mechanisms, and alternative currencies), Expansion of BRICS (modalities and implications of expansion), New Technologies (AI, digital governance, closing digital gaps), BRICS Declarations (establishing archival databases for monitoring implementation), and Sustainable Development Goals (reviewing BRICS performance against Agenda 2030).

The Council comprises member institutions from eight countries: IPEA (Brazil), the National Committee for BRICS Research/NRC (Russia), Observer Research Foundation/ORF (India), China Council for BRICS Think Tank Cooperation/CCBTC (China), SABTT (South Africa), Institute for Political and International Studies/IPIS (Iran), Institute of Foreign Affairs/IFA (Ethiopia), and the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy/AGDA (UAE).

Key leadership includes: Dr. Keiti Da Rocha Gomes (Brazil, IPEA), Dr. Victoria Panova (Russia, HSE University, Head of BRICS Expert Council and Vice-Rector), Dr. Samir Saran (India, ORF President, curator of Raisina Dialogue), Dr. Jin Xin (China, CCBTC), Prof. Mogomme A. Masoga (South Africa, SABTT, Dean of Humanities at University of the Free State), Dr. Alireza Khoda Gholipour (Iran, IPIS), H.E. Jafer Bedru Geletu (Ethiopia, IFA Executive Director), and H.E. Nickolay E. Mladenov (UAE, AGDA Director-General, former UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process).

Recent publications include BAR Issue 11 (January 2026) on the BRICS 2025 theme "Strengthening global south cooperation for more inclusive and sustainable governance," the Recommendations of the 17th BRICS Academic Forum 2025 (July 2025), and the 17th BRICS Summit Rio de Janeiro Declaration 2025 (held July 6-7, 2025, under the same theme). The 17th BRICS Academic Forum (FABRICS) was hosted by IPEA on June 25-26, 2025, during Brazil's 2025 BRICS Presidency. Contact details and addresses are provided for all eight member institutions across Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Iran, Ethiopia, and the UAE.

## BRICS Think Tanks Council

Established in 2013, the BRICS Think Tank Council (BTTC) is formed by research centers designated by each of the BRICS member countries, upon nomination by their respective governments. Its main function is to promote the exchange of ideas and cooperation between researchers, academics and other research institutions. The BTTC is chaired by the think tank of the country holding the rotating BRICS presidency that year.

The BTTC aims to strengthen, promote and develop cooperation in research activities, knowledge sharing, capacity building and the formulation of public policy recommendations for the BRICS countries. Its duties include: holding regular meetings at least once a year; organizing the BRICS Academic Forum (FABRICS); preparing policy recommendations to be submitted to the leaders of the group; identifying priority areas for cooperation; conducting joint studies; facilitating exchange programs between member countries; and supporting the production of strategic knowledge in the respective nations.

**BRICS Policy Center researchers have participated since the first edition of the BRICS Academic Forum**. The meetings deal with different themes and bring together experts and researchers from academic communities, as well as members and representatives of civil society, and usually take place before the BRICS Summit in the host country that year. At the end of each Forum, the participating institutions produce a document with long-term recommendations for the BRICS, which is delivered to the heads of state. In the context of Brazil’s presidency of BRICS in 2025, the BTTC’s main priority will be to contribute to the institutional strengthening of the bloc. In addition, the thematic priorities defined by the Brazilian presidency will also guide the recommendations made to the leaders and will be debated in specific sessions during the 17th BRICS Academic Forum (FABRICS).

  
 Among the planned deliverables are:  
 **(1)** the BTTC’s document of recommendations to BRICS leaders;

**(2)** the publication of the Research Report entitled Portfolio on BRICS cooperation mechanisms; and

**(3)** the organization of the 17th FABRICS itself. The Institute for Applied Economic Research (IPEA) represents Brazil in the BTTC.

Source*:© BRICS 2025 – Content developed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Social Communication Secretariat of the Presidency of the Republic of Brazil*

# 怎样认识全球南方

 来源：《求是》2025/16   作者：当代世界研究中心   2025-08-16 09:00:00 

**怎样认识全球南方**

当代世界研究中心

  当前，全球南方在国际舞台上日益活跃，正成为一股重塑世界秩序的关键力量。习近平总书记指出：“‘全球南方’群体性崛起，是世界大变局的鲜明标志。”我们应怎样认识全球南方？全球南方国家有什么共同属性和鲜明特征？怎样推动全球南方在促进人类进步方面发挥更重要作用？

**一**

  全球南方的概念来源于“南方”国家。现有研究认为，1926年意大利马克思主义理论家葛兰西正式提出了“南方”概念。他当时关注到意大利南北发展差距问题，并初步说明“南方”概念所蕴含的反剥削、求发展等特性。一般来说，全球南方被认为是新兴市场国家和发展中国家的集合体。它包括亚洲、非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、大洋洲地区的大部分国家，这些国家大多地处北半球南部和南半球，具有相似的历史遭遇、共同的发展任务、相近的国际事务立场。

  全球南方的崛起历经数十年的积淀。二战后，西方殖民体系逐步瓦解，在亚非拉等原殖民地建立起一大批实现了民族独立的主权国家。这些国家在民族解放、反殖反霸等方面具有共同诉求，逐渐联合成一股重要的国际力量。1955年，万隆会议在印度尼西亚召开，标志着亚非新兴民族独立国家作为一个集体正式走入世界政治的舞台，向世界展现了其推动建立公正合理国际秩序的智慧、信念与行动。1961年，不结盟运动正式形成。该运动的成立，反映了广大南方国家主张国际关系民主化的强烈诉求，推动了这些国家捍卫国家主权、反对霸权主义、振兴民族经济的历史进程。1964年，77国集团成立并提出关于国际经济关系、贸易与发展的一整套主张，旨在推动南南合作，建立国际经济新秩序。20世纪70年代，中国提出“三个世界”划分的理论，进一步推动发展中国家身份认同，鼓励发展中国家独立自主，在国际事务中形成联合阵线。

  20世纪八九十年代以来，随着世界多极化和经济全球化深入发展，一大批新兴市场国家和发展中国家经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗和广泛合作，走上发展的快车道。数据统计，新兴市场国家和发展中国家过去20年对世界经济增长的贡献率高达80%，过去40年国内生产总值的全球占比从24%增至40%以上。全球南方群体性崛起，深刻改写国际政治格局和世界经济版图。

  近年来，全球南方更加积极主动捍卫自身权益、推动全球治理变革。在慕尼黑安全会议上，呼吁坚持多边主义、加强集体行动；在南方首脑会议上，要求改变不公正的国际秩序，摆脱几个世纪以来被西方推入的“绝对不利境地”；在不结盟运动第十九次峰会上，强调要全面尊重国际法和国际共识原则……全球南方展现出的态度更加自信，国际地位和影响力显著提升，为世界多极化、经济全球化和国际关系民主化注入强大动能。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

**独立自主是全球南方的政治底色。**全球南方国家大多有过被侵略、被殖民、被掠夺的苦难经历，深知和平的宝贵，珍视自身的独立地位。当前，强权政治、霸权行径扰乱世界安宁，已成为国际和平面临的最大破坏性因素。全球南方对此始终保持高度警惕，日益重视战略自主，坚决反对一切形式的霸权主义和强权政治，反对冷战思维和阵营对抗，反对干涉别国内政，强调“生存权”、“发展权”，明确拒绝选边站队，为维护世界和平稳定发挥着重要作用。近年来，拉美和加勒比国家呼吁反对外来干涉，非洲一些国家提出“第二次独立”等政治主张。在乌克兰危机、巴以冲突等问题上，全球南方国家大多摆脱西方影响，坚持基于历史经纬和事情本身是非曲直确立本国立场，主张劝和促谈、停火止战。2024年9月，17个全球南方国家在联合国成立乌克兰危机“和平之友”小组，寻求妥善解决危机方案，发出客观、理性的声音，得到国际社会广泛认同和赞赏。

**发展振兴是全球南方的历史使命。**发展承载着各国人民对美好生活的向往，是全球南方国家的第一要务。全球南方多数国家发展任务艰巨，但拥有自然资源丰富、市场潜力大等优势和红利，发展前景广阔。然而，由于国际议程设置权和规则制定权长期由少数西方国家垄断，全球南方国家在国际经济利益分配格局中处于不利地位，经济和社会发展容易受到外部因素影响和干扰。当前世界经济复苏乏力，发展中国家面临的发展挑战尤其严峻。在此关键当口，全球南方国家普遍认为，应合力推动更加包容、更加普惠、更有韧性的全球发展，加快落实2030年可持续发展议程；坚持互利共赢的合作观，拒绝以邻为壑、自私自利的狭隘政策，摒弃垄断发展优势的片面做法，保障各国平等发展权利，促进共同发展繁荣。

  2024年7月11日至13日，全球共享发展行动论坛第二届高级别会议在北京举行，来自160多个国家、国际组织和其他机构的代表参会交流研讨。本届会议下设“推动全球南方现代化”等5场平行分论坛。图为7月12日，“分论坛一·推动全球南方现代化：新路径、新愿景”专题研讨环节。 中新社记者 田雨昊/摄

**怎样认识全球南方**

当代世界研究中心

  当前，全球南方在国际舞台上日益活跃，正成为一股重塑世界秩序的关键力量。习近平总书记指出：“‘全球南方’群体性崛起，是世界大变局的鲜明标志。”我们应怎样认识全球南方？全球南方国家有什么共同属性和鲜明特征？怎样推动全球南方在促进人类进步方面发挥更重要作用？

**一**

  全球南方的概念来源于“南方”国家。现有研究认为，1926年意大利马克思主义理论家葛兰西正式提出了“南方”概念。他当时关注到意大利南北发展差距问题，并初步说明“南方”概念所蕴含的反剥削、求发展等特性。一般来说，全球南方被认为是新兴市场国家和发展中国家的集合体。它包括亚洲、非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、大洋洲地区的大部分国家，这些国家大多地处北半球南部和南半球，具有相似的历史遭遇、共同的发展任务、相近的国际事务立场。

  全球南方的崛起历经数十年的积淀。二战后，西方殖民体系逐步瓦解，在亚非拉等原殖民地建立起一大批实现了民族独立的主权国家。这些国家在民族解放、反殖反霸等方面具有共同诉求，逐渐联合成一股重要的国际力量。1955年，万隆会议在印度尼西亚召开，标志着亚非新兴民族独立国家作为一个集体正式走入世界政治的舞台，向世界展现了其推动建立公正合理国际秩序的智慧、信念与行动。1961年，不结盟运动正式形成。该运动的成立，反映了广大南方国家主张国际关系民主化的强烈诉求，推动了这些国家捍卫国家主权、反对霸权主义、振兴民族经济的历史进程。1964年，77国集团成立并提出关于国际经济关系、贸易与发展的一整套主张，旨在推动南南合作，建立国际经济新秩序。20世纪70年代，中国提出“三个世界”划分的理论，进一步推动发展中国家身份认同，鼓励发展中国家独立自主，在国际事务中形成联合阵线。

  20世纪八九十年代以来，随着世界多极化和经济全球化深入发展，一大批新兴市场国家和发展中国家经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗和广泛合作，走上发展的快车道。数据统计，新兴市场国家和发展中国家过去20年对世界经济增长的贡献率高达80%，过去40年国内生产总值的全球占比从24%增至40%以上。全球南方群体性崛起，深刻改写国际政治格局和世界经济版图。

--- SOURCE 1: Postcolonialism and Orientalism: Said, Spivak, Bhabha, and the Critique of Colonial Discourse | Philosophy in Summary — Thinkers & Syntheses ---
URL: https://filosofiaemresumo.com.br/en/artigos/postcolonialism-orientalism-said-spivak-fanon

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive survey of postcolonial theory, tracing its precursors and key figures who consolidated the field. The article covers four main thinkers and the critical debates surrounding postcolonial theory.

**Precursors:**
- W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), an African-American sociologist, formulated "double consciousness" in *The Souls of Black Folk* (1903)—the inner experience of seeing oneself through others' eyes, divided between being American and Black. He also coined the "color line" thesis, arguing that racial boundaries (not just class) structure modern world politics.
- Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) analyzed colonized subjects' internalization of negative self-images in *Black Skin, White Masks* (1952), showing colonialism as a psychic and ontological wound, not merely economic/political domination.

**Key Theorists:**
- **Edward Said** (1935–2003), Palestinian-American critic at Columbia, founded postcolonial studies with *Orientalism* (1978). Drawing on Foucault's power/knowledge and Gramsci's hegemony, he argued "the Orient" is a Western discursive construction—an essentialized, backward, feminized Other that authorizes Western governance. He introduced "imaginative geographies" and later "contrapuntal reading" in *Culture and Imperialism* (1993).
- **Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak** (b. 1942), Derrida's translator, combined deconstruction, Marxism, and feminism. Her canonical essay "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) argued the subaltern's intelligibility is blocked by colonial and national representational codes. Using the example of *sati* (widow self-immolation), she showed the subaltern woman faces two competing representations (British "white men saving brown women from brown men" vs. Indian patriarchy), neither allowing her to speak. She coined "epistemic violence" and "strategic essentialism" (from which she later distanced herself).
- **Homi Bhabha** (b. 1949), author of *The Location of Culture* (1994), shifted focus to ambivalence in colonial relations. His concepts include "hybridity" (no culture remains pure), "mimicry" (colonial imitation that is "almost the same, but not quite," exposing colonial fragility), and the "third space" (interstitial site of cultural negotiation transcending binaries).

**Critiques and Debates:**
- Marxist critics like Aijaz Ahmad (*In Theory*, 1992) charged postcolonial theory with privileging discourse over political economy and class, and with being a comfortable product of the Western academy written by diasporic intellectuals.
- Latin American decolonial thought (Quijano, Mignolo, Dussel) differs by locating modernity/coloniality's origin in 1492 rather than 19th–20th century imperialism, and calling for a more radical epistemic break with European categories.

**Essential readings** listed include works by Du Bois, Fanon, Said, Spivak, Bhabha, and Ahmad. The article concludes that thinking the colonial inheritance is a condition of honest reflection on culture, identity, and power.
</summary>

"Orientalism is thus a historically structured set of knowledges and institutions — philology, literature, anthropology, colonial administration — that do not describe a pre-existing reality but fabricate it.", "Her provocative 'no' is less an ontological denial than a diagnosis of the conditions of listening: the problem is not that the subaltern has no voice, but that there is no place from which her speech can be heard as speech.", "Mimicry describes the subversive effect when the colonized imitates the colonizer: the copy 'almost the same, but not quite' exposes the artificiality and fragility of colonial authority.", "Du Bois also coined the thesis of the color line ('the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line'): the racial boundary, and not only class inequality, structures modern world politics.", "Far from invalidating the field, these controversies show its centrality: to think the colonial inheritance is, today, a condition of any honest reflection on culture, identity, and power."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an educational blog post by Dr. Vishwanath Bite, a Professor of English with over 15 years of experience and UGC NET English coach, explaining postcolonial theory and concepts for UGC NET English Literature aspirants. The post defines postcolonial theory as a framework critiquing the cultural, political, and literary legacies of colonialism, examining how power, identity, race, language, and history were shaped by colonial experience.

Key concepts covered include:
1. **Hybridity (Homi K. Bhabha)** – cultural mixing between colonized and colonizer cultures; example: Salman Rushdie's *Midnight's Children*
2. **Orientalism (Edward Said)** – from Said's 1978 work, how the West stereotyped the East to justify domination; example: E.M. Forster's *A Passage to India*
3. **Mimicry (Bhabha)** – colonized people imitating colonizers "almost the same, but not quite"; example: Chinua Achebe's *No Longer at Ease*
4. **Subaltern (Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak)** – marginalized populations denied voice; Spivak's question "Can the subaltern speak?"; example: Mahasweta Devi's "Draupadi"
5. **Othering** – defining another group as inferior to justify domination; example: Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness*
6. **Colonial Discourse** – texts reinforcing colonial ideology; example: 18th-19th century travel literature
7. **Language and Power** – colonial languages marginalizing native tongues; example: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's *Decolonising the Mind*

Major theorists listed: Edward Said, Homi K. Bhabha, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Frantz Fanon (*The Wretched of the Earth*), and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o. Indian authors with postcolonial themes include Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Amitav Ghosh, and Jhumpa Lahiri.

**Core Definition & Origins:** The concept of third space is attributed to postcolonial scholar Homi K. Bhabha (in *The Location of Culture*, 1994). It refers to a site of cultural hybridity where multiple cultures intersect, creating new cultural identities. These interstitial spaces arise from the colonizer/colonized dynamic and serve as sites of resistance where marginalized individuals (colonial subjects) can negotiate, transform, and redefine identities imposed by dominant cultural discourses. Key example: the dissemination of the English Bible in India, which resulted in a reinterpretation creating a space neither entirely English nor Indian. Physical examples include festivals, migrant-run restaurants, and the US-Mexico borderlands.

**Third Space in Postcolonial Studies:** Bhabha links third space to hybridity—Amar Acheraïou notes "hybridity is the third space." Third spaces are "liminal and interstitial sites where cultural meaning is not simply reflected but actively produced." Bhabha gives physicality to the concept through the Gacaca, a traditional Rwandan meeting space for post-genocide adjudication between Tutsis and Hutus, described as a "site of in-betweenness" between accused and accuser. Bhabha also examines a passage from Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* where a "white worsted" thread around a dying native's neck illustrates the third space—a commodity of colonial trade rendered untranslatable in the colonial context. Related theorists include Edward Said (*Orientalism*, 1978) on the "Orient" as a Western-created idea, and Gloria Anzaldúa (*Borderlands/La Frontera*, 1987) on borderlands as hybrid cultural spaces.

**Edward Soja's Thirdspace:** Soja applied Bhabha's concept to urban geography in *Thirdspace* (1996), drawing on Henri Lefebvre's "spatial triad" (*The Production of Space*, 1974): spatial practice (physical city space), representations of space (official/administrative conceptions), and spaces of representation (inhabitants' cultural understanding). Soja delineates three types: Firstspace (real/physical), Secondspace (imagined/conceived), and Thirdspace (hybrid of real and imagined). Using a market as example: firstspace is geographic location, secondspace is how planners conceive it, thirdspace is lived space where communities socialize. Soja coined "critical thirding as othering"—a rejection of either/or binary thinking (subject-object, male-female, black-white, etc.). Smagorinsky notes thirdspace focuses on how least affluent, privileged people inhabit and ascribe meaning to place.

**Third Space Feminism:** Feminist scholars have explored third spaces as sites for women to resist traditional roles. Golnaraghi and Daghar analyze how online third spaces allow Muslim women to renegotiate identities beyond Orientalist and traditionalist Islamic binaries (e.g., the 2013 "Somewhere in America #Mipsterz" video). Marissa Vigneault discusses Hannah Wilke's *S.O.S. Starification Object Series* (1974-1982) and the #MeToo movement as third-space resistance. Adela C. Licona's *Zines in Third Space* examines feminist-of-color zines (e.g., Mimi Nguyen's *Evolution of a Race Riot* 1997; Jackie Wang's *Memoirs of a Queer Hapa* 2007) as third-space radical rhetorical performances.

**Concluding Thoughts:** Shehrazade Emmambokus developed "Overlapping Space," fusing Third Space, diaspora space, and translation (focused on second-generation migrants). Third space theory has practical applications including LGBTQ+ inclusive curriculums (Steven P. Camicia's *Critical Democratic Education and LGBTQ-Inclusive Curriculum*, 2016). The concept now serves as a framework in postcolonial studies, queer theory, subaltern studies, and diaspora theory.

This is a Wikipedia article on "Decolonization of knowledge" (also called epistemic or epistemological decolonization), a concept in decolonial scholarship that critiques the hegemony of Western knowledge systems and seeks to construct and legitimize other knowledge systems through alternative epistemologies, ontologies, and methodologies.

**Background:** The concept inquires into historical mechanisms of knowledge production and their colonial and ethnocentric foundations. Scholars like Budd L. Hall, Jaco S. Dreyer, and Anibal Quijano argue that Western knowledge systems, which emerged during the Renaissance and Enlightenment, were deployed to legitimize European colonial endeavors and continue to "exclude, marginalise and dehumanise" those with different systems of knowledge. Linda Tuhiwai Smith's book "Decolonizing Methodologies" is a foundational text. Colonialism has ended legally and politically, but its legacy continues in "colonial situations" referred to as "coloniality."

**Origin and Development:** While rooted in resistance since 1492, its academic emergence is recent. It traces to Latin American thinkers, particularly Peruvian sociologist Anibal Quijano, who linked "coloniality of power" with "coloniality of knowledge." It developed from critical stances including postcolonialism, subaltern studies, and postmodernism, drawing on José Carlos Mariátegui, Frantz Fanon, and Immanuel Wallerstein. Political decolonization in the 20th century failed to achieve epistemological decolonization.

**Themes:** The concept involves a critique of objectivity as a colonial legacy, arguing that notions of truth and fact are "local" rather than universal. It holds that the Western knowledge system reduced epistemic diversity and suppressed other knowledge forms. Scholars like Lewis Gordon argue "knowledges" (plural) is more appropriate than "knowledge" (singular). Walter Mignolo describes the modern foundation of knowledge as territorial and imperial. Achille Mbembe says decolonization means contesting hegemonic Western epistemology.

**Significance:** Anibal Quijano argues epistemological decolonization is necessary for intercultural communication and alternative rationality. Ndlovu-Gatsheni says it addresses the "asymmetrical global intellectual division of labor" where Europe and North America produce theories consumed globally.

**Approaches:**
- **Indigenous decolonization:** Contests and reframes narratives about indigenous histories and colonial effects, adopts critical stance toward western-centric research, and seeks to reposition knowledge within Indigenous cultural practices. Some decolonial work relying on Western political thought has been criticized as paradoxically furthering dispossession.
- **Relational model of knowledge:** Louis Botha et al argue indigenous knowledges are relational, valuing relationships between actors, objects, and settings, and are fundamentally spiritual.
- **In academia:** Calls for greater representation of pluralistic ideas, inclusive curricula, expanded reading lists, and scrutiny of authority figures and epistemologies. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o emphasizes language as the starting point of decolonization; Mahmood Mamdani argues single-language universities are a colonial heritage and advocates for multilingual, diverse academic traditions.
- **Disciplines:** Proponents call for decolonization of history, science and history of science, philosophy (especially epistemology), psychology, sociology, religious studies, legal studies, and ethnomusicology.
  - **History:** The "colonialist worldview" has impacted the field; decolonial approach examines non-Western world on its own terms.
  - **Modern science:** Contests science as "purely objective, solely empirical, immaculately rational"; critics identify scientism as an ideology rooted in the Enlightenment. Boisselle argues for a "relational science" based on "relational ontology"; Samuel Bendeck Sotillos critiques modern science's rejection of metaphysics and promotes sacred science (scientia sacra).
  - **History of science:** Since the mid-1980s, postcolonial histories seek "decentered, diasporic, or 'global' rewriting" of nation-centred imperial grand narratives, acknowledging diverse global origins of science.
  - **Philosophy:** The decolonial turn liberates reason beyond Enlightenment rationality; scholars argue for inclusion of Islamic, African, Indian, Chinese, Asian, and Latin American philosophy.
  - **Psychology:** Decolonization is "essentially a psychological project" involving "recovery of self"; seeks to show colonialism and Eurocentric presumptions are ingrained in modern psychological science, creating space for indigenous knowledge and lived experiences.

URL: https://www.formajournal.org/essays/decolonial-sources-the-coloniality-of-power-reoriginalization-and-the-critique-of-imperialism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This essay by Abraham Acosta, published in FORMA Journal (Vol. 1, No. 1, 2019), is a critical examination of Aníbal Quijano's concept of "coloniality of power" within decolonial theory. The author argues that despite coloniality of power's centrality to decolonial thought, little rigorous scrutiny has been applied to Quijano's own formulations. Through close reading of two of Quijano's essays—"Colonialidad y modernidad/racionalidad" (1992) and "Colonialidad de poder, cultura y conocimiento en América Latina" (1997)—Acosta contends that the coloniality of power is riddled with ambiguity and contradiction, potentially undermining its status as the theoretical bedrock of decoloniality.

Key arguments include: (1) Quijano defines colonialism broadly as "a formal system of political domination by some societies over others," which does not limit colonialism to European domination, thereby undermining decoloniality's positioning against Western modernity specifically. (2) Acosta analyzes discrepancies between the Spanish original and two English translations of Quijano's essay, noting that the 2007 republished translation (also attributed to Sonia Therborn) added the qualifier "Eurocentered" to colonialism—a modification not present in the original or the 1999 translation—revealing an attempt to resolve an irreducible ambiguity. (3) Quijano distinguishes "political colonialism" (direct subordination/coercion, drawing on Gramscian notions of domination) from "cultural colonialism" (hegemonic, ideological colonization of the dominated's imagination), with coloniality of power springing from the latter. (4) Acosta argues that cultural colonialism/coloniality of power functions merely as a synonym for hegemony and "expresses nothing more than the ideology of any reigning form of hegemonic power," failing to account for the underlying political structures of domination. (5) Quijano's broader concept of "reoriginalization"—a transhistorical dynamic of cultural transformation of which coloniality of power is but one instance—creates further problems: if all cultures have been reoriginalized at some point, then there are no truly "original" cultures (Mayan, Aztec, Incan, etc.) to reclaim, nullifying the premise of decoloniality itself. (6) Acosta concludes that coloniality of power and reoriginalization "partake of the same deep ideological grammar" and are formally indistinct from one another, meaning decoloniality—as the oppositional countermeasure to coloniality—is equally undermined. The essay ultimately questions whether one can "de-reoriginalize" at all, since coloniality of power is the innermost mechanical activity of the very transhistorical process Quijano affirms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Thus colonialism, in the sense of a formal system of political domination by some societies over others seems a question of the past." (Quijano, 1999, 41)
</key_excerpts>

This is an Academia.edu page for the paper "Epistemology and domination: problems with the coloniality of knowledge thesis in Latin American decolonial theory" by Paul A Chambers (Faculty Member, Tecnologico de Antioquia), a 40-page academic paper.

--- SOURCE 15: Decolonising epistemologies - Alana Lentin ---
URL: https://www.alanalentin.net/2017/02/10/decolonising-epistemologies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the second post in Alana Lentin's "Race Critical and Decolonial Sociology" blog series, published February 10, 2017, focusing on decolonising epistemologies. The post examines the interconnections between postcolonial theory and decolonial approaches, exploring epistemological implications and possibilities for transformative social and political action.

**Postcolonial Theory**: Postcolonialism grew out of anti-colonial movements and theorizes both the legacy of European colonization and the aspiration for emancipation. Key thinkers discussed include Couze Venn (who frames postcolonialism as both postcolonial and post-occidental), Ella Shohat (questioning when the "post-colonial" begins), Gyan Prakash (arguing that both nationalism and Marxism reproduced colonial master narratives, and that postcolonial critique must "undo the Eurocentrism produced by the institution of the west's trajectory"), and Homi Bhabha (the postcolonial subject as hybrid, occupying an in-between position). The postcolonial is relational rather than territorial, with the Third World subject seen as deterritorialised and politics understood as a "politics of positionality."

**Dirlik's Critique**: Arif Dirlik offers a scathing critique of postcolonial theory, arguing it only became significant once Third World academics succeeded in the western academy. He contends that postcolonial discourse is "an expression not so much of agony over identity... but of newfound power," and that postcolonial critics generalize from local contexts to the global while denying global forces' impact on the local. Critics like O'Hanlon and Washbrook argue the focus on hybridity leads to a "depoliticising insulation of social from material domains," making postcolonialism conservative. David Macey's critique of the "post-colonial Fanon" is quoted at length—that the angry Third Worldist Fanon was replaced by one "worried about identity politics" who "is no longer angry."

**Historicism and Modernity**: Dipesh Chakrabarty's "Provincializing Europe" problematises history as a narrative of transition, showing how Indian nationalists internalised western universal presumptions. Gurminder Bhambra critiques modernisation theory as a "theory of convergence" and the multiple modernities approach for remaining Eurocentric, arguing instead that "colonisation was not simply an outcome of modernity, but, rather, modernity itself, the modern world, developed out of colonial encounters." Bhambra emphasises interrelatedness and "connected and entangled histories," exemplified by how cotton milling in Manchester depended on cotton from India.

**The Decolonial Approach**: Decolonial thinking originates mainly with Latin American scholars (Ramon Grosfoguel, Walter Mignolo, Enrique Dussel, Arturo Escobar, Gloria Anzaldua) and traces its genealogy through liberation theology, dependency theory, and Latin American autonomous social science. Unlike postcolonialism, decolonial thinkers call for "delinking" from modern colonial epistemology rather than merely deconstructing it. Mignolo states: "the rhetoric of modernity is that of salvation, whereas the logic of coloniality is a logic of imperial oppression... you cannot have modernity without coloniality."

**The Modernity/Coloniality Research Programme**: Escobar outlines five key points: (1) the conquest of the Americas as the starting point of modernity (Dussel's "first modernity"), not the Enlightenment; (2) colonialism as constitutive of modernity (Quijano's "coloniality of power"—colonial logics persisting after colonialism); (3) modernity as a worldwide process (Dussel's "transmodernity," giving voice to negated Others); (4) domination of non-Europeans as integral to modernity, with silenced knowledges; and (5) Eurocentrism as the knowledge form of modernity/coloniality.

**Impacts on the Academy**: Boaventura de Sousa Santos's "abyssal thinking" is discussed—modern knowledge and law divide social reality into visible and invisible realms, rendering indigenous and plebian knowledges nonexistent. Mignolo's "border thinking" (drawing on Gloria Anzaldua) rejects both Eurocentrism and anti-western fundamentalism, redefining concepts like citizenship, democracy, and human rights for non-western contexts, with the Zapatista movement as an example. Gender is introduced as a further power divide through Anzaldua and Maria Lugones.

A comment from Erik Ljungberg (April 19, 2019) challenges the claim that the Industrial Revolution depended on Indian cotton, noting England sourced cotton from America (citing "Empire of Cotton" by Sven Beckert), though acknowledging this doesn't change the overall argument about interconnectedness.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"the rhetoric of modernity is that of salvation, whereas the logic of coloniality is a logic of imperial oppression. They go hand in hand, and you cannot have modernity without coloniality; the unfinished project of modernity carries over its shoulders the unfinished project of coloniality." — Walter Mignolo
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: The South Centre | Revisiting the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and its legacy ---
URL: https://www.southcentre.int/question/revisiting-the-1955-bandung-asian-african-conference-and-its-legacy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the South Centre presents an article by Adriano José Timossi titled "Revisiting the 1955 Bandung Asian-African Conference and its legacy," published in South Bulletin 85 (15 May 2015). The article examines the historic Bandung Conference held April 18-24, 1955, in Bandung, Indonesia, which marked the first-ever summit-level meeting of independence leaders from 29 Asian and African countries. Key leaders included Chou En-Lai (China), Jawaharlal Nehru (India), U Nu (Burma), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), President Sukarno (Indonesia), and leaders from Liberia, Sudan, Gold Coast, Jordan, Iran, Ceylon, Nepal, Pakistan, and Philippines.

The article highlights Sukarno's opening speech, in which he declared that "colonialism is not yet dead" and warned of its "modern dress" in the form of economic, intellectual, and physical control. He called for Asian-African unity as essential for prosperity and world safety, emphasizing the conference's purpose to foster understanding, appreciation, and collective action among developing nations.

The Bandung Final Communiqué established the foundation for South-South cooperation, supporting UN human rights principles, deploring racial segregation, opposing colonialism in all forms, and advocating for universal UN membership and equitable Asian-African representation in the Security Council. The communiqué also established the Ten Bandung Principles, which include respect for fundamental human rights, sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of all races and nations, abstention from intervention in internal affairs, peaceful dispute settlement, and promotion of mutual interests and cooperation.

In the 60 years following the conference, the "Bandung Spirit" led to significant achievements: decolonization of most developing countries, establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) in 1961, the Group of 77 (G77) in 1964, and other Southern institutions including the South Centre and South Commission. Regional initiatives reflecting Bandung ideals include the African Union, UNASUR, CELAC, ASEAN, and SAARC. The article also cites the emergence of BRICS, the BRICS Development Bank, and the Bank of the South as continuing examples of Bandung's vision for South-South cooperation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are often told 'Colonialism is dead'. Let us not be deceived or even soothed by that. I say to you, colonialism is not yet dead... Colonialism has also its modern dress, in the form of economic control, intellectual control, actual physical control by a small but alien community within a nation." - President Sukarno, opening speech, 1955 Bandung Conference, "Our task is first to seek an understanding of each other, and out of that understanding will come a greater appreciation of each other, and out of that appreciation will come collective action." - President Sukarno, "The 1955 Bandung Conference led to the establishment in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). This was followed by the establishment of the Group of 77 (G77) in 1964." - Adriano José Timossi, "For many generations our peoples have been the voiceless ones in the world. We have been the unregarded, the peoples for whom decisions were made by others whose interests were paramount, the peoples who lived in poverty and humiliation." - President Sukarno
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Bandung Conference 1955 ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g5UQ7Z3C2QQ

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a video description and transcript from the Research Society of International Law (RSIL) commemorating the 70th anniversary of the Bandung Conference of 1955. Held from 18-24 April 1955 in Bandung, Indonesia, the conference brought together leaders from 29 Asian and African nations in what was the largest gathering of its kind on Asian or African soil at the time. The conference took place against the backdrop of the Cold War and the surging post-war national liberation movements in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It gave rise to the Non-Aligned Movement, the concept of the "third world," and the Global South, advocating for an alternative form of just global governance and countering colonialism in all its forms. The conference produced the "Ten Principles of Bandung," a political statement outlining guiding principles for developing countries to promote peace and cooperation. These principles include: (1) respect for fundamental human rights and UN Charter purposes; (2) respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations; (3) recognition of equality of all races and nations, large and small; (4) abstention from intervention or interference in internal affairs of other countries; (5) respect for the right of each nation to defend itself in conformity with the UN Charter; (6) abstention from using collective defense arrangements for big power interests and from exerting pressures on other countries; (7) refraining from aggression or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence; (8) peaceful settlement of all disputes; (9) promotion of mutual interests and cooperation; and (10) respect for justice and international obligations. The video notes that in the decades following Bandung, friction among conference members increased as decolonization progressed, making the concept of Asian-African solidarity less meaningful. On its 70th anniversary, the content asks whether the principles remain relevant today, noting that while they are deeply under threat, their observance is needed more than ever amid rising global tensions. The video was posted on 25 February 2025 and has received 8,247 views.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Bandung Conference set the stage for the Non-Aligned Movement and the rise of the Global South, advocating for self-determination, sovereignty, and global cooperation outside the influence of major powers."

--- SOURCE 4: Bandung Conference - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandung_Conference

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Bandung Conference (also known as the Asian–African or Afro–Asian Conference) was a landmark meeting of Asian and African states held from April 18–24, 1955, in Bandung, West Java, Indonesia. Twenty-nine countries participated, representing approximately 1.5 billion people (54% of the world's population). The conference was organized by Indonesia, Burma (Myanmar), India, Ceylon (Sri Lanka), and Pakistan, and was coordinated by Ruslan Abdulgani, secretary general of Indonesia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Its stated aims were to promote Afro-Asian economic and cultural cooperation and to oppose colonialism or neocolonialism by any nation.

Key organizers included Indonesian President Sukarno, Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, and Chinese leaders Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. The conference was motivated by the desire to create a unified non-aligned identity independent of both Western and Soviet influence during the Cold War, as well as concerns over Western reluctance to consult Asian nations on decisions affecting the region. Sukarno sought support for Indonesia's claim to West New Guinea (West Papua).

Major debate centered on whether Soviet policies should be censured alongside Western colonialism; a consensus was reached condemning "colonialism in all of its manifestations," implicitly censuring both the Soviet Union and the West. Zhou Enlai, who survived an assassination attempt (the Kashmir Princess incident) en route to the conference, displayed a moderate and conciliatory attitude, signing an agreement on dual nationality with Indonesia and endorsing the right of all nations to choose their own systems. Nehru, who advocated for non-alignment and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, received a generally negative reception and was criticized as arrogant. China also voiced support for Palestine at the conference.

The conference produced the Dasasila Bandung (Bandung's Ten Principles), a 10-point declaration on the promotion of world peace and cooperation, incorporating principles of the UN Charter and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. These principles covered respect for human rights, sovereignty, territorial integrity, equality of races and nations, non-interference in internal affairs, self-defense rights, abstention from collective defense arrangements serving big power interests, refraining from aggression, peaceful dispute settlement, promotion of mutual interests, and respect for justice and international obligations.

The United States was not officially represented (at the urging of Secretary of State John Foster Dulles), but formed a "Working Group on the Afro-Asian Conference" involving multiple agencies for propaganda and "Image Management." Representative Adam Clayton Powell Jr. attended unofficially, sponsored by Ebony and Jet magazines, and spoke in favor of American foreign policy. African American author Richard Wright also attended and later published "The Color Curtain: A Report on the Bandung Conference."

The conference was a step toward the eventual creation of the Non-Aligned Movement (formed at the Belgrade Summit in 1961), though the two initiatives ran in parallel and sometimes in confrontation during the 1960s. A proposed second Bandung Conference in Algiers failed due to events including the 1965 Algerian coup, the ouster of Sukarno, and the 1966 Ghanaian coup. A 50th anniversary Asian-African Summit was held in 2005 in Jakarta and Bandung, launching the New Asian–African Strategic Partnership (NAASP). A 60th anniversary summit was held in 2015 with delegates from 109 Asian and African countries. A 70th anniversary "Bharat Summit" was organized by the Telangana government in Hyderabad, India, in April 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The twenty-nine countries that participated represented a total population of 1.5 billion people, 54% of the world's population."

--- SOURCE 6: BRICS | Global South Studies ---
URL: https://www.globalsouthstudies.org/keyword-essay/brics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an academic keyword essay by Sitinga Kachipande (published August 19, 2022 on Global South Studies) providing a comprehensive overview of the BRICS coalition—Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa—and its significance as a major emerging economies bloc representing the Global South.

KEY FACTS AND STATISTICS:
- The five BRICS nations collectively represent approximately 41% of the world's population, 30% of the world's geographic area, 24% of GDP, and 16% of international trade (2019 World Bank data).
- The term "BRIC" was coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill to describe countries with the biggest potential for economic growth in the Global South. South Africa was added in 2010, creating the "BRICS" acronym.
- O'Neill's 2001 thesis predicted these nations would dominate global economic growth within 10 years; a 2003 follow-up by Dominic Wilson and Roopa Purushothaman projected BRIC economies would surpass existing global economic powers' wealth by 2050 due to low labor and production costs.

HISTORICAL EVOLUTION:
- 2006: Foreign ministers began formal meetings corresponding with the UN General Assembly.
- 2009: First high-level summit held in Russia, where heads of state agreed to strengthen financial ties and advocate for more prominent roles in multilateral organizations.
- Late 2010: South Africa invited to join.
- The BRICS maintain a physical headquarters (BRICS Towers in Shanghai) and operate a joint "virtual secretariat" (www.infobrics.org) rather than a conventional permanent secretariat.
- The BRICS formed the New Development Bank (NDB) in 2014 to address infrastructure financing challenges for Global South countries and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) in 2014 for short-term liquidity safeguards.

POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC ACTIVITIES:
- The BRICS have called for reforming global governance institutions like the UN Security Council to give greater voice to Global South nations, and opposed Global North interventions in Libya (2011) and Iraq (2003).
- They established the BRICS Business Council (2013), BRICS Film Festival (2016), academic forum (2009), and BRICS Think Tank (2013).
- China alone grew to become the world's second largest economy by 2010.

CRITICISMS AND CHALLENGES:
- Critics point to heterogeneity (geographic, economic, and political differences) undermining cooperation, including vast economic disparities between members (China and India's growth vastly outpacing Russia, Brazil, and South Africa).
- Some critics argue BRICS are "new imperialists" maintaining exploitative relationships and embracing neoliberal capitalism, which hinders social development goals.
- Critics cite failures including lack of influence on COVID-19 vaccine distribution despite G20 membership, low trade integration, and lack of coordination on priority issues.
- Supporters argue the informal structure and heterogeneity are points of strength allowing inclusivity and expansion.

FUTURE OUTLOOK:
- During Russia's 2014 Crimea invasion, BRICS members abstained from publicly endorsing UN resolutions condemning Russia and calling for peaceful resolution without sanctions, demonstrating refusal to support US-led Global North hegemony.
- During Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, China, India, and South Africa abstained from condemning Russia in UN resolutions; Brazil voted in favor but objected to economic sanctions. The group was exploring alternate channels for continued trade and finance with Russia.
- Analysts agree BRICS have seriously weakened the current world order and laid the foundation for a multipolar world order, representing an irreversible shift in global geopolitics.

The essay includes extensive references from scholars including Oliver Stuenkel, Harsh V. Pant, Immanuel Wallerstein, Patrick Bond, and others, and includes the author's biographical information as a sociology professor at Montgomery College with expertise in Global Political Economy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The acronym BRICS comprises the nations of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa which represent the five major emerging economies; that is, the countries in the Global South which had the biggest potential for economic growth."

- Connected the Zapotec concepts of *ombligo* (belly button) and *obligación* (obligation): obligation is a course of responsible action arising from being interconnected with each other and the non-human world. Knowledge requires "making relatives" and relationality that includes water, land, wind, and animals (expanding beyond human-centric relations per Melanie Yazzie).
- Warned against appropriation in academic settings when engaging colonized knowledge systems without obligation, and against reproducing Eurocentric hierarchies in citation and writing practices.
- Described the "University of Communality" project in Oaxaca/Tehuantepec isthmus, which enacts higher education as a communal responsibility, honoring communal practices, languages, values, and governance structures of Indigenous communities.
- Expressed concern about universities moving toward commercialization of knowledge where "objective" knowledge is valued by its ability to make profits.

**Opening segments:**
- Elder Colleen Sitting Eagle (Sipiyana'tokumiyaki), a Siksika language instructor and elder for the series, opened with a blessing in her language, sharing about the power of Indigenous people to fight battles (residential schools, current addictions crisis in Siksika), and promoting language and cultural preservation. She noted the Indigenous bishop for Canada is Bishop Sydney Black from Six Nations.
- Dr. Smith highlighted two inspirations: Violet King (Calgary-born first Black woman lawyer in Canada, who refused limits placed on her) and Maya Angelou ("courage is the most important of all virtues, because without courage, we can't practice any other virtue consistently").
- The session cited Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's idea that "decolonization is not a metaphor," and discussed prefixes (post-, neo-, decolonial), knowledge production in universities, curriculum and citational practices, and shifting from university to "pluri-university."

**Discussion:**
- Q&A addressed that decolonial thinking comes from battlefields, not classrooms, and that knowledge production is disconnected from land, place, and territories; the connection between degradation of a people's humanity and inability to achieve epistemic freedom was emphasized.

--- SOURCE 19: Towards an epistemological alliance for the decolonization of ---
URL: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/towards-epistemological-alliance-decolonization-knowledge-global-south-and-global-north

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This UNESCO "Idea" article, written by Obrillant Damus (socio-anthropologist, linguist, educator, and professor at the Université d'État d'Haiti, Université Quisqueya, and the University of Shebrooke), was published on 12 April 2021 and argues for a constructive epistemological alliance between the global North and global South to decolonize knowledge and shape the future of education. Damus contends that the monocultural educational paradigm "crushes local knowledge" in its multiple dimensions and promotes socio-epistemic separation that hinders the hybridization of knowledge essential for human survival. He advocates for integrating local and indigenous knowledge holders into formal education systems, using ancestral/local languages as vehicles of instruction in formerly colonized countries to achieve "intellectual liberation and autonomy," and building education on an "ecology of knowledge" that links Southern and Northern epistemologies. The article describes three harmful phenomena to address: auto-epistemicide (local knowledge disappearing because it is not valued, especially by youth), endo-epistemic practices (actors abandoning local knowledge), and exo-epistemic practices (Western-centred intervention causing disappearance of local knowledge, with destruction of traditional technical knowledge termed "technocide"). Damus argues that local and indigenous knowledge systems are crucial not only for human sustainability but also for planetary sustainability through biodiversity conservation. He calls for education that forms "cosmocentric (versus egocentric)" beings capable of overcoming unsustainable dichotomies (Man/Nature; Us/Them; Nature/Culture; Logical/Irrational) and emphasizes that "the future of education and human-planetary sustainability is not conceivable without a constructive alliance between the epistemologies of the North and the South." The article is based on a background paper prepared for the International Commission on the Futures of Education, and the ideas expressed are those of the author, not necessarily the official position of UNESCO.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Facebook post from the page "Black HistoryStudies" (dated April 16, likely 2026), which presents an educational graphic explaining the concept of "Coloniality of Knowledge." The post defines this concept as first introduced by Aníbal Quijano and expanded by scholars including Walter Mignolo and Dr. Sabelo Ndlovu-Gatsheni, describing how Eurocentric worldviews continue to dominate global knowledge systems.

The graphic highlights five interwoven mechanisms of Eurocentric Hegemony:
1. **Epistemicide** – the killing, destruction, and erasure of non-Western knowledge systems, replaced by colonial knowledge systems (attributed to Boaventura de Sousa Santos).
2. **Linguicide** – the killing or suppression of languages, popularized by Tove Skutnabb-Kangas and expanded by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o in "Decolonising the Mind," showing how linguistic domination serves cultural erasure.
3. **Cognitive Imperialism** – the imposition of Western thought as the universal standard (attributed to Marie Battiste).
4. **Hermeneutical Injustice** – structural gaps in interpretive resources that disadvantage marginalized groups (attributed to Miranda Fricker).
5. **Cultural Imperialism** – the domination of culture and imagination through language and power (attributed to Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o).

The post argues that together these forces uphold the Coloniality of Knowledge, and that decolonization involves reclaiming suppressed epistemologies and centering Africentric and Indigenous ways of knowing. It is described as rooted in Africentric and decolonial scholarship, shared to educate and invite critical reflection, with the statement that "truth precedes reconciliation." The post is credited to @ubuntucentredpractice and wellnessEmpowered.com. One commenter (Amanda Sutton) noted the utility of having words to describe these concepts.
</summary>

# 怎样认识全球南方

 来源：《求是》2025/16   作者：当代世界研究中心   2025-08-16 09:00:00 

**怎样认识全球南方**

当代世界研究中心

  当前，全球南方在国际舞台上日益活跃，正成为一股重塑世界秩序的关键力量。习近平总书记指出：“‘全球南方’群体性崛起，是世界大变局的鲜明标志。”我们应怎样认识全球南方？全球南方国家有什么共同属性和鲜明特征？怎样推动全球南方在促进人类进步方面发挥更重要作用？

**一**

  全球南方的概念来源于“南方”国家。现有研究认为，1926年意大利马克思主义理论家葛兰西正式提出了“南方”概念。他当时关注到意大利南北发展差距问题，并初步说明“南方”概念所蕴含的反剥削、求发展等特性。一般来说，全球南方被认为是新兴市场国家和发展中国家的集合体。它包括亚洲、非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、大洋洲地区的大部分国家，这些国家大多地处北半球南部和南半球，具有相似的历史遭遇、共同的发展任务、相近的国际事务立场。

  全球南方的崛起历经数十年的积淀。二战后，西方殖民体系逐步瓦解，在亚非拉等原殖民地建立起一大批实现了民族独立的主权国家。这些国家在民族解放、反殖反霸等方面具有共同诉求，逐渐联合成一股重要的国际力量。1955年，万隆会议在印度尼西亚召开，标志着亚非新兴民族独立国家作为一个集体正式走入世界政治的舞台，向世界展现了其推动建立公正合理国际秩序的智慧、信念与行动。1961年，不结盟运动正式形成。该运动的成立，反映了广大南方国家主张国际关系民主化的强烈诉求，推动了这些国家捍卫国家主权、反对霸权主义、振兴民族经济的历史进程。1964年，77国集团成立并提出关于国际经济关系、贸易与发展的一整套主张，旨在推动南南合作，建立国际经济新秩序。20世纪70年代，中国提出“三个世界”划分的理论，进一步推动发展中国家身份认同，鼓励发展中国家独立自主，在国际事务中形成联合阵线。

  20世纪八九十年代以来，随着世界多极化和经济全球化深入发展，一大批新兴市场国家和发展中国家经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗和广泛合作，走上发展的快车道。数据统计，新兴市场国家和发展中国家过去20年对世界经济增长的贡献率高达80%，过去40年国内生产总值的全球占比从24%增至40%以上。全球南方群体性崛起，深刻改写国际政治格局和世界经济版图。

  近年来，全球南方更加积极主动捍卫自身权益、推动全球治理变革。在慕尼黑安全会议上，呼吁坚持多边主义、加强集体行动；在南方首脑会议上，要求改变不公正的国际秩序，摆脱几个世纪以来被西方推入的“绝对不利境地”；在不结盟运动第十九次峰会上，强调要全面尊重国际法和国际共识原则……全球南方展现出的态度更加自信，国际地位和影响力显著提升，为世界多极化、经济全球化和国际关系民主化注入强大动能。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

**独立自主是全球南方的政治底色。**全球南方国家大多有过被侵略、被殖民、被掠夺的苦难经历，深知和平的宝贵，珍视自身的独立地位。当前，强权政治、霸权行径扰乱世界安宁，已成为国际和平面临的最大破坏性因素。全球南方对此始终保持高度警惕，日益重视战略自主，坚决反对一切形式的霸权主义和强权政治，反对冷战思维和阵营对抗，反对干涉别国内政，强调“生存权”、“发展权”，明确拒绝选边站队，为维护世界和平稳定发挥着重要作用。近年来，拉美和加勒比国家呼吁反对外来干涉，非洲一些国家提出“第二次独立”等政治主张。在乌克兰危机、巴以冲突等问题上，全球南方国家大多摆脱西方影响，坚持基于历史经纬和事情本身是非曲直确立本国立场，主张劝和促谈、停火止战。2024年9月，17个全球南方国家在联合国成立乌克兰危机“和平之友”小组，寻求妥善解决危机方案，发出客观、理性的声音，得到国际社会广泛认同和赞赏。

**发展振兴是全球南方的历史使命。**发展承载着各国人民对美好生活的向往，是全球南方国家的第一要务。全球南方多数国家发展任务艰巨，但拥有自然资源丰富、市场潜力大等优势和红利，发展前景广阔。然而，由于国际议程设置权和规则制定权长期由少数西方国家垄断，全球南方国家在国际经济利益分配格局中处于不利地位，经济和社会发展容易受到外部因素影响和干扰。当前世界经济复苏乏力，发展中国家面临的发展挑战尤其严峻。在此关键当口，全球南方国家普遍认为，应合力推动更加包容、更加普惠、更有韧性的全球发展，加快落实2030年可持续发展议程；坚持互利共赢的合作观，拒绝以邻为壑、自私自利的狭隘政策，摒弃垄断发展优势的片面做法，保障各国平等发展权利，促进共同发展繁荣。

  2024年7月11日至13日，全球共享发展行动论坛第二届高级别会议在北京举行，来自160多个国家、国际组织和其他机构的代表参会交流研讨。本届会议下设“推动全球南方现代化”等5场平行分论坛。图为7月12日，“分论坛一·推动全球南方现代化：新路径、新愿景”专题研讨环节。 中新社记者 田雨昊/摄

**公道正义是全球南方的共同主张。**在百年变局加速演进、全球治理赤字日益凸显的背景下，全球南方国家不畏强权、坚守正义，敢于对国际秩序中不公正不合理的安排说“不”，敢于为弱小者仗义执言。全球南方国家认为不能以多边主义之名行单边主义之实，要求践行真正的多边主义，不断促进权利平等、机会平等、规则平等。政治层面，支持扩大非洲国家在联合国安理会的代表性，呼吁遵守联合国宪章宗旨和原则，遵守国际法。经济层面，努力推动世界贸易组织改革，促进国际货币体系多元化，力争逐步摆脱经济依附的困境。全球治理层面，重视在全球治理体系变革道路上超越制度差异、强化集体行动，搭建“金砖国家数字经济伙伴关系框架”等新平台，为发展中国家提供安全、贸易、金融、产业机制新选项，努力消弭全球治理赤字。

**三**

  当前，全球南方声势卓然壮大，在人类进步事业中发挥着越来越重要的作用。习近平总书记指出，在世界百年变局中逐梦现代化，推动国际秩序朝着更加公正合理的方向发展，是全球南方国家肩负的神圣历史使命。中国是全球南方的坚定一员，也是推动全球南方发展振兴的中坚力量。总书记多次强调，中国“坚定维护发展中国家共同利益，推动增加新兴市场国家和发展中国家在全球事务中的代表性和发言权”，“愿同广大全球南方国家一道，践行真正的多边主义，倡导平等有序的世界多极化、普惠包容的经济全球化，携手推动构建人类命运共同体”，等等。总书记的重要论述，从世界之变、时代之变、历史之变的广阔视野和战略高度，深刻阐明深化全球南方团结合作的中国主张，激荡起全球南方开创人类光明未来的磅礴力量。

**推动全球南方做维护和平的稳定力量。**和平是全球南方实现发展繁荣的重要前提，也是各国人民的共同期盼。当前，全球安全形势动荡脆弱，地缘政治冲突此起彼伏，和平赤字成为制约全球发展的重要阻碍。习近平总书记提出全球安全倡议，超越“集团政治”、“势力范围”等陈旧狭隘观念和对立对抗思维，倡导共同、综合、合作、可持续的新安全观，强调恪守安全不可分割原则，尊重各国合理安全关切，构建均衡、有效、可持续的安全架构，为消弭国际冲突根源、实现世界长治久安指明了正确方向。全球南方应一道推动落实全球安全倡议，坚决反对霸权霸道霸凌，倡导尊重和保障每一个国家的安全，努力实现普遍安全、共同安全。面对国家间的分歧和争端，全球南方应共同呼吁冲突各方加强战略沟通，增进安全互信，化解矛盾，管控分歧，消除危机产生的根源。

**推动全球南方做开放发展的中坚力量。**开放合作是促进人类社会不断进步的时代要求。当前，经济全球化遭遇逆流，全球发展赤字有增无减，加强国际合作、破解发展困境成为国际社会尤其是广大全球南方国家的共同心愿与殷切期盼。习近平总书记提出全球发展倡议，致力于凝聚加快发展的政治共识、搭建发展合作的公共平台、促进发展经验的交流互鉴、增强协同发展的国际合力，推动全球发展迈向平衡协调包容新阶段，契合全球南方的迫切需求，也为南南合作提供了新机遇。全球南方应牢牢把握发展这个核心议题，一道推动落实全球发展倡议，既坚定支持各国探索符合本国国情、发挥自身优势的发展道路，又加强宏观经济政策协调，合作破解发展难题。同时，旗帜鲜明反对单边主义和保护主义，持续推进贸易和投资自由化便利化，共同建设开放型世界经济，推动经济全球化朝着更加开放、包容、普惠、均衡的方向发展。

  2025年3月19日至21日，以“融金聚智 点亮南方”为主题的2025全球南方金融家论坛在北京举行，来自全球30多个国家和地区的政府部门、金融机构负责人及专家学者等展开交流研讨。图为3月20日，以“金融合作促进平等共治”为主题的圆桌讨论环节。 新华社记者 李贺/摄

# 怎样认识全球南方

 来源：《求是》2025/16   作者：当代世界研究中心   2025-08-16 09:00:00 

**怎样认识全球南方**

当代世界研究中心

  当前，全球南方在国际舞台上日益活跃，正成为一股重塑世界秩序的关键力量。习近平总书记指出：“‘全球南方’群体性崛起，是世界大变局的鲜明标志。”我们应怎样认识全球南方？全球南方国家有什么共同属性和鲜明特征？怎样推动全球南方在促进人类进步方面发挥更重要作用？

**一**

  全球南方的概念来源于“南方”国家。现有研究认为，1926年意大利马克思主义理论家葛兰西正式提出了“南方”概念。他当时关注到意大利南北发展差距问题，并初步说明“南方”概念所蕴含的反剥削、求发展等特性。一般来说，全球南方被认为是新兴市场国家和发展中国家的集合体。它包括亚洲、非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、大洋洲地区的大部分国家，这些国家大多地处北半球南部和南半球，具有相似的历史遭遇、共同的发展任务、相近的国际事务立场。

  全球南方的崛起历经数十年的积淀。二战后，西方殖民体系逐步瓦解，在亚非拉等原殖民地建立起一大批实现了民族独立的主权国家。这些国家在民族解放、反殖反霸等方面具有共同诉求，逐渐联合成一股重要的国际力量。1955年，万隆会议在印度尼西亚召开，标志着亚非新兴民族独立国家作为一个集体正式走入世界政治的舞台，向世界展现了其推动建立公正合理国际秩序的智慧、信念与行动。1961年，不结盟运动正式形成。该运动的成立，反映了广大南方国家主张国际关系民主化的强烈诉求，推动了这些国家捍卫国家主权、反对霸权主义、振兴民族经济的历史进程。1964年，77国集团成立并提出关于国际经济关系、贸易与发展的一整套主张，旨在推动南南合作，建立国际经济新秩序。20世纪70年代，中国提出“三个世界”划分的理论，进一步推动发展中国家身份认同，鼓励发展中国家独立自主，在国际事务中形成联合阵线。

  20世纪八九十年代以来，随着世界多极化和经济全球化深入发展，一大批新兴市场国家和发展中国家经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗和广泛合作，走上发展的快车道。数据统计，新兴市场国家和发展中国家过去20年对世界经济增长的贡献率高达80%，过去40年国内生产总值的全球占比从24%增至40%以上。全球南方群体性崛起，深刻改写国际政治格局和世界经济版图。

  近年来，全球南方更加积极主动捍卫自身权益、推动全球治理变革。在慕尼黑安全会议上，呼吁坚持多边主义、加强集体行动；在南方首脑会议上，要求改变不公正的国际秩序，摆脱几个世纪以来被西方推入的“绝对不利境地”；在不结盟运动第十九次峰会上，强调要全面尊重国际法和国际共识原则……全球南方展现出的态度更加自信，国际地位和影响力显著提升，为世界多极化、经济全球化和国际关系民主化注入强大动能。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

**独立自主是全球南方的政治底色。**全球南方国家大多有过被侵略、被殖民、被掠夺的苦难经历，深知和平的宝贵，珍视自身的独立地位。当前，强权政治、霸权行径扰乱世界安宁，已成为国际和平面临的最大破坏性因素。全球南方对此始终保持高度警惕，日益重视战略自主，坚决反对一切形式的霸权主义和强权政治，反对冷战思维和阵营对抗，反对干涉别国内政，强调“生存权”、“发展权”，明确拒绝选边站队，为维护世界和平稳定发挥着重要作用。近年来，拉美和加勒比国家呼吁反对外来干涉，非洲一些国家提出“第二次独立”等政治主张。在乌克兰危机、巴以冲突等问题上，全球南方国家大多摆脱西方影响，坚持基于历史经纬和事情本身是非曲直确立本国立场，主张劝和促谈、停火止战。2024年9月，17个全球南方国家在联合国成立乌克兰危机“和平之友”小组，寻求妥善解决危机方案，发出客观、理性的声音，得到国际社会广泛认同和赞赏。

**发展振兴是全球南方的历史使命。**发展承载着各国人民对美好生活的向往，是全球南方国家的第一要务。全球南方多数国家发展任务艰巨，但拥有自然资源丰富、市场潜力大等优势和红利，发展前景广阔。然而，由于国际议程设置权和规则制定权长期由少数西方国家垄断，全球南方国家在国际经济利益分配格局中处于不利地位，经济和社会发展容易受到外部因素影响和干扰。当前世界经济复苏乏力，发展中国家面临的发展挑战尤其严峻。在此关键当口，全球南方国家普遍认为，应合力推动更加包容、更加普惠、更有韧性的全球发展，加快落实2030年可持续发展议程；坚持互利共赢的合作观，拒绝以邻为壑、自私自利的狭隘政策，摒弃垄断发展优势的片面做法，保障各国平等发展权利，促进共同发展繁荣。

  2024年7月11日至13日，全球共享发展行动论坛第二届高级别会议在北京举行，来自160多个国家、国际组织和其他机构的代表参会交流研讨。本届会议下设“推动全球南方现代化”等5场平行分论坛。图为7月12日，“分论坛一·推动全球南方现代化：新路径、新愿景”专题研讨环节。 中新社记者 田雨昊/摄

**公道正义是全球南方的共同主张。**在百年变局加速演进、全球治理赤字日益凸显的背景下，全球南方国家不畏强权、坚守正义，敢于对国际秩序中不公正不合理的安排说“不”，敢于为弱小者仗义执言。全球南方国家认为不能以多边主义之名行单边主义之实，要求践行真正的多边主义，不断促进权利平等、机会平等、规则平等。政治层面，支持扩大非洲国家在联合国安理会的代表性，呼吁遵守联合国宪章宗旨和原则，遵守国际法。经济层面，努力推动世界贸易组织改革，促进国际货币体系多元化，力争逐步摆脱经济依附的困境。全球治理层面，重视在全球治理体系变革道路上超越制度差异、强化集体行动，搭建“金砖国家数字经济伙伴关系框架”等新平台，为发展中国家提供安全、贸易、金融、产业机制新选项，努力消弭全球治理赤字。

**三**

  当前，全球南方声势卓然壮大，在人类进步事业中发挥着越来越重要的作用。习近平总书记指出，在世界百年变局中逐梦现代化，推动国际秩序朝着更加公正合理的方向发展，是全球南方国家肩负的神圣历史使命。中国是全球南方的坚定一员，也是推动全球南方发展振兴的中坚力量。总书记多次强调，中国“坚定维护发展中国家共同利益，推动增加新兴市场国家和发展中国家在全球事务中的代表性和发言权”，“愿同广大全球南方国家一道，践行真正的多边主义，倡导平等有序的世界多极化、普惠包容的经济全球化，携手推动构建人类命运共同体”，等等。总书记的重要论述，从世界之变、时代之变、历史之变的广阔视野和战略高度，深刻阐明深化全球南方团结合作的中国主张，激荡起全球南方开创人类光明未来的磅礴力量。

--- SOURCE 1: Latin American Dependency Theory | Global South Studies ---
URL: https://www.globalsouthstudies.org/keyword-essay/latin-american-dependency-theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This essay by Steven Schmidt (January 21, 2018, Global South Studies) traces the intellectual history of Latin American Dependency Theory, a political-economic school of thought that emerged from the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) shortly after World War II. Key scholars include Raúl Prebisch, Fernando Cardoso, Enrique Faletto, and Andre Gunder Frank, with later influence on world-systems analysis by Immanuel Wallerstein, Giovanni Arrighi, and Christopher Chase-Dunn.

Dependency theory argues that under-development in Latin America is the direct result of capital intervention and global economic forces, not a "lack" of development. It emerged as a response to modernization theory (associated with economist William Rostow's five stages of economic growth), which dependency theorists rejected as a false dichotomy between "traditional" and "modern" societies.

Central to the theory is the Prebisch-Singer thesis, developed by Prebisch (former Argentine chief trade diplomat) and UN economist Hans Singer, which demonstrated through trade data that an imbalance in terms of trade caused a constant flow of capital out of Latin America—as the region exported primary goods (food, lumber, minerals) while re-importing higher-value manufactured products from the Global North, creating a perpetual trade deficit.

The theory split into two camps: (1) liberal reformers like Prebisch, Cardoso, and Faletto, who advocated for import-substitution industrialization (ISI) and protectionist policies to develop domestic markets; and (2) neo-Marxists like Gunder Frank, who argued dependency could only be escaped through socialism and challenging the capitalist mode of production. A further offshoot was world-systems analysis (Wallerstein, Amin, Frank).

During the 1940s-1950s, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile adopted ISI policies, but debt crises in the 1980s led the World Bank and IMF to impose structural adjustment programs (SAPs), which dismantled these protections. While dependency theory is no longer widely applied as policy, its core insights remain valuable: understanding how global capital flows structure development disparities, challenging assumptions that Latin American economies are "feudal and backwards," that modernity equals industrialization, and that all nations can equally pass through development "stages." The theory laid groundwork for research on the international division of labor, commodity chains, and global cities (Sassen 1991).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory argues that under-development as experienced in Latin America and elsewhere is the direct result of capital intervention, rather than a condition of 'lacking' development or investment."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Dependency theory - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependency_theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikipedia article on Dependency theory, an international relations theory within the broader frameworks of imperialism studies and Marxist international relations theory. 

**Core concept:** Dependency theory posits that resources flow from a "periphery" of poor, exploited states to a "core" of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. The central contention is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by how poor states are integrated into the "world system." The theory was formally developed in the late 1940s following World War II as scholars sought to explain the lack of development in Latin America.

**Origins and History:** The theory arose as a reaction to modernization theory, which held that all societies progress through similar development stages. Dependency theory rejected this, arguing underdeveloped countries are not primitive versions of developed ones but have unique structures and are weaker members of the world market economy. The theory originated with two 1949 papers by Hans Singer and Raúl Prebisch, who observed deteriorating terms of trade for underdeveloped countries (the Prebisch–Singer thesis). Prebisch, an Argentine economist at the UN Commission for Latin America, advocated import-substitution industrialization (ISI) over export orientation. Paul A. Baran developed it from a Marxian perspective in 1957 with *The Political Economy of Growth*. Two main streams emerged: Latin American Structuralist (Prebisch, Celso Furtado, Aníbal Pinto) and American Marxist (Baran, Paul Sweezy, Andre Gunder Frank). The theory was popular in the 1960s-1970s as criticism of modernization theory. Walter Rodney's 1972 book *How Europe Underdeveloped Africa* applied it to Africa. Ruy Mauro Marini developed a specifically Marxist dependency theory focused on super-exploitation and unequal exchange. Fernando Henrique Cardoso (later Brazilian President 1995-2002) wrote extensively on dependency theory, developing the concept of "dependent development."

**Basic premises:** (1) Poor nations provide natural resources, cheap labor, destinations for obsolete technology, and markets for developed nations, without which the latter couldn't enjoy their standard of living; (2) Wealthy nations actively perpetuate dependence through economics, media control, politics, banking, finance, education, culture, and sport.

**Key concepts:** Baran placed surplus extraction and capital accumulation at the center of analysis, arguing that surplus in poor countries goes to luxury consumption rather than development investment. Latin American Structuralists argued for "dependent development" - partial development still controlled by outside decision-makers. Some argue the sine qua non of dependency is not technological difference but financial strength - particularly the inability of peripheral countries to borrow in their own currency, and US control of the international reserve currency (the dollar). Theotonio dos Santos described a "new dependency" based on Marxian analysis. The theory influenced world-systems theory developed by Immanuel Wallerstein, which added a third category of "semi-periphery" countries.

**Examples:** European colonization (1650-1900) of the Americas, Africa, and Asia, where wealth was transferred from colonized regions to Europe through control of materials, production, and distribution.

**Criticism:** India's economic improvement after moving to open trade is cited as evidence against the theory (though Indian economists Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik argue this may reflect a globalized reserve workforce). Import-substitution economies in Africa like Zimbabwe have performed poorly while trade-based economies like Egypt, South Africa, and Tunisia have succeeded. Economic historian Robert C. Allen argues dependency theory's claims are "debatable" because protectionism in Latin America failed, leading to excessive debt and recession, partly because national markets were too small to efficiently produce complex industrial goods.

**Other details:** The article also covers aid dependency, including instilling aid dependency, stunted economic growth, political dependency, corruption, and efforts to end aid dependency. Dependency theorists divide into liberal reformists (advocating targeted policy interventions) and neo-Marxists (proposing planned economies). The theory has lost influence with the growth of India and East Asian economies but still influences NGO campaigns like Make Poverty History and the fair trade movement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory is the idea that resources flow from a 'periphery' of poor and exploited states to a 'core' of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. A central contention of dependency theory is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by the way poor states are integrated into the 'world system.'"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Remembering Dependency Theory - New Politics ---
URL: https://newpol.org/issue_post/remembering-dependency-theory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Marxist-Humanist review article by Edward L. Tapia, published in New Politics (Summer 2017, Vol. XVI No. 3, Whole Number 63), titled "Remembering Dependency Theory." The article argues that dependency theory—a set of anti-colonial and anti-imperialist theoretical schemas that emerged after World War II—failed to properly grasp Marx's concept of value because it remained fixated on exchange value rather than penetrating into the social relations of production and abstract labor, which Tapia identifies as the defining principle of capitalism.

Key arguments and content:

1. **Origins and schools of dependency theory**: The theory emerged from anti-colonial/anti-imperialist struggles in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It argued that global capitalist expansion generated development in core locations (Western Europe, North America, Japan) and underdevelopment in peripheral locations (Africa, Asia, Latin America). It spanned from the revolutionary socialist school (Andre Gunder Frank, Samir Amin, Theotonio dos Santos) to the bourgeois nationalist/social-democratic school (Arghiri Emmanuel, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Enzo Faletto).

2. **Unequal exchange theory**: Dependency theorists relied on the Prebisch-Singer thesis, arguing primary commodity prices secularly fall relative to manufactured goods. They followed Ricardian theory of value, assuming commodities exchange at value and international equalization of profit rates, whereas Marx showed prices of production deviate from value due to abstract/socially necessary labor-time.

3. **Marx's counter-argument**: Marx demonstrated that advanced countries with higher organic composition of capital sell at prices of production above their value, exploiting less-advanced countries. Key quotes from Theories of Surplus Value, Grundrisse, and Capital Vol. III illustrate this—including Marx's statement that "three days of labor of one country can be exchanged against one of another country" and that "the richer country exploits the poorer one, even where the latter gains by the exchange."

4. **Industrialization and delinking strategies**: Two divergent theses emerged: "associated dependent development" (Cardoso and Faletto, involving semi-peripheral industrialization with international/local capital alliances) and "development of underdevelopment" (Frank). Both advocated "delinking"—either as mercantilist strategy to re-enter the world market later, or as disassociation toward socialism.

5. **Critique of delinking**: Tapia argues delinking fails because it addresses distribution rather than abstract value production, and socially necessary labor-time continues operating in national contexts. He cites Raya Dunayevskaya's Philosophy and Revolution on the whole human being and the persistence of the law of value.

6. **Failure of dependency theory**: It failed to anticipate the "new industrial division of labor" exemplified by the East Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan) in the 1970s. The article discusses John Smith's Imperialism in the 21st Century on globalization of production (foreign direct investment and "arm's length outsourcing"), noting the global economically active population grew from 1.9 billion (1980) to 3.1 billion (2006), a 63% increase. Tapia criticizes Smith's "super-exploitation" theory as an inadequate basis for understanding imperialism, siding with Michael Roberts that exploitation is determined by the ratio of surplus value to the value of labor power.

7. **Conclusion**: Tapia calls on today's revolutionary activists to choose between building freely associated human relations that negate the law of value, or repeating the "old illusions of past socialist experiments." He cites the fates of dependency theorists—Cardoso became a neoliberal Brazilian president, Amin remained a self-declared Maoist, and Frank argued capitalism and socialism never existed.

The article includes a substantial bibliography of works by Amin, Anderson, Birkan, Carchedi, Roberts, Cardoso/Faletto, Dunayevskaya, Evans, Frank, Grossman, Hudis, Marx, Pieterse, Pradella, and Smith.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Three days of labor of one country can be exchanged against one of another country. … Here the law of value undergoes essential modification. … The relationship between labor days of different countries may be similar to that existing between skilled, complex labor and unskilled, simple labor within a country. In this case, the richer country exploits the poorer one, even where the latter gains by the exchange." — Marx, Theories of Surplus Value
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Key Arguments of Dependency Theory: Understanding Economic Exploitation • PolSci Institute ---
URL: https://polsci.institute/international-relations/key-arguments-dependency-theory-economic-exploitation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from PolSci Institute provides a comprehensive explanation of dependency theory (theory of dependencia) and its key arguments regarding economic exploitation in the global system.

**Definition and Origins:** Dependency theory explains the underdevelopment of certain nations by emphasizing constraints imposed by the global economic and political order. It emerged in Latin America in the 1950s-1960s and gained influence through the 1970s. Its intellectual roots trace to Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch, executive director of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA/CEPAL) in 1950, whose work with Hans Singer produced the Prebisch-Singer thesis.

**Core-Periphery Structure:** The world economy is divided into core countries (wealthy, industrialised) and peripheral countries (poorer, raw material exporters). Theotonio Dos Santos defined dependence as a situation where some economies can expand and be self-sustaining while others only grow as a reflection of that expansion. Immanuel Wallerstein later added the semi-periphery category in his world-systems theory.

**Key Arguments:**
1. Underdevelopment is produced, not inherited—André Gunder Frank's "development of underdevelopment" concept (1966 essay, 1967 book) argues poor countries are poor because of how capitalism reached them, using a "metropolis and satellite" chain of exploitation. Frank noted that periods of less global integration (e.g., world wars) coincided with stronger local growth.
2. Unequal exchange and deteriorating terms of trade—prices of primary goods fall relative to manufactured goods, forcing peripheral economies to export ever-larger quantities to afford imports, making trade a mechanism of impoverishment.
3. Mechanisms of extraction include unequal trade relationships, foreign investment with repatriated profits, and brain drain.
4. Dependent development—Fernando Henrique Cardoso (with Enzo Faletto) argued peripheral nations could achieve some growth within the system, though lopsided and dependent on the core. Domestic elites often benefit from and maintain dependent relationships.

**Indian Experience:** British colonial rule exemplified dependency—raw materials (cotton, tea, minerals) were extracted and exported to Britain, then sold back as finished goods at higher prices. This resonates with the older "drain of wealth" theory by Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. Post-independence import substitution industrialisation was an attempt to break dependency.

**Criticisms:** The theory is criticized as overly deterministic and simplistic, neglecting internal factors (governance, institutions, human capital). The East Asian success stories (South Korea, Taiwan) challenge it—these countries achieved growth through export-oriented strategies and deep integration into the world economy. Samir Amin noted Frank's analysis was too generalised and failed to capture uneven development among peripheral states.

Despite criticisms, dependency theory retains explanatory value for debates on fair trade, debt relief, technology transfer, and Global South supply chains.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory is an approach that explains the underdevelopment of certain nations by emphasising the constraints imposed on them by the global economic and political order."
