<webpage_content>
# [artXchange Global Newsletter](/)

# Cultural Infrastructure: Examining the Cultural Dimensions of China's Belt and Road Initiative

[Ornela Ramasauskaite](https://substack.com/@ornelar)

[Map](https://www.asiagreen.com/en/news-insights/the-belt-and-road-initiative-and-the-rising-importance-of-china-s-western-cities) of The Belt and Road initiative

The Belt and Road Initiative represents far more than an infrastructure investment program – it constitutes a comprehensive cultural geopolitical strategy that seeks to reshape global connectivity through the deployment of cultural infrastructure, soft power mechanisms, and civilisational narratives. While presented as economic cooperation, the BRI functions as a cultural diplomacy platform, allowing China to present itself as a benevolent global leader while projecting cultural soft power and international influence.

**Introduction: Beyond Infrastructure – The Cultural Imperative**

As of early 2024, more than 140 countries were part of the BRI, representing almost 75% of the world's population and accounting for more than half of the world's GDP. Yet beneath this impressive scale lies a more complex cultural project. The BRI involves substantial investments in infrastructure, trade facilitation, and cultural exchange, which contribute to economic development and connectivity beyond purely geopolitical narratives.

Since 2004, China has been developing its "China story" narrative, with President Xi Jinping picking up this theme in 2013, urging Chinese leaders to play their role in improving China's international communication capacity to tell China's stories well and present a true, multi-dimensional, and panoramic view of China.

Cultural Infrastructure as Geopolitical Strategy

***The Five Pillars Framework***

The BRI's March 2015 action plan outlined specific policy goals, including improving intergovernmental communication, strengthening infrastructure coordination, encouraging soft infrastructure development such as trade deals and regulatory alignment, and bolstering people-to-people connections through cultural exchanges and tourism.

The cultural dimensions operate through what can be understood as "soft infrastructure" – institutional networks that facilitate cultural flow and shape normative frameworks. This includes:

**Cultural Institutions and Centers:** China has established 46 China cultural centers in 44 countries, of which 32 are partner countries, plus 20 tourism offices in 18 countries, eight of which are in partner countries.

**Educational Networks:** Chinese universities and colleges have opened 313 Confucius Institutes and 315 Confucius Classrooms in 132 partner countries, functioning as centers for Chinese language and cultural education, fostering a deeper understanding of Chinese traditions and values while helping establish trust relationships in intercultural trade.

**Cultural Platforms:** China has created cooperation platforms, including the Silk Road International League of Theaters, the Silk Road International Museum Alliance, the Network of Silk Road Arts Festivals, the Silk Road International Library Alliance, and the Silk Road International Alliance of Art Museums and Galleries, with 562 total members including 326 cultural institutions from 72 partner countries.

*People-to-People Connectivity as Strategic Foundation*

[Eight-leaf folding screen](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sc%C3%A8nes_de_palais,_l%E2%80%99arriv%C3%A9e_d%E2%80%99une_d%C3%A9l%C3%A9gation_et_les_festivit%C3%A9s_en_l%E2%80%99honneur_du_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9ral_Guo_Ziyi_(697-781)_des_Tang.jpg). Palace scene, the arrival of a delegation and festivities in honor of the Tang general Guo Ziyi (697-781)

People-to-people ties are identified as the social foundations of BRI cooperation, with participating countries carrying forward the spirit of friendly cooperation of the ancient Silk Road through culture, tourism, education, think tank and media exchanges, promoting mutual learning among civilisations and cultural integration.

Over 70% of survey respondents expressed enthusiasm for participating in projects that enhance their quality of life, with significant interest in Kenya, Indonesia, and Vietnam, particularly in cross-border tourism, cultural activities, traditional Chinese medicine exploration, and educational exchanges.

*Cultural Diplomacy and the "China Story"*

The BRI serves as one of the most ambitious expressions of China's objective to influence global perception, with Xi Jinping arguing that the BRI and affiliated institutions contribute to "a further rise in China's international influence, ability to inspire, and power to shape".

The cultural strategy operates through multiple channels:

**Academic and Research Networks:** In 2015, the Silk Road Research Institute of Beijing Foreign Studies University was founded to highlight "thematic studies to tell China stories, spread China voices and take Chinese culture to the world," while the University Alliance of the Silk Road, consisting of approximately 100 universities from 22 countries, was established to foster "institutional exchanges, talent training, joint research, and cultural communication".

**Cultural Events and Festivals:** The Cultural Silk Road was launched in China in 2016 and replicated in Lyon, France, the following year, while the Silk Road Music Industry Alliance, consisting of 18 countries, was created to "develop and expand the music, film/movie, entertainment, digital media and culture industries in China".

**Heritage Diplomacy:** China is fast emerging as a major player in heritage diplomacy, providing funds and expertise in maritime and land-based archaeology, and the conservation of historically significant landscapes and cities, invariably branded as promoting "people-to-people" contacts.

*The Confucius Institute Network*

Confucius Institutes have been indicated as a fundamental means in support of the BRI, holding dedicated lectures and events on the Silk Road, with 51 countries participating in the BRI having established 135 Confucius Institutes.

Confucius Institute logo

More than 525 Confucius Institutes and more than 1113 Confucius Classrooms operate worldwide, with 154 Institutes and 149 Classrooms located in 54 BRI countries, serving as the driving force of the BRI by teaching Mandarin and other languages, organising programs and lectures related to BRI countries, and offering free training and scholarships.

*Digital Cultural Infrastructure and the Metaverse*

The Digital Silk Road (DSR) is part of the BRI those finances and supports digital connectivity infrastructure, including both complex infrastructure like cellular networks and soft infrastructure like applications and mobile payment platforms to facilitate China's trade with developing countries.

The digital dimension extends cultural reach through:

* **Mobile Applications:** Mobile applications like Boomplay and Vskit are major players in Africa's social media ecosystem.
* **Technology Platforms:** Integration of Chinese digital platforms that carry cultural content and values.
* **Virtual Cultural Experiences:** The Metaverse presents unprecedented opportunities for promoting cultural tourism along the historic Silk Roads within the BRI framework, supporting sustainable tourism development and cultural exchange.

***Cultural Heritage Digitisation***

[Chinese red lights](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/culture/)

Recent research examines how the Metaverse can be harnessed to improve tourists' experiences, support sustainable tourism development, and promote cultural exchange along the Silk Roads through virtual and physical reality convergence.

*Heritage Preservation and Cultural Route Revival*

Systematic literature review from 2013 to 2023 reveals substantial potential for the development of new tourism products and destinations, improved urban renewal, and preservation of cultural heritage, provided that integrated policies, public-private collaboration, and equitable community participation frameworks are implemented.

The BRI's impact on cultural heritage operates through:

**Cultural Route Development:** Organisations like UNESCO have been supporting "cultural routes" for some time, but since the BRI launch, a wave of cultural projects themed around connected pasts has formed as multiple countries appropriate Silk Road histories for strategic advantage.

**Museum Networks:** Development of museum alliances and cultural preservation projects that both conserve heritage and project Chinese cultural influence.

**Archaeological Cooperation:** China's provision of expertise and funding for archaeological projects serves both preservation and diplomatic goals.

*Critical Perspectives and Challenges*

Research identifies significant challenges, including financial imbalances, uneven access to benefits, social disruption, cultural commodification, and environmental degradation that require careful, context-specific planning.

**Resistance and Limitations**

In Central Asia, soft power projects in the form of people-to-people initiatives are low priority within the BRI, and Confucius Institutes, while important for Chinese soft power, are not directly linked to the BRI and were launched independently.

Some Western governments have accused the BRI of being a form of neo-colonialism. However, academic research challenges these debt-trap narratives, with scholars noting that Chinese banks are willing to restructure loans and have never actually seized assets from countries.

**Geopolitical Tensions**

The influence of the United States has been declining due to its protectionist policies. At the same time, the USA views China's BRI as a strategic threat, concerned about China's investments in education sectors that could impact democratic values and create competition between Chinese and American workforces.

*Regional Case Studies*

**Middle East and Cultural Connectivity**

Cultural exchange is playing a pronounced role in the future of the BRI, with person-to-person cultural exchange increasingly defining China-MENA relations. Various countries across the region now host Confucius Institutes reflecting China's expanding soft power footprint.

Beijing's emphasis on promoting cross-civilisational dialogue through President Xi Jinping's Global Civilisation Initiative (GCI) is centring discourse around cultural connectivity in China's MENA diplomacy. At the same time, platforms like TikTok reflect China's increasing social media influence.

**Central Asia as Cultural Bridge**

Building depicting a boat in the [Chinese Garden](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gebouw_voorstellende_een_boot_in_de_Chinese_tuin_Het_Verborgen_Rijk_van_Ming_in_de_Hortus_Haren_02.jpg) The Hidden Empire Ming in the Hortus Haren in the Netherlands

Central Asia has returned as the liminal zone between two great centres of culture and civilisation, suggesting its history and culture emanate from elsewhere and the region is merely a "bridge" conjoining more historically significant areas, East and West.

[Share](https://artxchange.substack.com/p/cultural-infrastructure-examining?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

The region experiences tension between constructing cultural nationalisms that are distinctive yet speak to regional "shared heritage," while a Silk Road narrative driven by China looking to expand influence westwards represents a new landscape of cultural politics.

*Implications for Global Cultural Order*

The BRI's cultural dimensions represent an attempt to establish alternative frameworks for international cooperation based on "civilisational dialogue" rather than Western-dominated institutional arrangements. This involves:

**Narrative Competition:** The BRI competes with Western developmental models by offering an alternative vision of connectivity and cooperation rooted in historical Silk Road narratives.

**Institutional Innovation:** Creation of new cultural and educational networks that bypass existing Western-dominated international institutions.

**Value Proposition:** Promotion of "shared destiny" and "win-win cooperation" concepts that challenge liberal international order assumptions.

*Future Trajectories*

According to 2024 data, China's trade volume with BRI partner countries grew by 6.4 per cent year-on-year, accounting for over half of China's total trade volume for the first time. Meanwhile, 70 per cent of experts believe China will enhance cooperation with non-Western partners in 2025.

In the first half of 2023, over 100 BRI agreements were signed, valuing $43 billion –a roughly 20% increase from 2022, suggesting sustained momentum despite geopolitical tensions.

*Cultural Infrastructure as Geopolitical Architecture*

[Chinese Light Festival](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tianfu_Festival-7_A74189120240728.jpg) is a cultural event where you can enjoy large-scale light structures and traditional activities

The Belt and Road Initiative's cultural dimensions reveal a sophisticated strategy that deploys cultural infrastructure as geopolitical architecture. Rather than simply facilitating economic connectivity, the BRI constructs new networks of cultural influence, educational cooperation, and civilisational dialogue that challenge existing Western-dominated international frameworks.

The initiative is evolving and adapting in response to challenges and feedback from participating countries, demonstrating dynamism not captured by rigid geopolitical narratives. However, the long-term success of this cultural strategy will depend on its ability to balance Chinese strategic interests with genuine partnership and mutual benefit for participating countries.

The BRI represents a new model of cultural geopolitics – one that operates through infrastructure, education, heritage, and digital connectivity to reshape global cultural flows and power relations. *Understanding these cultural dimensions is essential for analysing contemporary shifts in the international order and the emergence of alternative frameworks for global cooperation.*

Neocolonial Belt or Road to Prosperity? A study on the framing of the Belt and Road Initiative Jonathan Höglund Master’s thesis in political science, Fall 2025 Department of Government, Uppsala University Supervisor: Camilla Reuterswärd Word count: 16 781 Abstract For decades, the development discourse has been dominated by Western voices. The voices of the Global South have long been ignored, both in media and academia. This study attempts to highlight these unheard voices by examining how the media in recipient countries of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) frame the major development initiative. This study utilises a comparative frame analysis, where the media reporting in Kenya and Pakistan, two major partners of the BRI, is analysed and compared based on a set of predetermined frame categories which draw on both framing and postcolonial theory. The study’s main finding is that the BRI is predominantly framed from a developmentalist perspective, where modernization, growth and progress are prioritized. This finding challenges previous studies on the BRI, which have primarily found it framed in geopolitical terms. This study contributes to academia by highlighting the valuable insights the Global South can offer and the important role it plays in shaping development discourses. 1 Acknowledgements I would like to thank my supervisor Camilla, who displayed such a genuine interest and dedication for my study and who was the lighthouse in the storm that has been this thesis project. Through illness, struggles with data access and doubts about deadlines, Camilla has stood steadfast, providing me with both academic and life advice, which I will continue to heed. Her trust and belief in me has provided me with a sense of calm and a confidence in my own ability to produce an adequate thesis on time. I am forever grateful for her vital impact on the progress of this study and for inspiring me to continue to pursue research in the future. I would also like to express my gratitude and appreciation for my loyal group of friends with whom I have spent countless hours shouting, laughing and crying about our shared thesis process as well as our overall journey through this Master’s programme. You know who you are. We have sat on more locations around the city than I count and studied for a longer period of time than I am able to comprehend. Whether we have taken a fika at Storken, a pubquiz at GH, danced the night away at Le Parc, or simply vented our frustrations to each other over lunch, the distraction and comfort these things have provided me have been invaluable, especially during this writing process. I will always cherish the bond, love and memories we have created and share. To say that this time spent with you, which has culminated with this thesis project, has been the highlight of my time in Uppsala, is an understatement. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).............................................................. 52 3 Chapter 1: Introduction Since the end of the Second World War and the colonial era, development has been a major political topic, particularly in the Western world, which has historically been the main orchestrator of development aid in the rest of the world (Escobar, 1995, p. 3-4). Starting with the Marshall Plan after the end of World War II and continuing with projects such as the Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAPs) up until the modern day, development remains a hot topic within political and economic sciences. The classical Western strategy behind development aid has been heavily debated both within the Western world and outside of it, with critical voices pointing to the traditional Western aid as being a form of neo-colonialism, further exploiting countries in the global south with conditional loans and making them more dependent on Western countries economically (Mireille et al, 2024). Over the decades, it has also been the Western world that has dominated the discourse surrounding development, both in the media and academia. However, Western voices are not the only voices that deserve to be heard. The voices of the Global South, the recipient countries of development assistance, have largely been ignored and obfuscated in the development discourse, with their views on major development programmes not represented in either the media or academia, despite these programmes often taking place in these countries. The purpose of this study is to show that recipient countries also play a role in the construction of development narratives and that their voices also carry weight. The People’s Republic of China (PRC), a country which saw its own rapid development during the second half of the 20th century, established its own international development programme, which has become the flagship of its foreign policy. This investment programme, called the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), was announced in 2013 by President Xi Jinping (Tsuji, 2025). The proposed aim of the investment programme was to improve connectivity, trade and communication between the continents, primarily in Eurasia and Africa (Ibid). The project consists of a “belt”, which refers to the construction and expansion of land routes for people and commerce over Eurasia and the Middle East and a “road”, which refers to the maritime Silk Road, which is an expansion of sea routes, mostly between South & East Asia, the Middle East and Africa (Feingold, 2023). The project has spread throughout most of the world, with over 150 countries and international organisations striking over 200 agreements with China under the BRI banner (Ibid). Infrastructure is the central part of the project, with large-scale construction of roads, railways, ports, and energy facilities such as dams, as well as digital infrastructure, being prioritized constructs (Ibid). 4 However, the evolution of the BRI has not been entirely positive, with concerns and accusations having been levied at the project, mainly from the west and its allies, claiming that it practices similarly predatory methods to the classical western development programmes, calling it things such as “debt trap diplomacy” (Clark, 2023) or a new form of colonialism (Kleven, 2019). The recipient countries of the BRI and their views on it have rarely been represented in the broader global news media, instead often reduced to passive bystanders. Both the stated goals of the BRI by Xi Jinping and the People’s Republic of China, and the mostly Western criticism of it, are two excellent examples of framing of a political issue. Framing refers to the practice of highlighting a particular aspect of a real-world phenomenon and giving it greater salience through a communicative medium to promote a specific interpretation of that phenomenon (Entman, 1993, p. 52). Framing is not only used by news media, as illustrated above, but also heavily used by politicians seeking to garner support for their preferred policy outcomes (Ibid. p. 55). Framing has been frequently applied in studies of social movements, analyzing how said movements utilize framing to promote their cause (Benford & Snow, 2000). Frames influence how people interpret complex phenomena, such as the BRI, whether it be as an opportunity, a threat or something in between. The use of frames affects how we interpret, evaluate, and act upon phenomena in the real world. Framing is a prevalent phenomenon in both media and academic circles, and in an increasingly polarized world, being cognizant of the potential framing of certain issues is becoming more relevant and important. As seen above, the BRI is a subject that is hotly contested and debated in media discourse (Clark, 2023; Kleven, 2019; Feingold, 2023), which makes studying the different frames and narratives that are being used about it, especially on a domestic level in recipient countries, important and relevant. It is not unreasonable to think that BRI projects, much like any other form of policy, can be framed in a certain way by actors in support of them in order to sell them to the public. While the BRI in general has been widely debated and scrutinized, the domestic perception of local BRI projects is less well-documented, which makes this study all the more relevant. The aim of this study, therefore, is to explore which frames are used domestically in recipient countries of key BRI projects, to discover whether the perception of the BRI differs between recipient countries, or whether there are any similarities in the framing of the BRI. Thus, the research question of this study is as follows: How is the Belt and Road Initiative framed in recipient countries? 5 This study will focus on two different recipient countries of the BRI: Kenya and Pakistan. Kenya is one of China’s major partners on the African continent and Pakistan plays a key role in achieving the goal of connecting the Asian and European continents. These two countries are each home to a major BRI project: the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) in Kenya and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) in Pakistan (Huang, 2022; Rauf, 2025). Kenya and Pakistan are two shining examples of the breadth of the BRI across continents and political systems, yet they share similar ambitions for development and growth. While Kenya is a relatively new acquaintance of China in the foreign policy field (Mwangi, 2024), the history between China and what is known as Pakistan today is more intimate and covers a significantly longer period of history (Rossi, 2025; Qingyan, 2021). This study employs a comparative frame analysis in which domestic English-language media in Kenya and Pakistan will be analysed to determine which frames are being used in relation to China and the Belt and Road Initiative in recipient countries. This thesis makes a number of contributions to academia. Most studies on the BRI have focused on its geopolitical aspects (Yang & Van Gorp, 2023; Dutta, 2021; Ittefaq et al, 2023). In contrast, this study focuses on the communicative dimension of the BRI, highlighting the importance of discursive legitimacy and exploring how different narratives shape international perceptions of China. There are not many studies that have focused on media reporting and framing of the BRI, and those that have done so have mainly focused on Western framing or the framing in Western-allied nations (Niu & Relly, 2021). In general, the vast majority of studies utilising a framing analysis have done so with a focus on Western contexts, often on American and/or European perceptions of international issues. Media in the Global South have been treated more as objects of Western analysis than as sources of vital opinion-making and narrative. This study sets itself apart by utilising frame analysis in the context of South-South cooperation. Whereas most countries portray recipient countries of Chinese investment in a passive light, this study aims to show that partner countries of the BRI also play a role in the construction of narratives and meanings relating to the BRI and to China in general and that the voice of actors in the Global South also carries weight. By doing so, this study demonstrates that the success of the BRI is not only contingent on the infrastructure and energy facilities built, but also on public perceptions and evaluations of it. By comparing Kenya and Pakistan, two key but geographically and politically distinct entities, this comparative study allows for insights into both similar and divergent framing patterns. This approach enables a deeper understanding of how domestic media, political systems and development priorities shape the meanings attributed to international cooperation and foreign investment. 6 Beyond its academic value, the study also carries societal and political relevance. Media is often discussed as the “fourth estate” (Gill, 2025) due to its societal influence, and it serves as a public forum where debate about political projects and policies unfolds. How media corporations choose to frame these projects can affect public opinion and the potential for policy accountability of local officials. By presenting the frames used in Kenyan and Pakistani domestic media, this study contributes to the ongoing discussions of transparency, public participation and governance in development cooperation. When it comes to China, the study also illustrates that its international image and power are not only negotiated in Beijing or at the UN, but also, or maybe especially, locally in its partner countries. Finally, this thesis makes a methodological contribution to the research topic by demonstrating the potential value of a qualitative comparative frame analysis based on publicly available media documents for studying international projects. Most existing studies of the BRI utilise elite interviews and hard-to-access economic indicators, which can give a skewed, top-down perspective of the BRI. By using publicly available newspaper articles, this study illustrates how academic scholars can still produce valuable insights into international communication, even if they lack the resources to conduct extensive fieldwork, demonstrating the study's replicability. By combining media studies with political science and development studies, this thesis bridges disciplinary gaps. The main finding of this study is that the BRI is framed primarily in developmentalist terms in recipient countries, with growth, prosperity, and modernization highlighted. This finding contrasts with the existing literature on framing of the BRI, which has mainly found it framed in geopolitical terms, indicating that the Global South may offer an alternative perspective to the one usually presented in Western media and academia, although further studies are required. Another conclusion from this study is that China is barely mentioned in the media reporting in recipient countries, which also deviates from the existing literature and should be examined further. In the following chapter, I present a review of what we currently know about how the Belt and Road Initiative is typically framed and discussed, followed by the theoretical framework. In Chapter 3, the research design is presented, with its operationalizations and limitations. In Chapter 4, the findings of the study will be presented and analysed. Finally, in Chapter 5, the main findings are summarized along with concluding remarks and reflections. 7 Chapter 2: Previous research & Theory 2.1 Literature Review 2.1.1 BRI as a neocolonial venture When speaking of neocolonialism and the continued exploitation of the Global South, the focus is usually on the relationship between former Western colonial powers and their former subjects. However, the term neocolonialism includes any major industrialised nation using its economic and technological advantage against weaker, emerging nations to exploit the latter’s resources for its own gain (Halperin, 2025). When it comes to the BRI, some studies point to some inherent neocolonial trends with China's behaviour as it pertains to foreign investment. For example, a study examining BRI projects in Sri Lanka and Kenya found that China has made unequal gains from its projects relative to its trade partners and has deprived local communities in project host countries of job opportunities by hiring Chinese companies and workers instead of local ones (Glysing, 2022, p. 18). Another aspect of possible neocolonial practices is the appropriation of land, which studies have claimed about the BRI, with its tendency to lease ports and other buildings it has constructed in other countries as an insurance policy in case the recipient countries cannot repay their loans (Glysing, p. 19, 22). Studies looking at the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), one of the flagship projects of the BRI (Sharif & Mansoor, 2025 p.462), have on the other hand argued that the BRI does not constitute a colonial project (Ibid., p. 464). Similarly, a study conducted on China’s investments in Egypt, parts of which were made under the BRI umbrella, did not find any tangible support for the claim of neocolonial practices by China, instead framing it as a relationship characterized by interdependence between the two nations (El Shafei & Metawe, 2022). However, others employ a more critical frame, citing how China potentially gets control over geographical territories when the host countries of BRI projects can’t pay back on their loans and how China uses this financial leverage for their geopolitical ambitions, which include aligning the host countries with Chinese policy and suppressing anti-China sentiments (Oberhauser, 2024). In sum, when it comes to the neocolonial frame that has been used against China and the BRI in the media, the scientific evidence seems more inconclusive, with some studies finding indicators of neocolonial and imperialist behaviour on the part of China. In contrast, others frame the relationship between China and its BRI partners as being more complex and interdependent, even if there are some imbalances present. 8 2.1.2 BRI & Geopolitical Implications Another aspect of the BRI that is among the more extensively studied is its geopolitical effects, which partly ties in with the discussion of the possible neocolonial and imperial ambitions of China. Studies tend to focus on the potential security concerns that the expansion of the BRI and thus China’s sphere of influence may entail, with the argument that China’s deepened integration and cooperation with developing nations may lead to the recipient countries of Chinese loans to align themselves with China more in foreign policy (Dutta, 2021). Furthermore, studies on this aspect of the BRI tend to highlight differences in framing between Chinese sources and major Western countries. While various Chinese actors choose to highlight the mutual benefits of the BRI and portray it as a simple economic and social programme, the Western powers instead portray the BRI as a cynical geostrategic attempt by the Chinese to expand their regional power and as a significant threat to the ruling Western order (Li, 2020). Comparisons of the framing by official sources and media sources in China and Western and Western-aligned nations found that official voices in China portrayed the BRI in an overwhelmingly positive light. In contrast, the official messaging from the foreign governments was significantly more critical, especially in the US and India, while the remaining countries were more cautious than outright critical (Yang & Van Gorp, 2023). The foreign media also framed the BRI in an overwhelmingly negative light, characterizing China as a cynical exploiter (Ibid.). However, another study found that media framing in the US and India is not purely negative, even if some of it is (Niu & Relly, 2021), bringing some nuance to the debate. Some academics argue that while the BRI is a tool for China to sustain its economic growth, it is not an overt attempt to overthrow the US-led global order or to expand its sphere of influence (Manzoor et al., 2022). Other studies have put their focus on the geopolitical implications of the BRI on specific cases, such as the Middle East, where a study argued that the expansion of the BRI in the Middle East could have severe geopolitical implications, such as Iran gaining significant power in the region due to its already existing ties to China, which could be perceived as a threat to the other countries in the Middle East. Furthermore, BRI investments in the Middle East were framed as potentially giving China greater influence over the region’s key energy sources and trade routes, such as the Suez Canal (Kamel, 2018). Other studies have found that China’s expansion in projects such as the CPEC and the series of ports in the Indian Ocean, called the “String of Pearls” (Mallick, 2024 p. 7), has led to unease among nations such as India and the western powers, while most other nations in the region see the BRI investments they receive in a more favourable light (Mallick, 2024). A study on the framing of China-Pakistan relations found that Pakistani media was overwhelmingly positive in its framing of China and the relations between the two countries (Ittefaq et al., 2023). 9 Zhang’s study on a Laotian BRI project found that western media outlets did not portray the BRI in a positive light, whereas media outlets from ASEAN member countries produced a more nuanced and diverse narrative regarding the project (Zhang 2024). While different studies have ended up on either side of this debate, other studies have found a middle ground and made the point that the BRI can be an economic development programme which encourages cooperation and mutual benefits, but still has geopolitical effects, whether they be intentional or not (Flint & Zhu, 2019). In sum, some of the existing academic literature on the potential geopolitical implications of the BRI seems to be quite suspicious of the investment programme, framing it as a potential threat to the current global order while also challenging the narrative that portrays the BRI as a purely socioeconomic venture that seeks to bring better interconnectivity and cooperation to the regions of the world. These critical voices, however, seem to stem mainly from China’s geopolitical rivals rather than from the media of recipient countries. Some more moderate voices show greater support for the idea that the BRI has no serious geopolitical ambitions. 2.1.3 BRI & The Economy Much of the focus on the BRI has been on its economic implications, which isn’t surprising, given that it is an initiative for trade and development. Studies showed that previous trade relations, pre-BRI, between China and the countries in question seemed to be more important than the impact of the BRI itself, suggesting that the BRI may be a product of these previous economic connections rather than a cause of it and thus may not be the driver of progress and growth as it has been portrayed by Chinese media (Wong & Downes, 2024). Fan (2023), however, found that the BRI leads to increased trade between China and its partner countries and that this trade leads to increased economic development in said partner countries. Other studies framed BRI investments as having increased economic complexity in the host countries of the projects, thereby enhancing production and sustainable growth in these countries, highlighting the positive economic and environmental impact of the BRI (Yeung & Huber, 2024). Brautigam (2020) challenged the media narrative that the BRI is an example of debt-trap diplomacy, which implies that China deliberately tries to ensnare its trade partners in a loan scheme with unpayable debts to gain political or strategic concessions (Brautigam, 2020). Brautigam found no evidence suggesting that China gains significant strategic assets from its BRI partner countries (Ibid). Wang et al (2023) examined Chinese OFDI between 2009 and 2020 and similarly found no relation between the BRI and increases in unpayable debt in partner countries, thus challenging the debt trap narrative (Wang et al, 2023). 10 Studying the perspectives of recipient countries of development is vital due to their voices being ignored historically, with more focus being put on the dominating Western perspectives surrounding development, thereby rendering Third World actors passive in the global discourse. While we do have a sense of which frames are being used about the BRI in general, less is known about what the recipient countries themselves actually say about the project. It is important to shed light on these domestic voices, as they can also have a significant impact on how these projects are perceived both domestically and potentially internationally, as well as have an impact on the future of Chinese foreign policy. 2.2 Theoretical framework 2.2.1 Framing Frames have been defined in a number of ways. Reese described frames as “[...]organizing principles that are socially shared and persistent over time, that work symbolically to meaningfully structure the social world” (Reese, 2001, p. 11). Frames are inherently socially constructed and can thus vary widely depending on geography, history and culture, among other factors, which can lead to different outcomes of the same phenomenon or event in different contexts (Zerubavel, 2024 p.530). Frames can thus be used unintentionally by actors due to these background factors. However, most of the time, actors use certain frames strategically and intentionally to package information in a way that is most relevant and convincing for their audience (Esaiasson et al., 2017 p.218). This notion is relevant when studying news media, as journalists choose which aspects of a news piece to accentuate and which to omit from their content in order to shape the interpretation of the audience (Entman, 1993 p. 55). Since frames are inherently socially constructed in quite specific and local contexts, it is expected that there will be some variation in the prevalence of certain frames between different recipient countries and different time periods, and perhaps also between news outlets within those countries, reflecting potential social and political differences that exist both between and within countries. Entman defined framing by saying that “to frame is to select some aspects of a perceived reality and make them more salient in a communicating text, in such a way as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and/or treatment recommendation” (Entman, 1993 p.52). This definition creates an expectation that the BRI is framed systematically around specific problems, which, based on previous literature on the BRI, could be development, resistance, debt etc. Entman described frames as having four core functions: Identifying problems, diagnosing causes, making moral judgement and suggesting a solution to it (Ibid). Identifying problems means to "determine what a causal agent is doing with what costs and benefits, usually measured in terms of common cultural values” (Ibid). Entman says that to diagnose causes is “to identify the forces creating the problem” (Ibid), while making moral judgements is to “evaluate causal agents and their effects” (Ibid). 11 Lastly, to suggest remedies is to “offer and justify treatments for the problems and predict their likely effects” (Entman, 1993 p.52). These four functions provide us with a set of questions we can ask of the empirical material to help us identify which frames are present in domestic news media in recipient countries. These questions relate to how the ‘issue’ is framed, which actors are involved with the ‘issue’, what the cause of the ‘issue’ is perceived to be and what choice of action is suggested by the author of the article, respectively (Esaiasson et al, 2017 p. 218-219). Framing can have a significant impact on how we perceive certain issues and how we choose to act on them (Entman, 1993. p.54). But it is important to note that frames are not only defined by what they choose to include, but also by what they choose to omit, as both the presence or absence of a certain aspect in communication will influence how we interpret the information (Ibid). As described above, framing plays a large role in political contexts, with politicians seeking re-election or specific policy outcomes using frames to garner support for their cause, often in competition with one another and with the news media (Ibid. p. 55). This aspect of frames is important, as it helps explain how meaning is constructed and reproduced in the context of political news media. Based on this reasoning, we can expect that newspapers that might be more government-aligned may choose to omit potential downsides of the major development initiatives and instead choose to frame them as a lucrative development partnership between countries. In contrast, newspapers that are more aligned with the political opposition may instead emphasize the potential risks of development investments. As this study aims to analyse which frames are present in domestic media in recipient countries of major development initiatives, the concept of competing frames is important to include, as it explains why certain frames are more prominent in the media. The strength of a frame relates to its resonance with the audience's shared values and its frequency (Chong & Druckman, 2007, p. 103-104). This aspect can help explain why certain patterns in media reporting of development initiatives are more prominent than others and builds the expectation that there will not be a random assortment of frames in the media, but instead a more limited set of frames that dominate the media discourse. This not only helps answer the question of which frames are present, but also gives us a base upon which we can start to try to explain why certain frames are present and others aren’t. 12 2.2.2 Postcolonialism Postcolonial thought is highly relevant to discussions of development and is often grounded in Said’s idea that the representation of the Third World (or the Orient) not only illustrates reality but also creates it through discourse (Said, 1979, p. 5-6). Said holds that the Third World is most often represented by other voices and actors than their own, and that this representation justifies domination by the West (Ibid.). Another essential part of Said’s postcolonial theory is the idea of imaginative geographies, which posits that the world is discursively divided into oppositional categories, such as ‘Occident vs. Orient’, ‘developed vs. underdeveloped’, ‘modern vs. backward’, etc. By doing this, certain regions are portrayed as threats, backward or inferior. In contrast, one's own region is often seen as civilized, modern and superior, thereby creating a hierarchy that justifies intervention by one’s own country (Ibid, p. 58-62). These imaginative geographies are used by all groups and countries, who construct their own identity by separating themselves from others through this categorization to pursue their interests (Ibid, p. 54). This is relevant to this study, as an industrialized power may construct a potential recipient country or region as ‘backward’ or as a battlefield for influence in competition with other major powers, in order to justify investment in development infrastructure in that region. Similarly, a recipient country may choose to construct their investor as a friend in order to justify the project in its country and resist outside interference. Said’s concept of constructing the Orient through discourse is relevant for this study, as discourses and representations of development are not neutral in any sense, they are shaped by colonial history and power. Positive framing of development led by an industrialized country in the Global South may thus reflect classic developmentalist thought, which holds development and modernization as necessary, whereas frames portraying that country as a neocolonial actor may reflect thoughts of foreign domination that were usually reserved only for the old empires. Additionally, postcolonial theory can help explain potential differences in framing between recipient countries, as these differences may reflect distinct colonial histories; however, that is not the primary aim of this study. An important part of postcolonial thought as it pertains to development discourse is that of an alternative to classical, Western development ideas and practices, preferably without the involvement of the former colonial powers. An example of this is South-South cooperation, which centers on countries in the Global South that often share a history of colonialism and exploitation and choose to cooperate on development. South-South discourse shies away from using terminology such as ‘donor-recipient’ and ‘foreign aid’, instead portraying the relationship as a mutually beneficial and equal partnership for both parties (Mawdsley, 2012 p. 159-160). Since this study focuses on cases of South-South development cooperation, this aspect is of importance, since it shapes an expectation that domestic media in recipient countries may choose to frame major developmental projects in more equal and favourable terms rather than the more classical Western terms, which carry more negative connotations, especially in the Global South. 13 Development itself has become a discourse, in which the Third World is characterized as underdeveloped, backward, and in need of Western aid and expertise, thus creating a narrative dichotomy between developed and underdeveloped countries (Escobar, 1995, p. 3-6). Development has been characterized as a continuation of colonial power dynamics through discourse and expertise, in which Western powers have maintained their dominance over their former subjects (Ibid). As this study focuses on South-South development, this aspect is of interest, as South-South relationships can potentially be framed in similar ways as classical Western development, with words of expertise of the investing country or a promise of prosperity being used in the media. Escobar introduced the concept of the “professionalization” (Escobar, 1995 p. 45) of development, which entrenches certain interpretations of concepts such as aid and poverty and frames development as something technical and apolitical (Ibid.). This professionalization removes political and social problems from the development discourse and also puts all the influential meaning-making in the hands of the “experts” (Ibid. p. 45-46). Furthermore, the dominant discourse surrounding development has normalized the inferiority and passivity of the Global South and the lack of agency of actors in recipient countries of development, with this inferiority often being internalized by the people in the Global South themselves (Ibid. p. 52-53). The postcolonial perspective leads us to expect that an industrialized, investing country may be presented as either a benevolent business partner or a neocolonial exploiter. Furthermore, it creates the expectation that the agency of local actors may be obscured as recipient countries continue to be portrayed as passive and inferior to the major developed powers. China’s status as both a member of the Global South and a major development investor thus creates an interesting juxtaposition in classic postcolonial discussions of power and discourse. The postcolonial perspective helps us identify possible explanations for why the domestic media frames the major development initiatives in a certain way by bridging the gap between media discourse today and the broader history of colonial power and representation. Another important aspect of postcolonial discourse is the agency of local actors. As previously mentioned, the First World typically portrays local Third World actors as passive and submissive; however, local actors also play an important and active role in shaping discourse, especially as it pertains to development and modernization, by redefining global projects in their own local contexts. Local actors do actively resist exploitative practices by imperial actors and try to provide local alternatives to the dominant development paradigm (Escobar, 1995 p. 15; 48-50; 95). This aspect of postcolonial discourse builds an expectation that there will be a corpus of domestic media articles that frame major development projects through a lens of resistance, highlighting the opposition and activism of local actors in recipient countries. 14 In sum, framing theory provides the analytical tools for identifying the frames through which news media construct meaning and highlight certain aspects of development initiatives. However, these meanings do not exist and are not produced in a vacuum; they are continuously influenced by contextual factors such as history, politics, geography, etc. Using a postcolonial lens allows this study to explore and understand how certain representations of development, cooperation and growth are reflective of existing and historical power relations. The postcolonial lens provides an interpretive tool to understand why certain frames are visible in recipient countries and what they imply about local discourses surrounding development, power and agency. The theoretical framework employed in this study expects that the frames identified in the empirical material will not be random but will instead form a systematic pattern that draws on postcolonial ideas of development, agency, and power. Postcolonial theory gives us certain expectations about which frames may be present in the empirical material. This study therefore utilises a set of predetermined frame categories, based on those theoretical expectations, that guide the coding process and provide structure and consistency for the identification and analysis of frames in the material. The first of these is the Development/Growth frame, which derives from classical development discourse, which posits that development projects facilitate economic growth, poverty reduction and modernization (Escobar, 1995 p. 74). The second frame is the Geopolitical frame, which derives from postcolonial discourse, in particular Said’s (1979) ideas of “imaginative geographies”, which is the idea that geographical regions and the peoples within them are discursively separated into categories (e.g. developer vs. recipient, secure vs. unstable). These dichotomies in turn justify the decisions of major powers to invest in Third World countries to strengthen their own influence over a geographical region in competition with other major powers and by extension their degree of control over those countries (Ibid). Similarly, recipient countries may construct investing powers as partners or friends in order to satisfy their interests. The third frame category is the Debt/Dependency frame, which is partly derived from postcolonial theory and the idea that developed countries invest in Third World countries to gain access to their natural resources and to exploit them for their own economic gain, and partly as the opposite side of the developmentalist coin (Escobar, 1995 p. 40). The fourth frame category is the Beneficial cooperation frame, which derives from South-South cooperation discourse, which posits development cooperation between countries as equal and mutually beneficial (Mawdsley, 2012 p. 159-160). The final frame category is the resistance frame, which derives from thoughts of postcolonial agency, where local actors are not passive; instead, they are actively reshaping development discourse in their own local context and providing resistance to potentially exploitative practices (Escobar, 1995, p. 15; 48-50; 95). 15 These frame categories are summarized in Table 1 under the Operationalizations section. The codebook used to collect the empirical material is also derived from these categories. Chapter 3: Methodology & Data 3.1 Research Design This study employs a qualitative comparative research design to analyze the framing of the BRI in domestic news media in recipient countries, with Kenya and Pakistan as the selected cases. The main aim of this study is to identify which frames are prominent in the domestic media. Given that framing is about meaning-making and interpretation, a qualitative research design seems the most suitable. Qualitative research designs allow for deeper analysis of how meaning is constructed and how that meaning reflects local political and historical contexts (Esaiasson et al, 2017 p. 211). This study utilises a comparative case study, in which the domestic media framing of the BRI in Kenya and Pakistan is analyzed. The comparative dimension enables us to explore how the same phenomenon, the BRI, is framed in two distinct postcolonial contexts and helps us identify potential shared patterns between the two countries, which could suggest common discursive logics among recipient countries of major developmental projects. Additionally, the comparative design also allows for differences in framing between the two countries to be highlighted, which may stem from their different national politics, histories, and each country’s relationship with China. 3.2 Case selection This study investigates the cases of Kenya and Pakistan. Both countries have a colonial past, largely at the hands of the United Kingdom (Black History Month Magazine, 2020; Burki, 2025), resulting in relatively recent independence for both (Ibid.). From a socio-political viewpoint, both countries have very diverse populations, with many different ethnic groups, often regionally divided (Ingham, 2025; Ziring, 2025). Both are also low-middle-income countries (Metreau et al, 2025). For Kenya, diplomatic relations with China began almost immediately after the former’s independence from British imperialism in 1963, with Kenya choosing to establish diplomatic relations with the PRC rather than Taiwan, showing its support for the PRC as the legitimate Chinese government (Mwangi, 2024). Furthermore, China has provided Kenya with developmental assistance since the 1970s and the trade between the two countries has continuously expanded , turning Kenya into a significant and strategically beneficial partner for China on the African continent. At the same time, Kenya has historically benefited greatly from China’s development assistance (Ibid.). In 2025, the two countries announced deepening of their ties with the aim to facilitate more stability in light of instability elsewhere in the world, with plans of further BRI projects also being announced (Master, 2025). 16 The flagship project of the BRI in Kenya is the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), an infrastructure project that links the vital port of Mombasa to the capital Nairobi and extends to trade hubs in the Great Lakes region to connect the countries located there to the sea. Construction of the first phase, the railway between Mombasa and Nairobi, started in 2014 and completed in 2017, with 90% of the financing coming through concessional loans given by the Export-Import Bank of China and the construction primarily being handled by Chinese contractors. The second phase, connecting Nairobi with the hinterland, broke ground in 2016 and followed a similar financing and construction pattern (Huang, 2022). In the case of Pakistan, the history with China is different. The two countries established diplomatic relations in the early 1950s after Pakistan’s independence from centuries of British colonial rule, with Pakistan being among the first countries to recognize the PRC as the legitimate ruler of the Chinese mainland. The two bordering countries have supported each other militarily over the years, with each country supporting the other in territorial disputes with India and internal security problems and have also established an expansive trade partnership, with the bond between the two countries often being referred to as the “Iron Brotherhood” (Rossi, 2025; Qingyan, 2021). The major BRI project in Pakistan is the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which was launched in 2015 and consists of multiple infrastructure projects with the goal of improving connectivity, trade and communication between the Eurasian countries by expanding ports, railways, roads and energy infrastructure along with establishing Special Economic Zones (SEZs) to promote further investment and trade (Rauf & Zeidan, 2025). These cases were chosen on a most different systems basis, which means that both cases differ on multiple points (Esaiasson et al, 2017 p.104), such as geography, politics, liberties, etc. Still, both are host to major BRI projects and have prominent relationships with China. Kenya is a presidential republic with a Christian majority population, while Pakistan is a Muslim majority country with a parliamentary democracy. A major difference between the countries is their geographical positions, with Kenya located far away from China on the African continent, while Pakistan borders China. This is sure to have a differentiated impact on the relationship between China and these two nations, with some issues having differing salience. For instance, the relationship between Kenya and China may be more ‘purely’ focused on economic trade and development, whereas the China-Pakistan relationship may have a more securitized tone due to their close proximity and the territorial disputes in the region. The point here is that this geographic factor may be reflected in how the media in each country frames projects related to the BRI. 17 Similarly, the shared yet distinct colonial legacies of the two countries are important to this study, as the selection of two postcolonial countries allows for an analysis of how major development projects are framed in related yet different historical and political environments. While both were British colonies, they looked very different in practice. Kenya was a settler colony marred by land dispossession, forced labour and racial segregation (Black History Month Magazine, 2020). Pakistan meanwhile, was part of the British Raj along with modern-day India and Bangladesh, where the muslim population that mostly constitutes Pakistan and Bangladesh today was rendered lowest in the local hierarchy, with the majority Hindu population being preferred by the British overlords when it came to political positions and influence (Burki, 2025). The two cases were also chosen on the basis of the considerable presence of English-language media sources in both countries, a result of English being an official language in both. Examining media frames of two countries with a shared language helps ensure greater comparability between the two countries as they then exist within the same language context, thus limiting potential loss of meaning as a result of translation. By using the same media language, the identification and analysis of the domestic media frames can be done more systematically and more effectively, since the same parameters can be applied to both cases seamlessly. Since the BRI is vast, with many different projects of varying sizes considered part of it, this study will focus on each country’s largest project: the SGR in Kenya and the CPEC in Pakistan. This is a Master's thesis in political science by Jonathan Höglund (Uppsala University, Fall 2025, supervised by Camilla Reuterswärd, ~16,781 words) examining how media in recipient countries of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) frame the major development initiative. The study employs a comparative frame analysis of domestic English-language media in Kenya and Pakistan, two major BRI partners, analyzing their reporting on the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) in Kenya and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) in Pakistan.

RESEARCH QUESTION: "How is the Belt and Road Initiative framed in recipient countries?"

THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: The study draws on framing theory (Entman's four core functions: identifying problems, diagnosing causes, making moral judgments, suggesting remedies) and postcolonial theory (Said's "imaginative geographies," Escobar's development discourse and "professionalization" of development, Mawdsley's South-South cooperation discourse). Five predetermined frame categories guide coding: (1) Development/Growth frame, (2) Geopolitical frame, (3) Debt/Dependency frame, (4) Beneficial cooperation frame, and (5) Resistance frame.

METHODOLOGY: Qualitative comparative case study design, selected on a "most different systems" basis. Both Kenya and Pakistan are postcolonial states (former British colonies), low-middle-income countries, with diverse populations, and English as an official language. Kenya established diplomatic relations with China in 1963 after independence; Pakistan recognized the PRC in the early 1950s and has an "Iron Brotherhood" relationship with China. The SGR (first phase Mombasa-Nairobi completed 2017, 90% financed by concessional loans from Export-Import Bank of China) and CPEC (launched 2015) are the flagship projects analyzed.

KEY FINDINGS: The study's main finding is that the BRI is predominantly framed from a developmentalist perspective, prioritizing modernization, growth, and progress in recipient countries. This challenges previous studies that primarily found the BRI framed in geopolitical terms. A second conclusion is that China is barely mentioned in the media reporting in recipient countries, which deviates from existing literature.

LITERATURE REVIEW CONTEXT: The thesis reviews three bodies of literature on the BRI: (1) BRI as a neocolonial venture (evidence is inconclusive, with some studies finding unequal gains, land appropriation, and loan-based leverage, while others find interdependence rather than colonialism), (2) BRI geopolitical implications (mostly Western critics frame it as a threat to the global order, while recipient country media is more positive), and (3) BRI economic implications (mixed evidence on trade and debt-trap claims, with Brautigam and Wang et al. challenging the debt-trap narrative).

SIGNIFICANCE: The study contributes to academia by highlighting insights from the Global South, demonstrating that recipient countries play an active role in constructing development narratives, using publicly available media documents rather than elite interviews (enhancing replicability), and bridging media studies, political science, and development studies.

args.summary:
This webpage contains the transcript and description of a SOAS World Philosophies Lecture delivered on October 29, 2021, by Boaventura de Sousa Santos, Emeritus Professor of Sociology at the University of Coimbra. The lecture, titled "The Epistemologies of the South and the Task of Decolonising the University," was posted on November 17, 2021, and has approximately 1,951 views.

KEY ARGUMENTS AND STRUCTURE:

1. **Decolonizing History**: Santos argues that decolonizing the university requires decolonizing history. He distinguishes between "inaugural generations" (who see the past as open, unaccomplished, and a mission) and "after generations" (who see the past as closed, accomplished, and a trophy). For the past 40 years, "after generations" have been promoted, reinforced by the fall of the Berlin Wall and the "end of history" narrative. Santos proposes a "wager" on inaugural generations, arguing that the pandemic (which he sees as marking the true beginning of the 21st century) signals both an ending and a new beginning.

2. **Three Epistemological Paradigms**: Santos identifies three paradigms of knowledge:
   - The Hegelian paradigm: knowledge after the struggle (the owl of Minerva flies at dusk), which dominates universities and means only the knowledge of winners survives.
   - The Marxist paradigm: knowledge before the struggle, which had accomplishments but also frustrations.
   - A third paradigm Santos proposes: knowledge born in struggle (a "thesis 12" extending Marx's thesis 11). This validates the knowledges of the oppressed, which combine counter-hegemonic uses of dominant knowledge with non-Western and non-dominant knowledges.

3. **The Abyssal Line**: Santos argues modern societies are divided by an invisible "abyssal line" separating "fully human beings" from "subhuman beings" — racialized and sexualized bodies degraded as ontologies. He notes that the first three US presidents (Jefferson, Washington, Madison) were both defenders of freedom and slave owners "without contradiction" because slaves were considered subhumans. This line persists today, as evidenced by the 20,000 deaths in the Mediterranean being treated as less significant because the victims were African or Bangladeshi.

4. **Epistemologies of the South**: Named by Santos in 2009 (though he says it names something "ancestral"), this framework includes:
   - Sociology of absences: identifying what is made inexistent.
   - Sociology of emergences: counter-hegemonic uses, ruin seas, and liberated zones.
   - Ecology of knowledges and intercultural translation.
   - Resistance to five "monocultures": knowledge, dominant scale, classification, linear time, and capitalist productivity.

5. **The University**: Santos traces colonial universities (30 Spanish universities in Latin America from the 16th century, 21 British universities in India, others in Africa) and identifies three phases of resistance: the 1918 Cordoba, Argentina student movement; the second phase of affirmative action and ethnic studies in the US; and the current third phase focused on changing curriculum, which requires changing epistemologies. He argues universities must move from monocultures to ecologies (including teaching popular, feminist, peasant, and cooperative economies alongside capitalist economics) and develop "post-abyssal science, law, and state."

6. **Challenges**: Santos warns that we are currently in a period of "recolonizing the university" rather than strong decolonization, citing capitalist pressure for online, commodified education ("knowledge with a price tag"), rankings, impact factors, and humanities departments closing. He identifies three post-pandemic scenarios: negationism (governments denying the pandemic's importance), Gattopardismo (changing things so nothing changes essentially), and a civilizational alternative. He also notes the fragmentation of resistance — anti-capitalist movements being racist, feminist movements being pro-capitalist, etc.

7. **Knowledge in the Plural**: In the Q&A, Santos explains why he insists on "knowledges" in the plural — the concept of unified science has been a metonymic reduction equating science with all knowledge. He advocates recognizing different knowledges for different purposes (science for going to the moon, indigenous knowledge for understanding Amazonian biodiversity). He cites examples of ecology of medical knowledges (indigenous communities using traditional medicine to improve immunity during the pandemic) and legal knowledges (legal pluralism). He references Amilcar Cabral's view that not all colonial knowledge should be discarded, and Spinoza versus Descartes on nature.

8. **Reciprocity**: Santos proposes that for every student from former colonies trained in European universities to study their own countries, there should be a student from those countries studying European societies, as they would better identify the abyssal lines Europeans often cannot see.

# 怎样认识全球南方

 来源：《求是》2025/16   作者：当代世界研究中心   2025-08-16 09:00:00 

**怎样认识全球南方**

当代世界研究中心

  当前，全球南方在国际舞台上日益活跃，正成为一股重塑世界秩序的关键力量。习近平总书记指出：“‘全球南方’群体性崛起，是世界大变局的鲜明标志。”我们应怎样认识全球南方？全球南方国家有什么共同属性和鲜明特征？怎样推动全球南方在促进人类进步方面发挥更重要作用？

**一**

  全球南方的概念来源于“南方”国家。现有研究认为，1926年意大利马克思主义理论家葛兰西正式提出了“南方”概念。他当时关注到意大利南北发展差距问题，并初步说明“南方”概念所蕴含的反剥削、求发展等特性。一般来说，全球南方被认为是新兴市场国家和发展中国家的集合体。它包括亚洲、非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、大洋洲地区的大部分国家，这些国家大多地处北半球南部和南半球，具有相似的历史遭遇、共同的发展任务、相近的国际事务立场。

  全球南方的崛起历经数十年的积淀。二战后，西方殖民体系逐步瓦解，在亚非拉等原殖民地建立起一大批实现了民族独立的主权国家。这些国家在民族解放、反殖反霸等方面具有共同诉求，逐渐联合成一股重要的国际力量。1955年，万隆会议在印度尼西亚召开，标志着亚非新兴民族独立国家作为一个集体正式走入世界政治的舞台，向世界展现了其推动建立公正合理国际秩序的智慧、信念与行动。1961年，不结盟运动正式形成。该运动的成立，反映了广大南方国家主张国际关系民主化的强烈诉求，推动了这些国家捍卫国家主权、反对霸权主义、振兴民族经济的历史进程。1964年，77国集团成立并提出关于国际经济关系、贸易与发展的一整套主张，旨在推动南南合作，建立国际经济新秩序。20世纪70年代，中国提出“三个世界”划分的理论，进一步推动发展中国家身份认同，鼓励发展中国家独立自主，在国际事务中形成联合阵线。

  20世纪八九十年代以来，随着世界多极化和经济全球化深入发展，一大批新兴市场国家和发展中国家经过艰苦卓绝的奋斗和广泛合作，走上发展的快车道。数据统计，新兴市场国家和发展中国家过去20年对世界经济增长的贡献率高达80%，过去40年国内生产总值的全球占比从24%增至40%以上。全球南方群体性崛起，深刻改写国际政治格局和世界经济版图。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

  近年来，全球南方更加积极主动捍卫自身权益、推动全球治理变革。在慕尼黑安全会议上，呼吁坚持多边主义、加强集体行动；在南方首脑会议上，要求改变不公正的国际秩序，摆脱几个世纪以来被西方推入的“绝对不利境地”；在不结盟运动第十九次峰会上，强调要全面尊重国际法和国际共识原则……全球南方展现出的态度更加自信，国际地位和影响力显著提升，为世界多极化、经济全球化和国际关系民主化注入强大动能。

**二**

  全球南方国家在国际舞台上彼此支持、携手同行，是因为有着相似的历史记忆和奋斗历程，对当前国际秩序和全球治理有着相近的看法和诉求。在变乱交织的国际形势下，全球南方反霸权、谋发展、求正义的共性和特征更加凸显。

**独立自主是全球南方的政治底色。**全球南方国家大多有过被侵略、被殖民、被掠夺的苦难经历，深知和平的宝贵，珍视自身的独立地位。当前，强权政治、霸权行径扰乱世界安宁，已成为国际和平面临的最大破坏性因素。全球南方对此始终保持高度警惕，日益重视战略自主，坚决反对一切形式的霸权主义和强权政治，反对冷战思维和阵营对抗，反对干涉别国内政，强调“生存权”、“发展权”，明确拒绝选边站队，为维护世界和平稳定发挥着重要作用。近年来，拉美和加勒比国家呼吁反对外来干涉，非洲一些国家提出“第二次独立”等政治主张。在乌克兰危机、巴以冲突等问题上，全球南方国家大多摆脱西方影响，坚持基于历史经纬和事情本身是非曲直确立本国立场，主张劝和促谈、停火止战。2024年9月，17个全球南方国家在联合国成立乌克兰危机“和平之友”小组，寻求妥善解决危机方案，发出客观、理性的声音，得到国际社会广泛认同和赞赏。

<summary>
This essay by Steven Schmidt (January 21, 2018, Global South Studies) traces the intellectual history of Latin American Dependency Theory, a political-economic school of thought that emerged from the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) shortly after World War II. Key scholars include Raúl Prebisch, Fernando Cardoso, Enrique Faletto, and Andre Gunder Frank, with later influence on world-systems analysis by Immanuel Wallerstein, Giovanni Arrighi, and Christopher Chase-Dunn.

Dependency theory argues that under-development in Latin America is the direct result of capital intervention and global economic forces, not a "lack" of development. It emerged as a response to modernization theory (associated with economist William Rostow's five stages of economic growth), which dependency theorists rejected as a false dichotomy between "traditional" and "modern" societies.

Central to the theory is the Prebisch-Singer thesis, developed by Prebisch (former Argentine chief trade diplomat) and UN economist Hans Singer, which demonstrated through trade data that an imbalance in terms of trade caused a constant flow of capital out of Latin America—as the region exported primary goods (food, lumber, minerals) while re-importing higher-value manufactured products from the Global North, creating a perpetual trade deficit.

The theory split into two camps: (1) liberal reformers like Prebisch, Cardoso, and Faletto, who advocated for import-substitution industrialization (ISI) and protectionist policies to develop domestic markets; and (2) neo-Marxists like Gunder Frank, who argued dependency could only be escaped through socialism and challenging the capitalist mode of production. A further offshoot was world-systems analysis (Wallerstein, Amin, Frank).

During the 1940s-1950s, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile adopted ISI policies, but debt crises in the 1980s led the World Bank and IMF to impose structural adjustment programs (SAPs), which dismantled these protections. While dependency theory is no longer widely applied as policy, its core insights remain valuable: understanding how global capital flows structure development disparities, challenging assumptions that Latin American economies are "feudal and backwards," that modernity equals industrialization, and that all nations can equally pass through development "stages." The theory laid groundwork for research on the international division of labor, commodity chains, and global cities (Sassen 1991).
</summary>

This is a Wikipedia article on Dependency theory, an international relations theory within the broader frameworks of imperialism studies and Marxist international relations theory. 

**Core concept:** Dependency theory posits that resources flow from a "periphery" of poor, exploited states to a "core" of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. The central contention is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by how poor states are integrated into the "world system." The theory was formally developed in the late 1940s following World War II as scholars sought to explain the lack of development in Latin America.

**Origins and History:** The theory arose as a reaction to modernization theory, which held that all societies progress through similar development stages. Dependency theory rejected this, arguing underdeveloped countries are not primitive versions of developed ones but have unique structures and are weaker members of the world market economy. The theory originated with two 1949 papers by Hans Singer and Raúl Prebisch, who observed deteriorating terms of trade for underdeveloped countries (the Prebisch–Singer thesis). Prebisch, an Argentine economist at the UN Commission for Latin America, advocated import-substitution industrialization (ISI) over export orientation. Paul A. Baran developed it from a Marxian perspective in 1957 with *The Political Economy of Growth*. Two main streams emerged: Latin American Structuralist (Prebisch, Celso Furtado, Aníbal Pinto) and American Marxist (Baran, Paul Sweezy, Andre Gunder Frank). The theory was popular in the 1960s-1970s as criticism of modernization theory. Walter Rodney's 1972 book *How Europe Underdeveloped Africa* applied it to Africa. Ruy Mauro Marini developed a specifically Marxist dependency theory focused on super-exploitation and unequal exchange. Fernando Henrique Cardoso (later Brazilian President 1995-2002) wrote extensively on dependency theory, developing the concept of "dependent development."

**Basic premises:** (1) Poor nations provide natural resources, cheap labor, destinations for obsolete technology, and markets for developed nations, without which the latter couldn't enjoy their standard of living; (2) Wealthy nations actively perpetuate dependence through economics, media control, politics, banking, finance, education, culture, and sport.

**Key concepts:** Baran placed surplus extraction and capital accumulation at the center of analysis, arguing that surplus in poor countries goes to luxury consumption rather than development investment. Latin American Structuralists argued for "dependent development" - partial development still controlled by outside decision-makers. Some argue the sine qua non of dependency is not technological difference but financial strength - particularly the inability of peripheral countries to borrow in their own currency, and US control of the international reserve currency (the dollar). Theotonio dos Santos described a "new dependency" based on Marxian analysis. The theory influenced world-systems theory developed by Immanuel Wallerstein, which added a third category of "semi-periphery" countries.

**Examples:** European colonization (1650-1900) of the Americas, Africa, and Asia, where wealth was transferred from colonized regions to Europe through control of materials, production, and distribution.

**Criticism:** India's economic improvement after moving to open trade is cited as evidence against the theory (though Indian economists Utsa and Prabhat Patnaik argue this may reflect a globalized reserve workforce). Import-substitution economies in Africa like Zimbabwe have performed poorly while trade-based economies like Egypt, South Africa, and Tunisia have succeeded. Economic historian Robert C. Allen argues dependency theory's claims are "debatable" because protectionism in Latin America failed, leading to excessive debt and recession, partly because national markets were too small to efficiently produce complex industrial goods.

**Other details:** The article also covers aid dependency, including instilling aid dependency, stunted economic growth, political dependency, corruption, and efforts to end aid dependency. Dependency theorists divide into liberal reformists (advocating targeted policy interventions) and neo-Marxists (proposing planned economies). The theory has lost influence with the growth of India and East Asian economies but still influences NGO campaigns like Make Poverty History and the fair trade movement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Dependency theory is the idea that resources flow from a 'periphery' of poor and exploited states to a 'core' of wealthy states, enriching the latter at the expense of the former. A central contention of dependency theory is that poor states are impoverished and rich ones enriched by the way poor states are integrated into the 'world system.'"
</key_excerpts>
